For Massey, his strategy/tactic distinction maps space onto power and time onto resistance — a binary that traps both terms and fails to think space as eventful.
commons/entities/michel-de-certeau.md.title: Michel de Certeau (1925–1986)

commons/entities/michel-de-montaigne.md.summary: Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592), French Renaissance writer who invented the personal essay form and modeled a philosophy of frank self-examination and epistemic humility.
commons/entities/michel-de-montaigne.md.title: Michel de Montaigne

commons/entities/michel-foucault.md.summary: French philosopher (1926–1984) whose analytics of power/knowledge, genealogy of disciplinary institutions, and concept of biopolitics have been foundational for critical theory; Bryant's gravity framework extends and partially critiques Foucault by adding the non-discursive, material-infrastructural dimension of power.
commons/entities/michel-foucault.md.title: Michel Foucault (1926–1984)

commons/entities/michel-serres.md.summary: French philosopher of science and communication (1930–2019) whose accounts of vortexes, noise, and topological time — especially the 'crumpled handkerchief' — are central to Bryant's spatial and temporal topology.
commons/entities/michel-serres.md.title: Michel Serres

commons/entities/miguel-de-cervantes.md.summary: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547-1616) - descendant of real Castilian knights-errant, wounded at Lepanto, five years a captive in Algiers, failed dramatist and tax collector, who gathered Don Quixote incidentally, treated it as a stepchild, and finished it only when a forged sequel forced him to kill his hero.
commons/entities/miguel-de-cervantes.md.title: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547–1616)

commons/entities/ming-dynasty-grand-secr.summary: Officials in the Ming dynasty who officially 'merely recorded imperial decisions' while wielding enormous de facto governing power — a paradigm case of antimemetic bureaucratic authority.
commons/entities/ming-dynasty-grand-secr.title: Ming Dynasty Grand Secretaries

commons/entities/mircea-eliade.md.summary: Romanian historian of religion whose concept of sacred consecration — the ritual act that incorporates new territory into a divine cosmos, erasing its prior existence — provides the religious-historical dimension of place-making through language and ceremony.
commons/entities/mircea-eliade.md.title: Mircea Eliade

commons/entities/modernity-machine-chaff.summary: David Chaffetz's Raiders, Rulers, and Traders argues that two of the Modernity Machine's ~1600 moving parts, the final eclipse of steppe military power and the Silk Road's obsolescence, are dated one to three centuries too early; this page records the friction and three ways to read it.
commons/entities/modernity-machine-chaff.term: Dating the Steppe's Eclipse: A Chaffetz Check on the Modernity Machine
commons/entities/modernity-machine-chaff.title: Dating the Steppe's Eclipse: A Chaffetz Check on the Modernity Machine

commons/entities/mughal-administration.m.summary: The administrative apparatus of the Mughal Empire, notable for its matrix reporting structure where provincial officials reported directly to the central government rather than to the provincial governor — a designed mechanism for central control and diffused accountability.
commons/entities/mughal-administration.m.title: Mughal Administration

commons/entities/naturgemalde.md.summary: Humboldt's 'painting of nature' — the Chimborazo cross-section that composed botany, climate, and geology on one sheet, and the method it became: a device for holding many domains together without reducing them to a common unit.
commons/entities/naturgemalde.md.title: Naturgemälde

commons/entities/necropolitics-carey.md.summary: John Carey's The Intellectuals and the Masses (1992) read as a prehistory of necropolitics: the documented, attributed discursive preparation (Augustine's massa damnata, the 'not fully alive' mass, the bacterial crowd metaphor, Wells's register) that made eliminating the 'mass' thinkable before any state acted on it.
commons/entities/necropolitics-carey.md.title: Necropolitics: Carey's Literary Prehistory

commons/entities/niccolo-machiavelli.md.summary: Florentine political thinker (1469–1527); in this wiki he appears primarily not as political theorist but as exemplar of the studiolo practice — nightly ritual of intellectual communion with ancient authors.
commons/entities/niccolo-machiavelli.md.title: Niccolò Machiavelli

commons/entities/nick-cave.md.summary: Australian musician and writer whose open letter arguing that AI creativity is soulless became an unexpected entry point for Sathe's argument about taste as an irreducibly experience-dependent faculty.
commons/entities/nick-cave.md.title: Nick Cave

commons/entities/nicolas-de-condorcet.md.summary: Marquis de Condorcet (1743–1794), Turgot's disciple and the philosophe who secularized the theory of progress into a would-be predictive science of history — a project 'to tame the future' that runs from probabilistic historical law through a self-governing republic of science to a state run by social mathematics, and ends with Progress installed as a substitute god.
commons/entities/nicolas-de-condorcet.md.title: Nicolas de Condorcet

commons/entities/niklas-luhmann.md.summary: German sociologist (1927–1998) whose systems theory treats society as composed solely of communications, autopoietically reproducing itself through recursive operations — a position Bryant's onto-cartography explicitly criticizes for neglecting material mediators.
commons/entities/niklas-luhmann.md.title: Niklas Luhmann

commons/entities/paul-carter.md.summary: Australian cultural historian whose The Road to Botany Bay (1988) argued that European exploration of Australia was constituted by the act of naming — that place emerged through spatial history, not through material transformation.
commons/entities/paul-carter.md.title: Paul Carter

commons/entities/paul-feyerabend.md.summary: Austrian philosopher of science known for epistemological anarchism — the claim that no single scientific method is universal and that 'anything goes' in productive inquiry — invoked as the epistemological correlate of dancer-style curiosity.
commons/entities/paul-feyerabend.md.title: Paul Feyerabend (1924–1994)

commons/entities/paul-ricoeur.md.summary: French hermeneutic philosopher whose account of feeling as 'strange intentionality' — directed outward toward things while also inwardly manifesting — grounds Tuan's understanding of how place-attachment is both about the world and about the self.
commons/entities/paul-ricoeur.md.title: Paul Ricoeur (1913–2005)

commons/entities/perplexity-ai.md.summary: An AI-powered search and answer engine that attempts to restore citations to LLM-generated responses — cited by Sathe as the most credible attempt to address the citation problem in LLMs, though with skepticism about whether it solves the underlying trust issue.
commons/entities/perplexity-ai.md.title: Perplexity AI

commons/entities/prapanca.md.summary: The Majapahit court poet whose 1359 Nagarakertagama was mocked in its own time as dull and unheroic, survived by Balinese copying and a single grab from a burning treasury in 1894, and became the primary documentary foundation for the empire — written by a chronicler who also deliberately buried his dynasty's real origin story.
commons/entities/prapanca.md.title: Prapanca

commons/entities/primekg.md.summary: A multimodal precision medicine knowledge graph that integrates multiple domain-specific KGs to enable cross-domain clinical reasoning — cited as an example of the kind of shared knowledge infrastructure that could accelerate healthcare.
commons/entities/primekg.md.title: PrimeKG

commons/entities/quentin-meillassoux.md.summary: French philosopher associated with Speculative Realism; author of After Finitude (2008), which introduced the concept of correlationism and argued for the speculative necessity of contingency.
commons/entities/quentin-meillassoux.md.title: Quentin Meillassoux

commons/entities/rabindranath-tagore.md.summary: Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, educator, composer, and philosopher — who shaped Indian national identity and spirituality as an intellectual rather than a revolutionary organizer.
commons/entities/rabindranath-tagore.md.title: Rabindranath Tagore

commons/entities/raphael-hythloday.md.summary: Raphael Hythloday — the fictional Portuguese philosopher-traveller of Utopia, who refuses to counsel princes in Book 1, diagnoses the evils of enclosure-era England at Cardinal Morton's table, and narrates the whole eyewitness account of the island in Book 2.
commons/entities/raphael-hythloday.md.title: Raphael Hythloday

commons/entities/richard-mcelreath.md.summary: Evolutionary anthropologist and statistician at the Max Planck Institute, author of 'Statistical Rethinking' — a Bayesian methods textbook that grounds causal inference in scientific epistemology and argues for honesty about model assumptions.
commons/entities/richard-mcelreath.md.title: Richard McElreath

commons/entities/richard-stallman.md.summary: Richard Stallman (b. 1953), founder of the Free Software Foundation and GNU Project, whose definition of hacking as 'playfully doing something difficult' anchors the Hack Hacky Hacker typology.
commons/entities/richard-stallman.md.title: Richard Stallman

commons/entities/robert-peake.md.summary: Robert Peake, contemporary poet and participant in the Summer of Protocols, who applied the infinite game framework to poetry and creative practice.
commons/entities/robert-peake.md.title: Robert Peake

commons/entities/robert-putnam.md.summary: Robert Putnam (b. 1941) is an American political scientist best known for Bowling Alone (2000), which documented the decline of social capital and civic engagement in America over the second half of the 20th century.
commons/entities/robert-putnam.md.title: Robert Putnam

commons/entities/ron-wakkary.md.summary: Canadian design researcher (b. 1960s) whose concept of 'more-than-human design' argues that designed things exceed their designers' intentions and must be understood as participants in ongoing relationships rather than completed objects.
commons/entities/ron-wakkary.md.title: Ron Wakkary

commons/entities/sancho-panza.md.summary: Don Quixote's squire - an afterthought in the novel's design who becomes its second centre: a rival epistemology of hunger, wages and proverbs, the author of Dulcinea's enchantment, an unexpectedly able governor of a fictional island, and the one who renounces office to keep a life he can actually operate.
commons/entities/sancho-panza.md.title: Sancho Panza

commons/entities/scottish-enlightenment..summary: The mid-eighteenth-century flowering of Scottish intellectual life — Hume, Smith, Robertson, Blair, Ferguson — which Rasmussen attributes not to any great man but to a convergence of parish schools, reformed universities, clubs, publishing, the 1707 union, and reforming Moderate clergy.
commons/entities/scottish-enlightenment..title: Scottish Enlightenment

commons/entities/simon-bolivar.md.summary: Liberator of northern South America (1783-1830), whose revolution Wulf presents as fought with Humboldt's statistics and Humboldt's imagery as much as with guns — and whose aftermath supplied Humboldt his sharpest disillusionment.
commons/entities/simon-bolivar.md.title: Simón Bolívar

commons/entities/simon-willison.md.summary: British developer and writer; creator of Datasette; prominent practitioner and theorist of ethical link blogging as a form of intellectual curation.
commons/entities/simon-willison.md.title: Simon Willison

commons/entities/skyhooks-and-cranes.md.summary: Dennett's organizing pair — a skyhook is a mind-first miracle that lifts without support, a crane is an evolved, itself-explicable subprocess that locally speeds up the accumulation of design — used across the book as a diagnostic for two centuries of resistance to Darwinism.
commons/entities/skyhooks-and-cranes.md.title: Skyhooks and Cranes

commons/entities/stacy-alaimo.md.summary: American feminist environmental humanities scholar who developed the concept of 'trans-corporeality' — the inseparability of human bodies from their more-than-human material environment — cited by Bryant as a key concept for inter-machine material entanglement.
commons/entities/stacy-alaimo.md.title: Stacy Alaimo

commons/entities/stato-da-mar.md.summary: The Venetian seaborne empire (1204–1797): not a territorial state but a network of ports, chokepoints, forts, and timetabled convoys, administered from the lagoon by an audit apparatus of extraordinary reach and lost by two and a half centuries of attrition rather than a single collapse.
commons/entities/stato-da-mar.md.title: Stato da Mar

commons/entities/stephen-fry.md.summary: English actor, writer, and public intellectual; in this corpus, notable as the narrator of Nick Cave's AI letter — and as a figure whose own public skepticism about AI dovetails with Cave's position.
commons/entities/stephen-fry.md.title: Stephen Fry

commons/entities/sun-wukong.md.summary: The stone-born Monkey King of Journey to the West, a figure of near-pure capture-resistance whose every containment by Heaven converts into either escape or instrumentalized service, until a golden headband he puts on willingly succeeds where mountains, braziers and armies had failed.
commons/entities/sun-wukong.md.title: Sun Wukong (Monkey King)

commons/entities/susanne-langer.md.summary: American philosopher of mind and symbolism whose account of experience as a construction — not a recording — of reality is the epistemological premise underlying Tuan's experiential perspective.
commons/entities/susanne-langer.md.title: Susanne Langer (1895–1985)

commons/entities/tarn-adams.md.summary: Creator of Dwarf Fortress — built the game over 20 years while completing a PhD and living on donations, representing an extreme case of sustained individual creative audacity.
commons/entities/tarn-adams.md.title: Tarn Adams

commons/entities/the-dynamo-and-the-virg.summary: Adams's paired figure for the two greatest forces he thought history had produced, and — more consequentially — his proposal to abandon causation and measure all historical force by the attraction it exerts on human minds, the only property dynamo and Virgin visibly share.
commons/entities/the-dynamo-and-the-virg.title: The Dynamo and the Virgin

commons/entities/the-eurasian-steppe.md.summary: The 3.1-million-square-mile grassland belt from Hungary to Manchuria, read by Chaffetz as an inland sea whose forage economy set the political ceiling for every empire on its shores until Qing China and Russia closed it in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
commons/entities/the-eurasian-steppe.md.title: The Eurasian Steppe

commons/entities/the-horse-road.md.summary: Chaffetz's name for the trans-Eurasian horse economy that the label 'Silk Road' obscures — caravans functioning as itinerant states, fairs that seeded pilgrimage sites, silk serving as currency rather than cargo, and the monopolies built to control it.
commons/entities/the-horse-road.md.title: The Horse Road

commons/entities/the-mass-as-fiction.md.summary: \"The mass\" as Carey analyzes it: not a sociological category but an invented rhetorical instrument with a theological ancestry in Augustine's massa damnata, a repertoire of interchangeable images (herd, bacillus, jelly, prole, peasant, slug), and a terminal use in eliminationist policy.
commons/entities/the-mass-as-fiction.md.title: "The Mass" as Fiction

commons/entities/the-scripture-pilgrimag.summary: The scripture mission of Journey to the West read as an institution: a chartered, document-bearing programme staffed entirely by condemned celestial exiles serving commuted sentences, disciplined by a pain-inflicting headband, and closed out by an audit of its own day-count and ordeal-count.
commons/entities/the-scripture-pilgrimag.title: The Scripture Pilgrimage

commons/entities/thomas-more.md.summary: Sir Thomas More (b. 1478) — Tudor humanist, lawyer, and royal servant; author of Utopia and, as the persona 'Mr. More', a character inside its dialogue who argues the case for engaged 'civil philosophy' against Hythloday's withdrawal.
commons/entities/thomas-more.md.title: Thomas More

commons/entities/thomas-nagel.md.summary: Philosopher at NYU, known for 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974) — an argument that subjective, first-person experience cannot be captured by objective physical description, used by Sathe as an exemplar of Socratic inquiry on an unsolvable question.
commons/entities/thomas-nagel.md.title: Thomas Nagel

commons/entities/thomas-paine.md.summary: English-American political pamphleteer whose writing provided key philosophical underpinnings for the American Revolution — exemplifying the intellectual role in the American independence typology.
commons/entities/thomas-paine.md.title: Thomas Paine

commons/entities/tim-ingold.md.summary: British social anthropologist whose relational vocabulary of correspondence, wayfaring, lines, and the education of attention offers a phenomenological counter-idiom to the World Machines legibility frame.
commons/entities/tim-ingold.md.title: Tim Ingold

commons/entities/timothy-morton.md.summary: British-American literary theorist and eco-philosopher; originator of 'dark ecology' and the concept of hyperobjects; argues that 'Nature' as a concept must be abandoned for genuinely ecological thought — Bryant engages Morton as a key interlocutor, agreeing on rejecting nature-as-outside while resisting the abandonment of the concept.
commons/entities/timothy-morton.md.title: Timothy Morton (b. 1968)

commons/entities/ulama.md.summary: Islamic legal and religious scholars who shaped law and public morality across pre-modern Islamic states through interpretive authority — an antimemetic power operating within the bureaucracy rather than above it.
commons/entities/ulama.md.title: Ulama

commons/entities/umberto-eco.md.summary: Italian semiotician, novelist, and intellectual historian — key figure in the history of language theory and the author of the observation that AI may be a revival of the perfect language dream.
commons/entities/umberto-eco.md.title: Umberto Eco

commons/entities/utopus.md.summary: Utopus — the conqueror-founder-legislator who, in Book 2, digs the island free of the continent, lays out its uniform civic plan while leaving its completion to successors, and establishes its founding law of religious toleration; a paradigmatic World Machines 'Dawn' founder.
commons/entities/utopus.md.title: Utopus

commons/entities/vaclav-smil.md.summary: Czech-Canadian environmental scientist (b. 1943) and energy historian whose quantitative accounts of civilisational metabolism — energy, food, materials — are the principal source for the historical energy data in 'The Lightening of Intent'.
commons/entities/vaclav-smil.md.title: Vaclav Smil

commons/entities/vaughn-tan.md.summary: Vaughn Tan — academic, consultant, and author focused on organizational uncertainty and innovation; creator of the Four Questions of Uncertainty framework used by Commoncog for AI sensemaking.
commons/entities/vaughn-tan.md.title: Vaughn Tan

commons/entities/venkatesh-rao.md.summary: Venkatesh Rao is the author of the Ribbonfarm and Contraptions newsletters, known for machinic, systems-oriented frameworks applied to history, technology, and culture; key concepts in this wiki include the Divergence Machine, Configurancy, and Liveness.
commons/entities/venkatesh-rao.md.title: Venkatesh Rao

commons/entities/virgil.md.summary: The Roman poet Virgil as Dante's guide through Hell and Purgatory — emblem of unaided human reason and the classical inheritance, an ordering intelligence whose competence has an explicit terminus and who unwittingly authored a prophecy legible only to later readers.
commons/entities/virgil.md.title: Virgil

commons/entities/virginia-tufte.md.summary: Virginia Tufte (1922–2020), linguist and professor, author of Artful Sentences — a 270-page analysis of sentence mechanics placed in the anti-library, awaiting the right reader.
commons/entities/virginia-tufte.md.title: Virginia Tufte

commons/entities/voltaire.md.summary: Voltaire (1694–1778) — French Enlightenment writer, playwright, and entrepreneur who transformed the intellectual's social role, pioneered celebrity, advanced political and epistemic legibility, and made early contributions to the Divergence Machine through Candide and tolerance campaigns.
commons/entities/voltaire.md.title: Voltaire

commons/entities/walter-wriston.md.summary: Citibank chairman (1919–2005) whose Hayekian conviction that information technology and mobile capital would dissolve state sovereignty made him, in Farrell and Newman's reading, the chief unwitting architect of the chokepoints that gave the United States more leverage over the world economy than it had ever had.
commons/entities/walter-wriston.md.title: Walter Wriston

commons/entities/weaponized-interdepende.summary: Farrell and Newman's term for the conversion of a state's inherited centrality in global economic networks — financial messaging, dollar clearing, fiber routing, chip design IP — into instruments of surveillance and exclusion, exercised through the commercial dependency of the private firms that operate those networks.
commons/entities/weaponized-interdepende.title: Weaponized Interdependence

commons/entities/werner-herzog.md.summary: Werner Herzog is a German filmmaker whose philosophical remarks about the jungle — 'the harmony of overwhelming and collective murder' — serve as Rao's touchstone for the authentic relationship between liveness and death that civilization suppresses and New Nature requires.
commons/entities/werner-herzog.md.title: Werner Herzog

commons/entities/william-baumol.md.summary: William Baumol (1922–2017) was an American economist best known for Baumol's cost disease — the observation that labor-intensive service sectors experience chronic relative price inflation as economy-wide productivity rises.
commons/entities/william-baumol.md.title: William Baumol

commons/entities/william-zinsser.md.summary: William Zinsser (1922–2015), American writer and writing teacher, author of On Writing Well and Writing to Learn — foundational texts in the series of essays on documentation, dictionaries, and prose craft.
commons/entities/william-zinsser.md.title: William Zinsser

commons/entities/zach-adams.md.summary: Co-creator of Dwarf Fortress alongside his brother Tarn Adams — handles the business, community, and operational side of Bay 12 Games.
commons/entities/zach-adams.md.title: Zach Adams

commons/glossary/legibility.md.summary: The condition of being readable by a system that has the power to act on what it reads — mapped, predicted, categorized, managed. In this project legibility is treated as the core optimization target of the Modernity Machine, and therefore as a precondition for scale rather than a neutral technique.
commons/glossary/legibility.md.title: Legibility

commons/glossary/psychohistory.md.summary: Asimov's fictional science of forecasting the statistical behaviour of civilizations, adopted here as the project's guiding conceit rather than its method — the thing we are building toward while remaining explicit that we cannot currently do it.
commons/glossary/psychohistory.md.title: Psychohistory

commons/glossary/world-machine.md.summary: A civilization-scale contraption — institutions, technologies, practices and assumptions interlocked — that embodies the logic of how the world works for a period of centuries, and that rises, operates and decays on a roughly thousand-year lifecycle.
commons/glossary/world-machine.md.title: World Machine

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Writing of himself in the third person as a specimen of education, Henry Adams describes his 1838 Boston birth into an eighteenth-century Puritan-Revolutionary inheritance, and the doubled childhood world of Quincy and Boston that shaped him until his grandfather John Quincy Adams's death in 1848 closed what he calls the "ancestral and Revolutionary" chapter of his life.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Quincy: The Ancestral Chapter (1838-1848)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Adams recounts his Boston boyhood (age ten to sixteen) inside his father Charles Francis Adams's Free Soil household, arguing that the political, religious, and educational certainties of self-satisfied 1850s Boston trained him for a world that industrial change was already dissolving.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Boston, 1848–1854: Trained for a World Already Closing
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Boston, 1848–1854: Trained for a World Already Closing

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Adams recounts his boyhood between Boston and Washington from 1850 to 1854 — blackguard violence and antislavery ferment at home, a slave-state journey that fixes George Washington as an unresolvable moral paradox at Mount Vernon, and an early taste of corrupt machine politics electing Charles Sumner — framing his entire eighteenth-century upbringing as already obsolete by the century's end.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Washington and the Boy's Political Education, 1850–1854
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Washington and the Boy's Political Education, 1850–1854

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Adams recounts four intellectually barren but socially formative years at Harvard College (1854-1858), where a near-total curricular failure -- redeemed only by Agassiz's lectures and Lowell's tutorials -- left him stamped with reflexive self-possession and, inexplicably, elected Class Orator.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Harvard College (1854-1858)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Adams's 1858–59 attempt at a Berlin education collapses through a worthless University Civil Law lecture and forces him into a Prussian Gymnasium classroom of twelve-year-olds, and its only real lesson—an unbidden feel for Beethoven—arrives by accident rather than instruction.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: The Berlin Failure: Civil Law, the Gymnasium, and an Accidental Beethoven (1858–1859)
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Berlin Failure: Civil Law, the Gymnasium, and an Accidental Beethoven (1858–1859)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams drifts through a second sterile year of German study, then is pulled by his sister Mrs. Kuhn into an Italy where mediaeval, unrestored Rome resists any law of progress and a five-minute audience with Garibaldi in besieged Palermo shows him a revolutionary who, by his own later account, never understood the acts he was serving, closing two years of self-styled "accidental education" that leave him, by his own admission, nothing but a tourist.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Accidental Education: Dresden, Rome, and Garibaldi's Palermo (1859–1860)
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Accidental Education: Dresden, Rome, and Garibaldi's Palermo (1859–1860)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Serving as his father's private secretary in Washington through the secession winter of 1860-61, Henry Adams finds every statesman he studies—Southern and Northern alike—groping in as much ignorance as himself, and suffers a private rupture with Charles Sumner over the family's conciliatory tactics that teaches him the lasting political axiom that a friend in power is a friend lost.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Treason: An Education in Universal Ignorance (Washington, Winter 1860-61)
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Treason: An Education in Universal Ignorance (Washington, Winter 1860-61)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Adams sails to London in 1861 as his father's unpaid private secretary, where England's swift recognition of Confederate belligerency, the Trent Affair, and total social ostracism teach him that his family's inherited, eighteenth-century assumptions about American diplomacy are worthless, and that deliberate obscurity, not usefulness, is the only survivable posture.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Diplomacy (1861): The Cabin-Boy's Education

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: In 1862 London, Henry Adams learns to survive a society that treats Lincoln and Seward as demons by masking every feeling among nominal friends as carefully as before enemies, watches his father read Lord Palmerston's hidden motives through the near-rupture of the Butler "woman-order" crisis, and then, at Monckton Milnes's Fryston house party, finds his cultivated taste dwarfed by the genius of Algernon Swinburne.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Foes or Friends: London Diplomacy and the Discovery of Swinburne (1862)
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Foes or Friends: London Diplomacy and the Discovery of Swinburne (1862)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: As his father's unofficial private secretary in London during 1862, Henry Adams tests two rival philosophies of political trust against the Alabama crisis and the British Cabinet's near-recognition of the Confederacy, only to learn decades later from private correspondence that the conspiracy he thought he had detected was in fact contradiction, vacillation, and chance.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Political Morality (1862)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: As private secretary to his father in the London legation, Henry Adams narrates the 1863 diplomatic crisis over the Confederate ironclad rams — Charles Francis Adams's ultimatum that forced Earl Russell to stop the ships — then, writing decades later, revises his own verdict on Russell after new evidence surfaces in an 1889 biography.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Battle of the Rams (1863)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Recalling his years as private secretary at the London Legation, Henry Adams argues that English eccentricity, though it made society vivid and gave the illusion of force, was in fact weakness — and that Confederate sympathizers who staked their diplomacy on English eccentrics (Mason, Roebuck) lost precisely because they mistook eccentricity for strength.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Eccentricity (1863)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams recounts nearly a decade of failed social apprenticeship in 1860s London, mapping the city's mutually illegible social circles and interrogating Lothrop Motley's claim that "the London dinner and the English country house were the perfection of human society," before a chance breakfast introduction to Charles Milnes Gaskell opens a lasting Yorkshire friendship.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Perfection of Human Society

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Back in London after the Civil War ends, Henry Adams finds diplomacy and law closed to him, drifts into English art-collecting and antiquarian history as substitute educations, and concludes both were false starts that taught him nothing except the unreliability of expert authority.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Dilettantism: The Failure of Art and Antiquarianism as Careers (1865-1866)
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Dilettantism: The Failure of Art and Antiquarianism as Careers (1865-1866)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: In London and on Shropshire's Wenlock Edge in 1867-1868, Henry Adams takes up Darwinism and geology as intellectual sport under Sir Charles Lyell's tutelage, only to conclude that the fossil record proves mere change rather than uniform evolution, and that his own Darwinism is psychological convenience rather than conviction.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Darwinism, Deep Time, and the Failure of Uniformity
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Darwinism, Deep Time, and the Failure of Uniformity

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Landing in New York in July 1868 after seven years abroad, Henry Adams finds his gentleman's education worthless in an America suddenly reorganized around coal, iron, steam, and railway capital, and, shut out of Boston's press and Newport's society, gambles on Washington journalism under Evarts's patronage, where a village-scale capital hands him close studies of President Andrew Johnson, Secretary Seward, Treasury Secretary Hugh McCulloch, Chief Justice Chase, and Senator Charles Sumner.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: The Press (1868): Return to a Machine-Made America
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Press (1868): Return to a Machine-Made America

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Newly returned to Washington as a would-be political journalist under the incoming Grant administration, Henry Adams watches his hopes for a reforming, second-Washington presidency curdle into disillusionment as he studies Grant himself: an intellectually inert, purely instinctive "force of nature" whose elevation to the nation's highest office, Adams concludes, is proof enough to upset Darwin.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: President Grant (1869)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams recounts his second Washington season (1869-70) — Jay Gould's Gold Conspiracy, the Erie Railway exposé he and his brother Charles wrote, and Grant's Cabinet dissolving into paired personal wars (Boutwell's silent Treasury, the Fish-Sumner rift over annexation, Hoar versus Chief Justice Chase over Legal Tender) — that convince him the constitutional system of 1789 has broken down beyond repair.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Free Fight (1869-70)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: In the summer of 1870, the sudden death of Adams's sister from tetanus and the eruption of the Franco-Prussian War reveal Nature and history alike as chaotic, purposeless forces, ending Adams's faith in steady 'education' and leaving him, adrift, to accept an unwanted Harvard professorship.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Chaos (1870)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Adams closes his account of seven years as Harvard's Assistant Professor of History and editor of the North American Review by declaring both careers failures, then ends the chapter — and the book's first movement — meeting Clarence King in the Colorado Rockies in 1871, a friendship he frames as the one unambiguous success of the period.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Failure (1871): The Harvard Professorship, the North American Review, and Clarence King
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Failure (1871): The Harvard Professorship, the North American Review, and Clarence King

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Resuming the narrative after a twenty-year gap, Henry Adams returns from a lonely London hospital stay in 1892 to a changed but strangely inert Washington, taking stock of a finished education, an accelerating industrial civilization he can no longer be taught by, and a Gilded-Age social and political order he can no longer read as meaningful, crystallized in his silent visits to the Rock Creek Cemetery memorial Saint-Gaudens made for him.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Twenty Years After (1892): An Education Declared Finished
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Twenty Years After (1892): An Education Declared Finished

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams narrates 1893 as a single arc from his cloistered life inside the Cameron-Hay-Lodge circle and the silver-versus-gold quarrel, through the banking Panic that nearly ruins him and delights him as a spectacle of anonymous mechanical force, to a fortnight studying the Chicago World's Fair, where the dynamo confronts the trained historian with a form of causation he has no vocabulary for, closing with the nation's formal submission to the gold standard and "the capitalistic system with all its necessary machinery."
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Chicago (1893): Panic, the Exposition, and the Question the Dynamo Asks
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Chicago (1893): Panic, the Exposition, and the Question the Dynamo Asks

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Between the Panic of 1893 and the sinking of the Maine in 1898, Adams abandons every systematic theory of "education" -- Clarence King's ruined scientific-education scheme, statistics, the religious press -- and settles instead into restless world travel and a deliberate philosophy of silence, broken only by a chance family trip to Normandy that quietly relaunches his medieval scholarship.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Chapter XXIII — Silence (1894–1898)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: In 1898-99 Henry Adams watches John Hay's diplomatic career vindicate a century of Adams-family effort to bind England to America, then drifts from Sicily to Chartres to a paralyzed Washington before resolving, since "chaos cannot be taught," to hunt Kepler-style for a mathematical law of historical attraction.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Indian Summer: Hay's Diplomatic Harvest and the Turn to a Dynamic Theory of History (1898–1899)
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Indian Summer: Hay's Diplomatic Harvest and the Turn to a Dynamic Theory of History (1898–1899)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: At the 1900 Paris Exposition, Henry Adams reads the dynamo as the new age's occult, unmeasurable god of force and sets it against the Virgin and Venus as history's greatest attractive force, arguing that American culture, unlike French or medieval culture, never learned to feel sex or the sacred as force at all.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Dynamo and the Virgin (1900)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: In 1901, Adams weighs John Hay's unilateral diplomatic triumph in the Boxer Rebellion crisis and the mounting exhaustion of the men around him against his own failed lifelong search for scientific unity, as a child's magnet, a stack of geological literature, and a stalled Darwinism all reveal multiplicity where he had expected convergence.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Twilight (1901)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Touring Paris, Baireuth, Russia, Scandinavia, and the Rhineland in 1901, Henry Adams tests his invented private philosophy of "conservative Christian anarchy" -- in which order and anarchy resolve into one chaotic unity -- against Russia's ancient inertia, the new electro-industrial "empire of Coal," and news of President McKinley's assassination reaching him by telegraph inside the Arctic Circle.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Teufelsdrockh (1901)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Reeling from the deaths of Del Hay, McKinley, and Clarence King and displaced from intimacy with power by Theodore Roosevelt's sudden ascension, Adams treats 1901-02 as the peak of his and John Hay's political education, watching Hay triangulate a global balance between Anglo-French "Coal-power" and German-Russian "Gun-power" combinations while concluding that reaching the height of available knowledge only reveals the full scale of his own ignorance.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Height of Knowledge (1902)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: At sixty-five, Adams hunts for a single "unit of force" to ground a science of history, and finds every candidate — occult attraction, Pascal's ennui, the Virgin's Love, Aquinas's Multiplicity, the kinetic theory of gases, the new psychology's dissolving self — collapsing the promised Unity back into Multiplicity, so he converts the unresolved philosophical question into a historiographical method: two books measuring motion between a thirteenth-century pole of Unity and his own pole of Multiplicity.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Abyss of Ignorance

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Tracking John Hay's 1903 fight to keep China's "open door" against a rolling, unstoppable Russia, Adams borrows the physics of inertia to build a fatalistic theory of historical force, then applies it at far greater length to the American woman's paradoxical, directionless "freedom."
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Vis Inertiae (1903)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Reading Karl Pearson's Grammar of Science alongside Poincare, Mach, and Haeckel in the aftermath of Crookes, Roentgen, and Curie, Adams concludes that turn-of-the-century physics has replaced a lawful, unified nineteenth-century universe with an admitted supersensual chaos, dating the rupture precisely to 1900 and closing with the image of the mind's own self-made unity - man's abstract, woman's procreative - destroyed by that chaos.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: The Grammar of Science (1903)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: In the year of the Russo-Japanese War's outbreak, Hay's last diplomatic triumph, the St. Louis World's Fair, and a summer automobile pilgrimage among French cathedrals, Adams tests his private measure of historical force against Russian inertia, Rooseveltian candor, the dynamo-born "new American," and the Virgin's still-active power, until Plehve's assassination pushes him to resolve on building his own Dynamic Theory of History.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Chapter XXXII: Vis Nova (1903-1904)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams proposes a mechanics of history in which Progress is redefined as the development and economy of Forces that capture and educate man — from fetish, the Cross, and Rome's slave-system through the Baconian reversal of mind and nature to the accelerating "supersensual forces" of 1900.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: A Dynamic Theory of History (1904)

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams proposes a mechanics-inspired 'dynamic theory' of history, using coal-output as a dynamometer to argue that historical force has been accelerating on a roughly ten-year doubling since 1840 and must soon drive the human mind into a new equilibrium.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: A Law of Acceleration

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Returning to a New York convulsed by the raw power of Trusts and corporations in November 1904, Adams reframes Roosevelt's antitrust fight as a physical contest over whether the new forces can breed a "new man," then closes the memoir with John Hay's decline and death in July 1905, ending the shared education of the three friends.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Nunc Age: The Trusts, the New Man, and the Death of John Hay
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Nunc Age: The Trusts, the New Man, and the Death of John Hay

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Henry Cabot Lodge's 1918 editor's preface recounts how Henry Adams conceived The Education of Henry Adams as the twentieth-century-multiplicity companion to Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres' thirteenth-century-unity, why Adams left it privately printed and unpublished until his death, and why the Massachusetts Historical Society now issues it posthumously.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Editor's Preface: The Making and Withholding of The Education of Henry Adams
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Editor's Preface: The Making and Withholding of The Education of Henry Adams

commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.summary: Adams's preface rejects Rousseauian confession in favor of an impersonal "manikin" method, casting the self as a model figure onto which the garment of education is fitted so young men can be trained in economy of force rather than moral self-display.
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.term: Preface: The Manikin in Place of Confession
commons/reading/adams-education/adams-ed.title: Preface: The Manikin in Place of Confession

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Appleby opens her history of capitalism by posing not its triumph but its four-thousand-year delay as the real puzzle, arguing that a scarcity-bound, custom-governed world broke apart uniquely and contingently in seventeenth-century England rather than in wealthier rivals or in Ming China, and redefines capitalism, against Smith, Marx, and Weber, as a cultural rather than natural or inevitable system.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Capitalism’s Puzzle: Why England, Why So Late
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Capitalism’s Puzzle: Why England, Why So Late

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Between roughly 1500 and 1700, Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, English, and French trading empires stitched the Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Pacific into one commercial system, but Appleby argues this explosion of trade was not itself capitalism — aristocratic Iberia and France converted commerce into bullion and royal extraction without transforming their societies, the commercially brilliant Dutch stalled short of industrialization, and only England's institutional peculiarities let trade eventually feed into capitalism proper.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Trade Is Not Capitalism: Empire, Commerce, and Institutional Divergence, 1500–1700
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Trade Is Not Capitalism: Empire, Commerce, and Institutional Divergence, 1500–1700

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Premodern Europe's economies were bound in a demographic-agricultural vise—scarcity-driven grain regulation, a widening but double-edged Columbian-Exchange food supply, and Malthusian population cycles—that kept some 80 percent of people farming and starved every other enterprise of labor and capital until agricultural productivity and Europe's distinctive late-marriage pattern began to loosen the trap.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: The Vise of Scarcity: Food, Population, and the Preconditions for Capitalism
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: The Vise of Scarcity: Food, Population, and the Preconditions for Capitalism

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: New crop-rotation techniques pioneered in the Netherlands and adopted by English freeholders and landlords broke the age-old cycle of soil exhaustion and famine, and Appleby argues that the market society and social upheaval that followed were the consequence of this agricultural transformation, not, as Marxist historians hold, its coercive cause.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Priming the Pump of Capitalism: The Agricultural Revolution in England and the Netherlands
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Priming the Pump of Capitalism: The Agricultural Revolution in England and the Netherlands

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century England argued the market economy into moral legitimacy through a vibrant public pamphlet culture, replacing a picture of impulsive, sin-prone human nature with the durable image of self-interested, calculating economic man, via the 1620s clothiers' crisis and Thomas Mun's mercantilist theory of an autonomous market, the slow erosion of the biblical usury taboo, English fascination with the inexplicable Dutch economy, and the calico craze's proof that consumer desire could itself drive growth.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Debating the Market: Discourse, Mercantilism, and the Decline of the Usury Taboo
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Debating the Market: Discourse, Mercantilism, and the Decline of the Usury Taboo

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: England's 1690s recoinage crisis pitted John Locke's mistaken intrinsic-value theory of money against practical critics who saw legal tender as a social convention, and the deflationary aftermath, the founding of the Bank of England, and France's contrasting Mississippi-Bubble and physiocratic experiments together illustrate Appleby's larger claim that capitalism took root in England through trust and decentralized trial-and-error rather than top-down design or historical inevitability.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: The Recoinage Crisis and the Making of Economic Thought in England and France
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: The Recoinage Crisis and the Making of Economic Thought in England and France

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Atlantic plantation slavery and Britain's steam-powered mechanization arose as parallel, capital-hungry responses to the same capitalist imperative, one built on coerced African labor and invented racial rationalizations, the other on an English combination of high wages, cheap coal, and a freed-up agricultural workforce.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Sugar and Steam: Slavery, Plantation Capitalism, and the Roots of Industrial Invention
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Sugar and Steam: Slavery, Plantation Capitalism, and the Roots of Industrial Invention

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: The seventeenth-century marriage of experimental science and craft knowledge — from Bacon's empiricism and Newton's mechanics through Watt's steam engine and Wedgwood's clock-disciplined factories — built industrial capitalism's technical base, while Enlightenment thinkers like Adam Smith and Thomas Paine supplied its ideological case for self-interested progress, even as Luddite machine-breaking and the entangled, then diverging, histories of wage labor and Atlantic slavery exposed its costs.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: How Science Became Machines: Invention, Factory Discipline, and the Enlightenment Case for Progress
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: How Science Became Machines: Invention, Factory Discipline, and the Enlightenment Case for Progress

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Nineteenth-century Germany and the United States overtook Britain in industrial output and innovation by fusing economic development with nation-building — Germany through state-directed unification and the Zollverein, the United States through decentralized private initiative, westward expansion, and (in the South) slave-based cotton agriculture.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Two Roads to Industrial Ascent: Germany and the United States Overtake Britain
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Two Roads to Industrial Ascent: Germany and the United States Overtake Britain

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Germany and the United States leapfrogged Britain's early industrial lead by adapting borrowed railroad and telegraph technology, building bank-centered capital markets and incorporation law, and weathering the prolonged depression of 1873 and the rigidities of the gold standard, despite starkly different national temperaments toward risk and enterprise.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Overtaking Britain: Technology, Finance, and the Long Depression of 1873 in Germany and the United States
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Overtaking Britain: Technology, Finance, and the Long Depression of 1873 in Germany and the United States

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Self-made industrial magnates in America and Germany built monopolistic leviathans of railroads, steel, and oil on the back of a fifty-million-person transatlantic migration, provoking rival syndicalist, anarchist, and Marxist labor movements whose political fortunes diverged sharply by country, while a new mass consumer economy of department stores, advertising, and demand-driven wages emerged to reshape capitalism itself.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: The Leviathans of Industry, Their Workers, and the Rise of the Consumer
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: The Leviathans of Industry, Their Workers, and the Rise of the Consumer

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Flush with capital accumulated over two centuries of market growth, European governments turned to state-directed empire-building in Africa—producing Leopold's Congo atrocities, the Scramble for Africa, and a belated moral reckoning over its hypocrisy—while Meiji Japan modernized along Western capitalist and military lines without submitting to colonization, emerging as an imperial power in its own right.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Capitalism's Imperial Turn: The Scramble for Africa and Japan's Meiji Counter-Model
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Capitalism's Imperial Turn: The Scramble for Africa and Japan's Meiji Counter-Model

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Between the 1880s and 1920s, capitalist competition pushed American, German, and British firms toward three different organizational solutions—bureaucratic mergers and trusts in the United States, state-tolerated cartels in Germany, family-firm continuity in Britain—while electricity and Henry Ford's automobile assembly line remade production, consumption, and daily life atop new global chains in oil and rubber, a transformation Appleby argues was politically contingent rather than an inevitable unfolding of capitalist logic.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Bureaucracy, Cartels, and the Automobile: Remaking Industrial Capitalism, 1880s–1920s
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Bureaucracy, Cartels, and the Automobile: Remaking Industrial Capitalism, 1880s–1920s

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: The wealth capitalism generated financed the arms race and alliance system that made World War I feel overdetermined, and the punitive peace, agricultural gluts, and gold-standard rigidities that followed set up a Great Depression whose failures of leadership incubated fascism, a second and deadlier world war, and the slow, incomplete unraveling of the European empires.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Two World Wars and a Global Depression, 1914–1945
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Two World Wars and a Global Depression, 1914–1945

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Postwar governments rebuild shattered economies along three divergent paths—European state planning, Soviet command control, and American reliance on market signals—while the Marshall Plan, Bretton Woods, and a deliberately anti-nationalist European integration movement restore growth and contain Cold War rivalry, even as a credit-financed boom in cars, television, air travel, and plastics remakes the texture of American daily life.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Postwar Capitalism Remade: The Marshall Plan, European Integration, and America's Consumer Boom
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Postwar Capitalism Remade: The Marshall Plan, European Integration, and America's Consumer Boom

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Sputnik-triggered expansion of American higher education, Cold War military R&D (rocketry, computers, pharmaceuticals), and the rise and erosion of organized labor set the stage for the 1973 oil shock and stagflation that ended capitalism's postwar golden age.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Sputnik, the Computer State, and the Unraveling of the Postwar Boom
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Sputnik, the Computer State, and the Unraveling of the Postwar Boom

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Stagflation discredited Keynesian orthodoxy and opened the door to Friedman-inspired deregulation that delivered mixed results, while Japan's state-guided industrial rise and the American personal-computer boom emerged as the era's two most consequential new growth engines.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Friedman, Deregulation, and the Rise of Japan and the Personal Computer
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Friedman, Deregulation, and the Rise of Japan and the Personal Computer

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: The Internet, the Asian Four Little Tigers, and Walmart's information-driven retailing together close out Appleby's account of late-twentieth-century capitalism, with a coda on birth control, genomics, and capitalism's ambiguous ties to democracy and inequality.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: The Internet, the Four Little Tigers, and Walmart's Information Machine
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: The Internet, the Four Little Tigers, and Walmart's Information Machine

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: China's three-decade party-managed transition from Maoist collectivism to a market economy—special economic zones, dual-track pricing, and the “bird cage economy” doctrine of controlled liberalization—together with India's parallel rise, has undermined Western assumptions linking free markets to democracy and left the World Trade Organization straining to hold its multilateral consensus after the 2008 Doha round collapsed.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: China's Market Transformation and the WTO's Fraying Consensus
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: China's Market Transformation and the WTO's Fraying Consensus

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Post-Soviet Russia's rushed, adviser-driven privatization breeds oligarchy, criminal capture, and demographic decline while India, still shaped by Britain's deindustrializing colonialism and its own caste hierarchy, dismantles the License Raj after 1991 and, guided by the contrasting legacies of Gandhi and Mao, becomes a consumer-driven capitalist power alongside China.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Eastern Europe's Shock Therapy and India's Long Road from Empire to Boom
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Eastern Europe's Shock Therapy and India's Long Road from Empire to Boom

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Three decades of financial deregulation, unregulated credit default swaps, and leveraged mortgage securitization built a globally interconnected house of cards whose 2008 collapse -- amplified by the unintended consequences of individually rational choices and capitalism's contagious optimism -- forced worldwide bailouts and revived the case for regulation and for the legal and civic scaffolding capitalism depends on.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: The 2008 Financial Crisis: Deregulation, Leverage, and the House of Cards
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: The 2008 Financial Crisis: Deregulation, Leverage, and the House of Cards

commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.summary: Closing out the book, Appleby recapitulates capitalism's rise from the periphery of aristocratic society to the center of modern life, surveys practical anti-poverty innovators (Yunus, Sen, De Soto, Barnes, Lappé/Bello/Patel) and a nascent green-technology wave, then argues that capitalism is decentralized, amoral, and locked in permanent tension with democracy and equality — a relentless revolution, but not a mindless one.
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.term: Capitalism's Legacy: Poverty, the Green Revolution, and the Book's Final Reckoning
commons/reading/appleby-relentless-revol.title: Capitalism's Legacy: Poverty, the Green Revolution, and the Book's Final Reckoning

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Between roughly 1400 and 1800 a near-equilibrium of births and deaths, chronic famine, and cyclical epidemic disease formed a structural 'biological ancien regime' across Europe and Asia that only began to break, unevenly and reversibly, with the eighteenth century.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Biological Ancien Regime: Famine, Plague, and the Weight of Numbers, 1400–1800
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Biological Ancien Regime: Famine, Plague, and the Weight of Numbers, 1400–1800

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel reconstructs approximate global population figures for 1300-1800 from radically uneven regional evidence, solid only for Europe and China, and argues that the near-synchronous demographic doubling he finds across otherwise unconnected regions cannot be explained by specifically European causes and is best attributed, provisionally, to shared climatic fluctuation.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Guessing the World's Population, 1300-1800
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Guessing the World's Population, 1300-1800

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel argues that population numbers shape civilizations' fates -- barbarian conquerors are absorbed by the civilizations they defeat, nomadic power collapses once gunpowder closes the open frontier, and colonized 'cultures' either vanish into empty space or mount durable resistance -- before naming numbers one of material life's lasting constraints, distinct from the coming volume's account of economic life and capitalism.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Many Against the Few
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Many Against the Few

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel builds a translation scale for reading pre-industrial numbers — showing that small pre-1800 towns, armies, and fleets carried proportionally far greater weight than their raw figures suggest, that "overpopulation" is relative to a country's carrying capacity rather than absolute density, and that Gordon W. Hewes's 1500 map of the world's civilizations traces a narrow, persistent belt of dense settlement ringed by vast, thinly peopled wildernesses.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: A Scale of Reference: Small Numbers, Great Weight
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: A Scale of Reference: Small Numbers, Great Weight

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel traces maize from its Mesoamerican archaeological origins and role in Inca, Aztec and Maya civilization through its slow, two-century, world-spanning diffusion alongside the potato into an eighteenth-century dietary revolution that let European peasants eat cheap new-world starches while wheat became a market crop, closing on the racially charged 1697 Mexico City bread riot.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Maize, Potatoes, and the Dietary Revolutions of the Eighteenth Century
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Maize, Potatoes, and the Dietary Revolutions of the Eighteenth Century

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Rice's paddy-field agriculture, far more calorically productive per hectare than wheat but far more labor-, water-, and state-intensive, built the demography, social discipline, and diet of China, Japan, and India across centuries while foreclosing the highland pastoral economies that Europe's wheat-and-livestock agriculture exploited.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Rice: The Tyrannical Grain and the Making of the Far East
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Rice: The Tyrannical Grain and the Making of the Far East

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Beyond the great grain civilizations lies a vast, remarkably homogeneous world of hoe- and digging-stick cultivators — and, below them, still more marginal gathering-hunting peoples — whose technological difference from plough agriculture Braudel treats not as a lower rung on one ladder but as a distinct layer of material life coexisting, in the very same fifteenth-to-eighteenth centuries, with grain civilizations and advancing European capitalism.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Rest of the World: The People of the Hoe and the Primitive Peoples
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Rest of the World: The People of the Hoe and the Primitive Peoples

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Opening his chapter on 'Daily Bread,' Braudel first surveys the world's vegetable-versus-meat diets as markers of civilization before narrowing to wheat as one of three 'plants of civilization', tracing its Old World geography, its inseparability from companion grains and livestock in a fixed rotation system, and its stubbornly low, only slowly rising, seed-to-harvest yields across early modern Europe.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Daily Bread: World Diets and the Wheat System
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Daily Bread: World Diets and the Wheat System

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Local self-sufficiency dominated Europe's grain supply while long-distance trade stayed structurally marginal in volume, and the price of grain — converted into calories, hours of labor, and loaf weight — functioned as the master barometer of the poor's standard of living and the recurring trigger of bread riots.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Grain Rules Europe: Trade, Price, Calories, and Bread
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Grain Rules Europe: Trade, Price, Calories, and Bread

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Europe's drink hierarchy runs from water — scarce and often foul even in wealthy cities — through wine's climate-bounded belt from the Loire to the Crimea and the northern beer-and-cider zone, to the sixteenth-to-eighteenth-century rise of distilled brandy and grain spirits from apothecary medicine into a mass-consumed, state-taxed, exchange-quoted commodity.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Drinks: Water, Wine, Beer, Cider, and the Rise of Alcohol
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Drinks: Water, Wine, Beer, Cider, and the Rise of Alcohol

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel traces luxury as an ever-shifting relational category in food and material goods, documents Europe's unusually meat-rich diet from roughly 1350 to 1550 giving way to a three-century retreat of meat after 1550, and sets both trends inside a world-scale comparison of eating habits across China, Japan, India, the Ottoman lands, Egypt, and colonial Brazil and Argentina.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Superfluity and Sufficiency: Luxury, Diet, and the Long Retreat of Meat
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Superfluity and Sufficiency: Luxury, Diet, and the Long Retreat of Meat

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Alcohol, chocolate, tea, coffee and tobacco each spread from non-European origins into worldwide use between roughly 1500 and 1800, moving from local material-life habits into commodities that colonial powers weaponized for dependency and that an organized capitalist sector eventually mass-produced for profit.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Stimulants and Their Global Circuits: Alcohol, Chocolate, Tea, Coffee and Tobacco
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Stimulants and Their Global Circuits: Alcohol, Chocolate, Tea, Coffee and Tobacco

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: A small European elite's extravagant table, and the centuries-slow spread of forks, individual plates, and napkins across the continent, opens onto a world-scale survey of everyday foods — salt, dairy, fish, pepper, and sugar — whose trade networks bind material life to a market economy and, in sugar's case, to plantation slavery.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Table Manners and the World Trade in Everyday Foods
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Table Manners and the World Trade in Everyday Foods

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel argues that costume changes almost nowhere except where political rupture disturbs a stable social order, and that Europe's turn toward perpetual fashion — crystallizing as a concept around 1700 — makes dress a visible index of prosperity, social mobility, and a civilization's willingness to break with tradition, all riding on top of a much slower geography of textile production and trade.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Costume and Fashion
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Costume and Fashion

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel surveys vernacular housing across Europe, Islam, China, India, and the Americas from the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries to show how tradition and the local availability of stone, brick, wood, or earth set durable limits on what could be built, while town wealth, fire risk, and social rank progressively reshape rural land, roofing materials, and the layout of urban houses.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Houses Throughout the World: Materials, Tradition, and the Rural–Urban Divide
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Houses Throughout the World: Materials, Tradition, and the Rural–Urban Divide

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Domestic interiors reveal a world where most civilizations' material culture stayed nearly frozen for centuries while only the West made constant renovation of houses, furniture, and comfort its habit, and where furniture itself — chairs, heating, privacy — marks the deepest fault lines between cultures.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Interiors: the furniture of civilizations
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Interiors: the furniture of civilizations

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Between the fifteenth and eighteenth centuries pre-industrial societies ran on human muscle and an unevenly distributed menagerie of draft animals — llamas and mules in the Americas, camels under Islamic caravan trade, oxen, and horses whose medieval collar multiplied their pulling power fourfold — with Braudel arguing throughout that a technology's actual use, not its invention, is set by a society's readiness to adopt it.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Human Engine and the Animal Engine: Power Before Coal
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Human Engine and the Animal Engine: Power Before Coal

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Iron remained a marginal, technically stagnant, geographically dispersed industry from the fifteenth through the eighteenth century — dwarfed by textiles, outpaced by a Chinese head start that mysteriously stalled after the thirteenth century, and excluded from the speculative capital that silver, gold, and copper attracted to early capitalism.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Iron: A Poor Relation
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Iron: A Poor Relation

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel surveys pre-industrial Europe's entire energy base — watermills, windmills, sails, wood and charcoal, and the slow, socially resisted arrival of coal — and closes with a quantified ranking showing draught-animals and wood, not machines, as the two dominant power sources before the eighteenth century.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Energy Budget of Pre-Industrial Europe: Wind, Water, Wood, and Coal
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Energy Budget of Pre-Industrial Europe: Wind, Water, Wood, and Coal

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Artillery and firearms spread across Eurasia over three centuries as a slow, contested, and ultimately non-monopolizable technology whose diffusion — through trade, itinerant gunners, and capitalist arms production — reorganized state finance and siege warfare without redrawing the frontiers of the world's great civilizations.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Artillery as a 'Revolution' in Slow Motion
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Artillery as a 'Revolution' in Slow Motion

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Paper's mere cheapness (not quality) made movable-type printing economically viable and turned it into a capitalist enterprise whose deepest effects were unplanned, while Europe's parallel monopoly on ocean navigation is explained, against a purely technical account, by the post-thirteenth-century rise in Europe's material life and the driving hunger of its capitalist towns.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: From Paper to the Printing Press, and Why Only Europe Took to the High Seas
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: From Paper to the Printing Press, and Why Only Europe Took to the High Seas

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Pre-industrial transport and technology alike stayed fixed, slow, and largely unchanged across centuries and civilizations, and real technological breakthroughs occurred only when accumulated social pressure forced society past the 'ceiling of the possible', never from any autonomous drive to innovate.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Transport, Technology, and the Limits of the Possible
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Transport, Technology, and the Limits of the Possible

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Opening Chapter 7, Braudel argues money is best read not through received metaphors but as a function of an economy's own complexity, then catalogues the world's commodity and "imperfect" currencies — cowries, manillas, wampum, coral olivette, salt, slave-priced cloth — before showing that barter itself never disappeared, surviving as pockets inside supposedly monetized Europe and its colonies.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Money as Indicator: The World's Imperfect Currencies and Persistent Barter
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Money as Indicator: The World's Imperfect Currencies and Persistent Barter

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Across seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Japan, the Ottoman Empire and Persia, India, and China, metallic coin layered onto rather than replaced older moneys, while bullion migrated along a chain that Braudel traces from the Americas through the Levant into Persia and, above all, India, leaving China more self-contained and less "sophisticated" but more internally coherent.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Outside Europe: Early Economies and Metallic Money
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Outside Europe: Early Economies and Metallic Money

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel traces paper money and instruments of credit—bills of exchange, bank notes, scriptural money—as an ancient, world-spanning technique whose boundary against metallic money economists themselves cannot settle, closing with money-and-credit as a universal 'language' that unifies the world only into a hierarchy of favoured and handicapped economies.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Money and Credit as a Universal Human Technique
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Money and Credit as a Universal Human Technique

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Europe's stratified gold-silver-copper currency, doubled by an abstract layer of 'moneys of account' and multiplied by its velocity of circulation, formed a single world-spanning monetary net whose bullion flowed east and whose hoarding drained it, while a barter and subsistence economy persisted largely outside its reach.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Some Rules of the Currency Game
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Some Rules of the Currency Game

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel closes his chapter on the great cities of the ancien régime — and the whole volume — by pushing the parasitical-capital thesis to its extremes in Peking and London, then arguing that cities are a yardstick of their society rather than an autonomous force, and that the real pivot toward industrial modernity bypassed the old capitals entirely.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Peking and London: Parasitical Capitals and the Verdict on Urbanization
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Peking and London: Parasitical Capitals and the Verdict on Urbanization

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries a handful of European capitals overtook the historically larger cities of the East because capital status was created by political centralization rather than trade, leaving London, Paris, Naples and St Petersburg as economically top-heavy "unbalanced worlds" sustained by court, office and rent rather than commerce.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Big Cities: States, Capitals, and the Political Arithmetic of Growth
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Big Cities: States, Capitals, and the Political Arithmetic of Growth

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Medieval and early-modern Western European towns achieved a uniquely durable freedom from territorial-state control, becoming self-governing city-states that invented the financial and institutional machinery of early capitalism, while comparable towns in colonial Latin America, Muscovite Russia, and the Islamic and Far Eastern empires never escaped subordination to prince, tsar, caliph, or mandarin because the state (or its equivalent) reasserted itself before an independent closed-city phase could take hold.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Originality of Western Towns
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Originality of Western Towns

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Town walls, street plans, siting, and networks of civic dependency are read as direct expressions of each civilization's distinct way of building and controlling urban space, from Chinese ramparts repurposed as instruments of internal surveillance to the sharp grid-versus-maze divide between planned and organically grown towns and the market-driven hierarchies binding small towns to great capitals.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: The Self-Consciousness of Towns: Walls, Grids, and Hierarchies
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: The Self-Consciousness of Towns: Walls, Grids, and Hierarchies

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Opening Chapter 8, Braudel argues that a town is defined not by population size but by a recurring bundle of functions — market, division of labour, coercive power, self-consciousness, and external trade — then shows through comparative demography (France, Britain, Russia, Japan, colonial America, Germany, China) how unstable any size threshold is, before tracing the mutual, non-sequential creation of town and countryside and the chronic dependence of urban growth on stratified immigration of both poor labourers and skilled elites.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Towns and Cities: Defining, Measuring, and Peopling the Urban World
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Towns and Cities: Defining, Measuring, and Peopling the Urban World
