commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel closes Volume I by defending its scope and method — the long term, the anonymous 'dust of history,' civilizations as non-convergent bonding orders, and society reframed as socio-economy — before restating the three-storey house of material life, ordinary economic life, and real capitalism, and locating capitalism's power in its comparative freedom of movement relative to the other two, inflexible floors.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Braudel Closes Volume I: Scope, Method, and the Three-Storey House
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Braudel Closes Volume I: Scope, Method, and the Three-Storey House

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel recounts how a 1952 commission from Lucien Febvre to summarize pre-industrial European economic history grew into a rejection of the classical single-economy narrative and a proposal instead of a tripartite schema of material life, the market economy, and capitalism as distinct, coexisting strata that structures all three volumes of the book.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Introduction: Three Economies, Not One
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Introduction: Three Economies, Not One

commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.summary: Braudel's preface justifies Volume I's method by defining "the limits of the possible" — the slow-moving, largely unchanging border between what pre-industrial societies could and could not do — and by arguing that the routine-bound "material civilization" beneath the market economy, together with the unremarked repetitions of everyday life, deserves history's attention as much as its unique events.
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.term: Preface: The Limits of the Possible
commons/reading/braudel-civilization-cap.title: Preface: The Limits of the Possible

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Surveying Ortega y Gasset, Nietzsche, and a chorus of early-twentieth-century European writers, Carey shows how the literary intelligentsia responded to newly literate mass publics, popular newspapers, and universal education by inventing modernism, eugenics fantasies, and theories of the avant-garde as mechanisms for excluding and dehumanizing 'the masses,' before arguing that the mass itself is only a metaphor that denies individuality to other people.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: The Revolt of the Masses

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey traces how early-twentieth-century intellectuals (Ortega, Hardy, Nietzsche, Eliot, Woolf, Pound, Le Bon, Freud, Canetti, Forster, Lawrence, Priestley, and above all Orwell) invented and reinvented images of "the mass" — herd, bacillus, jelly, peasant, pastoral child, prole — in order to strip actual people of individuality and secure the intellectual's own superiority and control.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: Rewriting the Mass: Metaphor as Instrument of Control
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Rewriting the Mass: Metaphor as Instrument of Control

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey traces how the explosive growth of suburbs and clerical white-collar work between 1880 and 1939 gave English intellectuals a concrete target — "the suburban" and "the clerk" — onto which they projected and then despised an invented, homogeneous mass, with writers from Chesterton and Bullock to Betjeman and Stevie Smith occasionally breaking ranks to reclaim that territory with sympathy.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: The Suburbs and the Clerks

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey traces how early-twentieth-century intellectuals (Nietzsche, Lawrence, Yeats, Pound, Bell, Huxley, Greene, Steiner) invented a doctrine of "natural aristocracy" to reassert distinction and authority once mass literacy and democracy had eroded the old bases of cultural and social hierarchy.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Natural Aristocrats

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: John Carey shows how George Gissing, using twin diagnostic devices of physiognomy and bookshelf-contents to sort people into innate categories, became the first and most thorough architect of the modern intellectual case that the working-class "masses" are congenitally ineducable, a doctrine inseparable from his own class self-exile, his cruelty toward his two lower-class wives, and a virulent misogyny toward educated women, even as his lived knowledge of London poverty kept generating a sympathy his theory could not suppress.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: George Gissing and the Doctrine of the Ineducable Masses
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: George Gissing and the Doctrine of the Ineducable Masses

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey traces H. G. Wells's lifelong population anxiety—rooted in childhood grief over the suburban ruin of Bromley—into an explicit eugenicist and genocidal program in his non-fiction, and into a fiction obsessed with annihilating the human masses altogether, arguing that destruction, not progress, was Wells's deepest imaginative pleasure.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: H. G. Wells and the Extermination of the Masses
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: H. G. Wells and the Extermination of the Masses

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey traces H. G. Wells's fiction and essays to show a writer permanently split between two irreconcilable drives — a Nietzschean program of eugenic system, classification, and contempt for "the masses," and an imaginative sympathy that keeps siding with the failures, clerks, and excluded lower-middle-class characters his own doctrines condemn.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: H. G. Wells Against H. G. Wells: System, Freedom, and the Masses
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: H. G. Wells Against H. G. Wells: System, Freedom, and the Masses

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey presents Arnold Bennett as the book's counter-hero, a self-made shopkeeper's son turned bestselling novelist and mass-market critic whose fiction and journalism systematically refute the modernist claim that ordinary, uneducated people live shallower or less worthy inner lives than intellectuals.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: Narrowing the Abyss: Arnold Bennett as Anti-Elitist Novelist
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Narrowing the Abyss: Arnold Bennett as Anti-Elitist Novelist

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey traces Wyndham Lewis's lifelong misogyny to a personal psychology of bodily disgust and resentment, shows how he generalized it into a theory that democracy, mass culture, and even relativity and stream-of-consciousness fiction were symptoms of a 'feminization' of the West, and follows that logic through to his apologetics for Mussolini and Hitler and his racism and antisemitism.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: Wyndham Lewis and the Feminization of the West
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Wyndham Lewis and the Feminization of the West

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: Carey argues, using Mein Kampf and Table Talk, that Hitler's cultural ideas—reverence for canonical genius, contempt for mass media and the bourgeoisie, the aristocratic principle set against parliamentary democracy, and a series of interchangeable images of the mass as woman, child, nation, worker, or exterminable vermin—were not an aberration but continuous with mainstream early twentieth-century English intellectual orthodoxy.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: Hitler's Cultural Orthodoxy and the Rewriting of the Mass
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Hitler's Cultural Orthodoxy and the Rewriting of the Mass

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: In the book's postscript, Carey traces intellectual mass-phobia from Virginia Woolf's self-tormenting fantasy of loathsome working-class women through Rayner Heppenstall's near-genocidal outbursts, then updates the story to the late twentieth century, where real population explosion literalizes the old fear of the swarming mass and post-structuralist "theory" replaces modernist difficulty as the intellectual's new defense against a culturally enfranchised majority.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Coda: Mass-Phobia After Modernism

commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.summary: In the preface to "The Intellectuals and the Masses," John Carey states his book's thesis that modernist literature and art were a deliberate strategy by which the late-Victorian and early-twentieth-century literary intelligentsia sought to exclude the newly literate reading public created by educational reform, and traces the theological genealogy of the word "mass" from Augustine's massa damnata to its terminal expression in Hitler's death camps.
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.term: Preface: The Thesis of "The Intellectuals and the Masses"
commons/reading/carey-intellectuals-and-.title: Preface: The Thesis of "The Intellectuals and the Masses"

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: A biographical essay reconstructs Cervantes's obscure ancestry and youth amid Spain's transition from chivalric to absolutist rule, then follows him through his wounding at Lepanto and five years of captivity and repeated, self-sacrificing escape attempts in Algiers, arguing that this documented life supplies the real ground beneath Don Quixote's treatment of chivalry.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Making of Cervantes: Ancestry, Lepanto, and Captivity in Algiers
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Making of Cervantes: Ancestry, Lepanto, and Captivity in Algiers

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: A biographical sketch follows Cervantes from his penniless return to Spain through failed careers as playwright and tax collector, the accidental gathering of material that became Don Quixote, the novel's contested reception, Avellaneda's spurious sequel that forced him to finish Part Two, and his death in 1616, closing with a defense of his life against the charge that Spain neglected him.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Making of Don Quixote: Cervantes's Later Life and Death
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Making of Don Quixote: Cervantes's Later Life and Death

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: John Ormsby's critical essay traces Don Quixote's uniquely cosmopolitan-yet-national popularity, argues Cervantes attacked not chivalry itself (already a century dead) but its degraded theatrical mockery, reconstructs the book's unplanned, accretive composition (Sancho, Cid Hamete Benengeli), and locates its humor in the deadpan incongruity between Don Quixote's ideal and the mean, prosaic Manchegan world he moves through.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Meaning and Making of Don Quixote
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Meaning and Making of Don Quixote

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: John Ormsby's prefatory essay surveys a century-and-a-half of English translations of Don Quixote—Shelton, Phillips, Ward, Motteux, Jervas, Smollett, and lesser imitators—to argue that fidelity to Cervantes's spirit and plain, unaffected style, not archaism or comic embellishment, is the translator's real duty, and to state the principles guiding his own version.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Prefatory: The History and Ethics of Translating Don Quixote
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Prefatory: The History and Ethics of Translating Don Quixote

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Cervantes frames Don Quixote with a self-mocking prose Preface staged as a dialogue with a friend who supplies a mock-recipe for faking scholarly authority, followed by a set of comic commendatory verses spoken by chivalric-romance characters themselves, and closes with a conventional dedication to the Duke of Béjar.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Author's Preface, Commendatory Verses, and Dedication to the Duke of Béjar
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Author's Preface, Commendatory Verses, and Dedication to the Duke of Béjar

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: An aging hidalgo, driven mad by chivalric romances, invents himself as the knight Don Quixote, rides out alone, gets a tavern-keeper to mock-dub him a knight, tries and fails to enact chivalric justice on a farm boy's behalf, and is finally carried home broken and raving while his household resolves to burn the books that unmade him.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Don Quixote Reads Himself into Knighthood
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Don Quixote Reads Himself into Knighthood

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: The curate and barber conduct a mock inquisition of Don Quixote's chivalric library, condemning most of it to the bonfire (sparing a self-referential handful, including Cervantes's own Galatea), after which Don Quixote recruits the farmer Sancho Panza with promises of an island governorship and rides out on his second sally, mistaking windmills for giants and provoking an inconclusive sword duel with a Biscayan squire whose outcome the narrator claims to have lost and later recovered from a manuscript by the fictitious Moorish historian Cide Hamete Benengeli.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Book-Burning, the Windmills, and the Found Manuscript
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Book-Burning, the Windmills, and the Found Manuscript

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: After the joust with the friars' escort, Don Quixote and Sancho banter over the fictional balsam of Fierabras and a chivalric vow before lodging with goatherds, where Don Quixote delivers his Golden Age discourse on lost innocence and property, and the goatherd Pedro (followed by Vivaldo and Ambrosio) tells the tale of the scholar-turned-shepherd Chrysostom, who died of love for the independent shepherdess Marcela, whose funeral the company then attends.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Sancho's Balsam, the Golden Age, and the Death of Chrysostom
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Sancho's Balsam, the Golden Age, and the Death of Chrysostom

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Chrysostom's despairing pastoral lay is read and he is buried, the shepherdess Marcela appears to defend her right to refuse love without blame, and Don Quixote and Sancho are then twice beaten senseless — first by muleteers after Rocinante's misadventure, then in a rural inn Don Quixote insists on perceiving as an enchanted castle, culminating in a farcical night of mistaken identity, a vomit-inducing placebo balsam, and Sancho's blanket-tossing.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Marcela's Refusal, the Yanguesan Beating, and the Castle That Was an Inn
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Marcela's Refusal, the Yanguesan Beating, and the Castle That Was an Inn

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Across Chapters XVIII–XX, Don Quixote mistakes two flocks of sheep for warring armies and a priestly funeral procession for a train of phantoms, then spends a terrified night paralyzed by imagined monsters that turn out to be fulling-mill hammers, while Sancho's earthy skepticism, storytelling, and a rope trick on Rocinante repeatedly puncture (without ever quite deflating) his master's chivalric self-mythology.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Sheep Armies, a Funeral Procession, and the Fulling Mills
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Sheep Armies, a Funeral Procession, and the Fulling Mills

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote seizes a barber's brass basin as "Mambrino's helmet" and spins Sancho a full chivalric-romance fantasy of future glory, then, encountering a chained gang of galley slaves being marched to the king's oars, "liberates" them by force of arms in the name of free will and justice, only to be stoned and stripped by the very men he freed.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Barber's Basin and the Chain of Galley Slaves
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Barber's Basin and the Chain of Galley Slaves

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: In the Sierra Morena, Don Quixote and Sancho find a dead traveler's valise full of gold, a sonnet, and a despairing love letter, then track down and befriend its mad, half-wild owner—Cardenio, the Knight of the Thicket—who begins the story of his betrayal by Don Fernando over Luscinda before a chance mention of Amadis-adjacent chivalry, and then of Queen Madasima's honor, sends him into a violent fit that ends the storytelling in a brawl.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Ragged Knight of the Sierra Morena
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Ragged Knight of the Sierra Morena

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote withdraws into the Sierra Morena to stage a deliberately unmotivated, literary-modeled madness in imitation of Amadis of Gaul and Roland, dispatches Sancho with a love letter to Dulcinea, and the curate and barber, having intercepted Sancho, plot a disguise scheme to lure the knight home.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Don Quixote's Penance in the Sierra Morena
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Don Quixote's Penance in the Sierra Morena

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: The curate and barber costume themselves to lure Don Quixote from his penance in the Sierra Morena, but are diverted first by Cardenio's completed confession of Luscinda's forced betrothal to Don Fernando and then by the discovery of a cross-dressed peasant girl who turns out to be Dorothea, Don Fernando's other, secretly-wronged betrothed.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Two Tales in the Sierra Morena: Cardenio Concludes, Dorothea Begins
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Two Tales in the Sierra Morena: Cardenio Concludes, Dorothea Begins

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Dorothea and the newly-identified Cardenio join forces and Dorothea disguises herself as the fictitious Princess Micomicona so the curate's party can lure Don Quixote out of his mountain penance, a scheme repeatedly stress-tested by Sancho's self-interested fantasies, Don Quixote's rationalizing devotion to Dulcinea, the boy Andres's furious report that the knight's earlier 'rescue' only made things worse, and, at the inn, a landlord's fierce insistence against the curate that the romances of chivalry are literal truth.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Micomicona Ruse and the Reckoning at the Inn
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Micomicona Ruse and the Reckoning at the Inn

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Obsessed with converting his trust in his wife Camilla into verified proof, Anselmo orders his best friend Lothario to seduce her as a test of her virtue, and the staged trial curdles into real adultery, layered deception, and Anselmo's eventual death from the truth his own curiosity manufactured.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Novel of the Ill-Advised Curiosity (El Curioso Impertinente)
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Novel of the Ill-Advised Curiosity (El Curioso Impertinente)

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote's dream-battle with wineskins closes the tale of "The Ill-Advised Curiosity," after which chance reunites all four lovers (Dorothea, Don Fernando, Luscinda, and Cardenio) at the inn, and the arrival of a Christian captive and his veiled Moorish companion Zoraida opens a new thread just as Don Quixote launches into a discourse on arms versus letters.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Wineskin Battle, the Lovers' Reunion, and the Arrival of the Captive
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Wineskin Battle, the Lovers' Reunion, and the Arrival of the Captive

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote closes his discourse on the miseries of the soldier's life and the superiority of arms over letters, cursing the anonymity of gunpowder warfare, and the narrative then turns to the Captive, who begins the "true story" of his life: his father's division of the family patrimony among three sons destined for the church, trade, and arms, his own path through the wars in Flanders and the Battle of Lepanto, his capture and enslavement in Constantinople and Algiers, and the start of his secret courtship-by-letter with Zoraida, the rich Moor's daughter who wants to become a Christian.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Arms and Letters, and the Captive Begins His Tale
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Arms and Letters, and the Captive Begins His Tale

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: The captive concludes his tale of stealing away with Zoraida from Algiers, their perilous voyage and robbery at French hands, and landing in Spain, after which the narrative frame resumes at the inn where a traveling Judge turns out to be the captive's long-lost brother.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Captive's Escape with Zoraida, and the Reunion of Brothers
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Captive's Escape with Zoraida, and the Reunion of Brothers

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Doña Clara confesses that the muleteer-singer is her disguised suitor Don Luis just as Maritornes tricks Don Quixote into hanging by the wrist all night, and the inn then descends into a farcical brawl over whether a barber's basin is Mambrino's helmet, settled by a mock vote, before an officer of the Holy Brotherhood recognizes Don Quixote from an arrest warrant and provokes his final tirade that knights-errant answer to no law but their own.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Enchantment, Consensus, and the Law of Chivalry at the Inn
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Enchantment, Consensus, and the Law of Chivalry at the Inn

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote's companions stage his "enchantment," caging him for the journey home, while Sancho tries and fails to talk him out of his unfalsifiable belief system, and a chance-met Canon of Toledo delivers an extended literary manifesto against the improbability of chivalric romances and the market-driven absurdities of contemporary Spanish theatre.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Caging of Don Quixote and the Canon's Case Against the Romances
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Caging of Don Quixote and the Canon's Case Against the Romances

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Sancho tries to reason Don Quixote out of believing himself enchanted, the freed knight and a skeptical canon stage a full debate over whether chivalric romances are lies or history, Don Quixote rapturously narrates a stock romance adventure as proof of their delight, and the unit closes with a goatherd's pastoral tale of Leandra, whose elopement with a swaggering soldier has turned a valley full of spurned suitors into a shepherds' Arcadia of lament.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Canon's Quarrel with Chivalry and the Tale of Leandra
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Canon's Quarrel with Chivalry and the Tale of Leandra

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote brawls with an offended goatherd, then charges a rain-procession he mistakes for an abduction and is beaten to the ground, after which Sancho carries him home by ox-cart to end the first sally, and the chapter closes with a mock scholarly apparatus of epitaph-sonnets "by the Academicians of Argamasilla" that ironically monumentalize the knight, his lady, and his squire.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Fall Before the Penitents, and the Mock Epitaphs of Argamasilla
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Fall Before the Penitents, and the Mock Epitaphs of Argamasilla

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: The curate and barber test Don Quixote's sanity through veiled parables and political talk, Sancho reports the village's mixed verdict on his master's madness, and both men learn with astonishment that their adventures have already been published as a book, prompting them to plan a second sally to the joust at Zaragoza.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Cure That Wasn't: Testing Don Quixote's Sanity and Discovering His Fame
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Cure That Wasn't: Testing Don Quixote's Sanity and Discovering His Fame

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Sancho bargains with his social-climbing wife Teresa and then with Don Quixote over wages and titles, Don Quixote answers his niece's and housekeeper's objections with a discourse on lineage and the nature of knight-errantry, and after the trickster bachelor Samson Carrasco maneuvers Don Quixote into departing, master and squire ride out by night on their third sally, debating fame, saints, and immortality on the road to El Toboso.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Bargaining for the Third Sally: Teresa, the Niece, and the Road to El Toboso
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Bargaining for the Third Sally: Teresa, the Niece, and the Road to El Toboso

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote and Sancho fail to find Dulcinea's nonexistent palace in El Toboso, so Sancho fabricates an enchantment by presenting a peasant girl as the transformed Dulcinea, after which the pair survive a farcical run-in with a cart of actors dressed as Death and company, and finally meet a lovesick, sonnet-singing Knight of the Grove who mirrors Don Quixote's own madness without either man recognizing it.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Enchantment of Dulcinea and the Knight of the Grove
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Enchantment of Dulcinea and the Knight of the Grove

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Sancho and the squire of the Grove trade cynical talk of squirely rewards before Don Quixote defeats the self-proclaimed Knight of the Mirrors in a farcical joust and unmasks him as the bachelor Samson Carrasco in disguise, a plot Don Quixote's own theory of enchantment lets him explain away, and the party then falls in with the sane, moderate Don Diego de Miranda, prompting Don Quixote's set-piece discourse on poetry.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Knight of the Mirrors and the Gentleman in Green
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Knight of the Mirrors and the Gentleman in Green

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote faces down two caged lions and takes the name Knight of the Lions, then spends four days debating poetry and the 'science' of knight-errantry at the rational household of Don Diego de Miranda, before setting out toward Camacho's wedding, where a bystander's fencing match settles a dispute between raw strength and trained skill.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Knight of the Lions: Courage, Reason, and the Road to Camacho's Wedding
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Knight of the Lions: Courage, Reason, and the Road to Camacho's Wedding

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: At Camacho's lavish wedding feast, the poor but clever Basilio fakes a suicide to force Quiteria's consenting hand before he 'dies,' then springs up unharmed to reveal the trick as a legitimate stratagem of love, after which Don Quixote and Sancho travel on to the mouth of the Cave of Montesinos, where Don Quixote is lowered by rope and, on being hauled back up asleep, wakes reporting a rapturous vision he has not yet recounted.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Camacho's Wedding, Basilio's Stratagem, and the Descent into the Cave of Montesinos
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Camacho's Wedding, Basilio's Stratagem, and the Descent into the Cave of Montesinos

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote recounts an elaborate, dreamlike descent into the Cave of Montesinos before a skeptical Sancho and cousin, after which Cide Hamete's own marginal doubt, a soldier-boy's meditation on a good death, the tall tale of the braying towns, and the arrival of Master Pedro's divining ape all keep circling back to the same unresolved question of what, in this narrative, can be believed.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Cave of Montesinos and the Question of What Can Be Believed
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Cave of Montesinos and the Question of What Can Be Believed

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote's chivalric literalism destroys Master Pedro's puppet show and provokes a beating in the braying-town affair, after which Cervantes reveals Master Pedro as the fraud Gines de Pasamonte, Sancho needles Quixote into a comic reckoning over wages and the twenty-years-delayed island, and the pair's "enchanted bark" on the Ebro turns out to be a rowboat wrecked on an ordinary mill-wheel.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Puppets, Brays, and the Enchanted Bark: Chapters XXVI–XXIX
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Puppets, Brays, and the Enchanted Bark: Chapters XXVI–XXIX

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote and Sancho arrive at the country estate of a duke and duchess who, having read Part I of the history, stage an elaborate mock-chivalric reception to amuse themselves, provoking a censorious ecclesiastic's attack on Don Quixote's madness and Don Quixote's dignified self-defense, while Sancho is promised an island and twice rebels against degrading "washing" ceremonies.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Don Quixote at the Duke and Duchess's Castle
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Don Quixote at the Duke and Duchess's Castle

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: In private conversation the duchess draws out Sancho's confession that he invented Dulcinea's enchantment, and the duke and duchess then convert that confession into an elaborate hunting-ground spectacle in which a costumed "Merlin" decrees that only 3,300 self-administered lashes from Sancho can disenchant Dulcinea, a penance Sancho haggles down to a countable, consensual transaction before Trifaldin arrives to herald the next contrived adventure, the Distressed Duenna.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Manufactured Disenchantment of Dulcinea
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Manufactured Disenchantment of Dulcinea

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: The Countess Trifaldi delivers her elaborate, self-interrupting tale of the bearded duennas before the Duke and Duchess's court, and Don Quixote and Sancho then "fly" on the wooden horse Clavileño to a staged, fireworks-punctuated non-adventure that the aristocratic hosts have engineered purely for their own entertainment.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Trifaldi's Tale and the Flight of Clavileño
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Trifaldi's Tale and the Flight of Clavileño

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote delivers two sets of counsels—spiritual and bodily—to Sancho before his departure to govern the isle of Barataria, after which Sancho arrives, endures Altisidora's mock love-serenade heard by Don Quixote, and takes up the governor's seat, where he issues three shrewd, proverb-flavored judgments (the hidden gold-crowns, the extorted purse, and the five caps) that confound expectations of his folly.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Don Quixote's Counsels and Sancho's First Judgments as Governor
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Don Quixote's Counsels and Sancho's First Judgments as Governor

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: A cruel practical joke of bells and cats mauls Don Quixote in the duke's castle, and the scene shifts to Sancho Panza's first hours as governor of Barataria, where a starvation-inducing court physician and a grotesque farmer's petition expose the comic absurdity of instant, unearned power.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Cat Fright and the First Trials of Sancho's Government
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Cat Fright and the First Trials of Sancho's Government

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote's midnight standoff with the weeping duenna Doña Rodriguez, whose family history exposes the duke's household as a place where money buys impunity and cruelty is staged as sport, gives way to Sancho's night rounds as governor, in which his proverb-driven rulings on a gambling dispute and a cross-dressed brother and sister reveal a shrewd, humane justice undercut by his own conventional moralizing.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Duenna's Grievance and the Governor's Rounds
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Duenna's Grievance and the Governor's Rounds

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: The duchess and Altisidora are revealed as the 'enchanters' who tormented Don Quixote and flogged Doña Rodriguez out of wounded vanity, the duke's page delivers gifts and letters that turn Teresa and Sanchica's heads with fantasies of rank, and Sancho proves an unexpectedly wise governor by resolving a liar's-paradox lawsuit through equity and absorbing Don Quixote's mirror-of-princes advice, even as hunger and a second aggrieved duenna signal that both his government and his master's idyll are running out.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Enchanters Unmasked, Teresa Panza's Letters, and Sancho's Rule of Mercy
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Enchanters Unmasked, Teresa Panza's Letters, and Sancho's Rule of Mercy

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Sancho's governorship of Barataria collapses in a staged mock-siege that leaves him bruised and disabused of ambition, and on the road back to Don Quixote he meets the exiled Morisco Ricote, falls into an underground pit, and is rescued, before the unit closes with Don Quixote's near-duel against the duke's lacquey Tosilos.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Fall of Barataria, Ricote's Exile, and the Sham Duel
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Fall of Barataria, Ricote's Exile, and the Sham Duel

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote leaves the ducal castle amid Altisidora's mock love-lament, delivers a set-piece on freedom, is trampled by a herd of bulls after rashly vowing to defend some masquerading shepherdesses' beauty, and at a roadside inn overhears two strangers discussing Avellaneda's spurious sequel, provoking him to divert his route to Barcelona to disprove the impostor's account of him.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Leaving the Castle: Freedom, Folly, and the False Don Quixote
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Leaving the Castle: Freedom, Folly, and the False Don Quixote

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Escorted by the bandit-captain Roque Guinart through the Catalan hills toward Barcelona, Don Quixote witnesses Roque's rough but scrupulous justice and the tragic murder-suicide of Claudia Jeronima before entering the city to a hero's welcome staged around his status as the 'true' Don Quixote against the spurious Avellaneda sequel, culminating in Don Antonio Moreno's mechanical 'enchanted head' hoax.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Roque Guinart's Mountains and the Talking Head of Barcelona
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Roque Guinart's Mountains and the Talking Head of Barcelona

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: In Barcelona, the captured Morisco corsair Ana Félix reveals her forced-exile family history and her father Ricote's paradoxical defense of the Moorish expulsion, before Don Quixote is unhorsed and disenchanted of his knighthood by the Knight of the White Moon, who turns out to be his neighbor Samson Carrasco in disguise.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Ana Félix's Exile and the Fall of Don Quixote
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Ana Félix's Exile and the Fall of Don Quixote

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: On the road home after his defeat, Don Quixote proposes a pastoral retirement with Sancho, the pair are trampled by a drove of pigs and later abducted to the duke's castle, where they are forced to endure a staged catafalque ceremony in which Sancho's whipped face and pinched arms supposedly resurrect the feigned-dead Altisidora, whose plot is then revealed as Samson Carrasco's and the duke's joint contrivance.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Pastoral Dreams, a Pig Stampede, and Altisidora's Staged Resurrection
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Pastoral Dreams, a Pig Stampede, and Altisidora's Staged Resurrection

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Don Quixote and Sancho journey home through the comic bargaining over Sancho's disenchantment-whipping and a metafictional encounter with a character from Avellaneda's spurious sequel, and the unit closes with Don Quixote's fever, his sudden recovery of sanity as Alonso Quixano the Good, his will, and his peaceful Christian death, followed by Cide Hamete Benengeli's valedictory address to his pen.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: Homecoming, the Rival Knight, and the Death of Alonso Quixano
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: Homecoming, the Rival Knight, and the Death of Alonso Quixano

commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.summary: Cervantes dedicates the finished Second Part to his patron the Count of Lemos with a wry anecdote about a Chinese emperor's invitation, then in the preface answers the spurious Avellaneda "Second Part" with wounded pride, two comic dog parables about the ease of criticizing books, and a promise to kill Don Quixote off for good so no counterfeit continuation can follow.
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.term: The Dedication to the Count of Lemos and the Author's Preface to Part II
commons/reading/cervantes-don-quixote/ce.title: The Dedication to the Count of Lemos and the Author's Preface to Part II

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: The horse's early relationship with humans on the Eurasian steppe moved through distinct, archaeologically reconstructible stages -- hunting, corralling, milking, and finally riding -- each deepening an entanglement that remained, even so, only ever superficially domesticated.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: Horse and Herder: The Making of the Steppe Partnership
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Horse and Herder: The Making of the Steppe Partnership

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: The chariot and then the mounted, gelded, bow-armed horse transformed steppe herders' low-status animal into the era's decisive weapon, remaking warfare and the balance of power between steppe and settled empires from the Bronze Age into the Scythian cavalry revolution.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: Horses for Heroes: From Chariots to Mounted Archers
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Horses for Heroes: From Chariots to Mounted Archers

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: Horse power builds and unmakes the first great Eurasian empires as Assyria's cavalry dependence on the horse-breeding Medes gives way to Cyrus's Persia, which institutionalizes state-run horse breeding to escape steppe dependence, while Mauryan India develops a parallel but geographically constrained cavalry tradition set against the rival power of the elephant, all shadowed by an enduring, unresolved rivalry with mounted steppe nomads like the Scythians.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Engines of Empire

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: China's chronic inability to breed its own quality warhorses forced a centuries-long dependency on steppe suppliers, a dependency that the Huns under Modun turned into history's first steppe empire, culminating in Emperor Wudi's costly expedition for the legendary blood-sweating horses of Ferghana.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: Heavenly Horses and the Birth of the Steppe Empire
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Heavenly Horses and the Birth of the Steppe Empire

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: The Yuezhi's flight from the Huns seeds the Kushan Empire, whose horse-breeding, caravan, and fair economy across China and India was in fact the dominant Eurasian trade system that the later, silk-centered name "Silk Road" obscures.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Silk Road or Horse Road

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: Under the Tang dynasty, mastery of horses became simultaneously a bureaucratic-military project of unprecedented scale and a spiritual, artistic, and courtly obsession shared across Turks, Iranians, and Arabs, until the An Lushan rebellion of 755 shattered the system that sustained it.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: The Tang Horse Cult: Hard Power and Soft Power on Hooves
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: The Tang Horse Cult: Hard Power and Soft Power on Hooves

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: The hunt, refined on the steppe into the mass encirclement tactic called the nerge or battue, doubled as war-college training that let Eurasian horse-breeding peoples like the Khitans, Seljuks, and Ghaznavids convert hunting bands into conquest states across China, Iran, Anatolia, and India after the Tang collapse.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Hunting for Supremacy

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: Genghis Khan converts the steppe's chronic surplus of geldings and its cyclical raid-and-retreat pattern of conquest into a permanent, disciplined empire, and the horse-pasture logistics that made this possible also set the hard ecological limits that eventually broke it in China while letting it endure in Iran and the Golden Horde.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire of Grass
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire of Grass

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: From Timur's death-interrupted invasion of Ming China through Babur, Akbar, and the Mughal emperors to Nader Shah's ruinous sack of Delhi and Ahmad Shah Durrani's rise, the chapter traces three centuries of Eurasian mounted conquest as a self-consuming cycle in which horse power both compels rulers to endless campaigning and, in the end, bankrupts them.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Riding the Whirlwind

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: Eighteenth-century Qing China and Muscovite Russia each finally overpower and absorb their steppe horse-breeding neighbors, closing the two-thousand-year era of independent nomadic horse power on the eastern and western steppe.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: The Steppe Closes: Qing China and Russia's Conquest of the Horse Frontier
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: The Steppe Closes: Qing China and Russia's Conquest of the Horse Frontier

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: The eighteenth-century collapse of Mughal power touched off a scramble among Indian horse powers (Marathas, Afghans, Sikhs) that the cavalry-poor British ultimately won through money and diplomacy rather than horseflesh, setting up a century-long, horse-starved Anglo-Russian Great Game across Central Asia that climaxed in the Qing bannermen's defeat by sea powers and Russia's brutal conquest of the last independent Turkmen horse breeders.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: The Great Game: India's Horse Powers and the Scramble for Central Asia
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: The Great Game: India's Horse Powers and the Scramble for Central Asia

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: In the decades before and during World War I, Russian and British colonial breeding schemes to industrialize Central Asian and Indian horse stock repeatedly failed against local practice and ecology, even as both empires staged their largest-ever cavalry forces and pageantry, only for airpower and petroleum to render horse power strategically obsolete within a single generation.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: The Last Horse Powers: Breeding Failures, Imperial Pageantry, and the Petroleum Transition
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: The Last Horse Powers: Breeding Failures, Imperial Pageantry, and the Petroleum Transition

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: The book closes at a 1950s-60s royal buzkashi match in Kabul, using King Zaher Shah's staging of the anarchic steppe horse-game as national spectacle to frame how twentieth-century Soviet collectivization, Iranian state-building, and imperial border-closing crushed Central Asian pastoral horse culture everywhere except Afghanistan, which became its last refuge.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: Epilogue: The Last Refuge of the Horse
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: Epilogue: The Last Refuge of the Horse

commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.summary: A personal visit to a Mongolian yurt camp frames the book's thesis that the domestication and riding of the horse, more than any other technology, drove the rise and interaction of Eurasian empires from prehistory to the twentieth century.
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.term: The Horse as the Engine of Eurasian History
commons/reading/chaffetz-raiders-rulers-.title: The Horse as the Engine of Eurasian History

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A dreamer, having spent a day absorbed in Cicero's account of the Dream of Scipio, is led by the elder Scipio through a garden and Temple of Venus to Nature's parliament of birds on Saint Valentine's Day, where three tercel eagles plead in courtly rhetoric for a peerless formel eagle, the lower birds erupt into comic squabbling over the dispute, and Nature resolves the impasse by granting the formel a year's respite and the free choice of her own mate.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Assembly of Fowls (The Parliament of Fowls)
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Assembly of Fowls (The Parliament of Fowls)

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A Canon and his soot-stained Yeoman gallop up to overtake Chaucer's pilgrims, and once the ashamed Canon flees mid-conversation, the Yeoman confesses seven ruinous years of practicing alchemy before narrating how a fraudulent canon fleeces a credulous London priest with rigged demonstrations of transmuting quicksilver into silver, closing with a moral verdict that the philosopher's stone is unattainable because God has reserved its secret to himself.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Canon's Yeoman's Prologue and Tale: Confession of an Alchemical Fraud
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Canon's Yeoman's Prologue and Tale: Confession of an Alchemical Fraud

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A dream-vision poem of disputed Chaucerian authorship allegorizes a knight's forced abduction of an isle's queen, her death and miraculous resurrection by a bird bearing a magic herb, and a mass wedding, traditionally read as a coded account of John of Gaunt's marriage to Blanche of Lancaster with the poet's own courtship woven in as a subplot.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Chaucer's Dream
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Chaucer's Dream

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Clerk retells Petrarch's Latin version of the Griselda story (via Boccaccio): a young marquis marries a peasant girl on condition of her total, unquestioning obedience, subjects her for years to escalating staged cruelties — the pretended murder of both her children, a faked papal annulment, and public repudiation — before revealing it was all a test of her constancy, only for Chaucer's own closing envoy to mockingly reverse the tale's ostensible moral by urging wives never to imitate her.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Clerk's Tale: Griselda's Patience and Chaucer's Ironic Envoy
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Clerk's Tale: Griselda's Patience and Chaucer's Ironic Envoy

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Cook, Roger of Ware, banters with the Host and Reeve before telling of Perkin Revellour, a dancing, dice-mad London apprentice whose riotous living finally gets him dismissed and packed off to live with a comrade and his prostitute wife — at which point the tale, notoriously, breaks off unfinished.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Cook's Prologue and the Unfinished Tale of Perkin Revellour
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Cook's Prologue and the Unfinished Tale of Perkin Revellour

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A Cambridge clerk called Philogenet is summoned by Mercury before the King and Queen of Love, sworn under a codified oath to twenty binding Statutes of Love, and wins the favor of the lady Rosial, in a dream-vision poem of disputed Chaucerian authorship that closes with a choir of birds parodying the Latin Matins in praise of Cupid.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Court of Love
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Court of Love

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A dreamer overhears a debate between a scornful Cuckoo and a devoted Nightingale over whether Love is a blessing or a curse, sides with the Nightingale by stoning the Cuckoo away, and the birds resolve to refer the quarrel to a parliament to be held under a maple at Woodstock the morrow after Saint Valentine's Day.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Cuckoo and the Nightingale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Cuckoo and the Nightingale

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A judge's lust for a beautiful, virtuous girl corrupts the machinery of law itself, and her father kills her with her own consent rather than surrender her to a false judgment.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Doctor's Tale: Virginia and the Corrupt Judge
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Doctor's Tale: Virginia and the Corrupt Judge

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: D. Laing Purves's editorial preface to his combined Victorian popular edition of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales and Spenser's Faerie Queene explains and defends his method of modernizing spelling, abridging prose and epic bulk, and rehabilitating Chaucer's reputation for a mass nineteenth-century readership.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Purves's Preface: Popularizing Chaucer and Spenser for the General Reader
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Purves's Preface: Popularizing Chaucer and Spenser for the General Reader

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In a dream-vision spring allegory (likely a later imitation rather than Chaucer's own work), a sleepless gentlewoman watches two courtly companies — knights and ladies of the Leaf, who are scorched by sun and battered by storm yet endure, and knights and ladies of the Flower, whose beauty withers at the first heat and rain — and learns from a lady in white that the Leaf signifies enduring virtue and perseverance in honour, while the Flower signifies fleeting pleasure and idle beauty.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Flower and the Leaf
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Flower and the Leaf

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In Chaucer's Franklin's Tale, a knight and his wife found their marriage on mutual freedom rather than mastery, and when the wife's rash promise to a lovesick squire is made good by an astrologer's illusion, three men in turn outdo one another in acts of unrewarded generosity, ending in an open question about which was 'most free.'
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Franklin's Tale: Troth, Mastery, and the Contest of Gentillesse
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Franklin's Tale: Troth, Mastery, and the Contest of Gentillesse

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In the Friar's Tale, a corrupt ecclesiastical summoner who extorts money from sinners under threat of church prosecution swears brotherhood with a devil disguised as a fellow bailiff, learns from him that a curse only takes effect if meant in earnest, and is dragged bodily to hell when an old widow he tries to swindle damns him with genuine sincerity.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Friar's Tale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Friar's Tale

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Chaucer's General Prologue frames a spring pilgrimage to Canterbury as the occasion for a storytelling contest, then catalogues the roughly thirty pilgrims — knight, squire, prioress, monk, friar, merchant, clerk, lawyer, franklin, guildsmen, cook, shipman, doctor, wife of Bath, parson, ploughman, miller, manciple, reeve, summoner, and pardoner — as a cross-section of English estates ranging from idealized virtue to open venality.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A dreamer borne aloft in a golden eagle's claws visits the ice-built House of Fame, where a monstrous, ever-changing goddess grants or denies renown to nine successive companies of petitioners with no regard for their actual deserts, and then the neighboring whirling House of Rumour, where every tiding on earth arrives, mutates mouth to mouth, and flies back out into the world, before the unfinished poem breaks off at the sight of "a man of great authority."
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The House of Fame
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The House of Fame

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Duke Theseus of Athens conquers Thebes to avenge grieving widows, takes the cousins Palamon and Arcite captive, and must arbitrate when their sworn brotherhood shatters into rivalry over his sister-in-law Emily, resolving the feud not with more bloodshed but with a decreed hundred-a-side tournament a year hence.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Knight's Tale (Part One): Theseus, Fortune, and the Rivalry of Palamon and Arcite
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Knight's Tale (Part One): Theseus, Fortune, and the Rivalry of Palamon and Arcite

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Theseus completes the lists at Athens with three temples to Venus, Mars, and Diana whose grim iconography previews the outcome, then stages a rule-bound tournament between Palamon and Arcite for Emily's hand that Arcite wins by combat but loses by a Saturn-sent accident, dying after commending Palamon to Emily, after which Theseus's First Mover oration reframes the death within a providential cosmic order and marries Palamon to Emily.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Knight's Tale, Part 2: The Lists, the Tournament, and the First Mover
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Knight's Tale, Part 2: The Lists, the Tournament, and the First Mover

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In a May dream-vision, Chaucer is arraigned by the God of Love for writing Troilus and Criseyde and translating the Romance of the Rose as slanders against women, and is pardoned only through the intercession of Alcestis, who imposes as penance the writing of a legendary of good women.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Prologue to the Legend of Good Women
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Prologue to the Legend of Good Women

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: An editorial biography reconstructs Geoffrey Chaucer's life from court, customs, and pension records — his birth, marriages, diplomatic missions to Italy, patronage under John of Gaunt, and precarious civil-service fortunes tied to Lancaster-Gloucester factional strife — before laying out the scope, frame narrative, and textual conventions of The Canterbury Tales.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Life of Geoffrey Chaucer
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Life of Geoffrey Chaucer

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In his Prologue the Man of Law debates the theft of time, the miseries of poverty, and his own literary debts before telling of Constance, the Roman emperor's daughter, who is twice married into foreign courts and twice set adrift on a rudderless ship by the schemes of two murderous, order-defending mothers-in-law, her serial survival offered throughout as proof that Christian providence, not the stars or Fortune, governs human affairs.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Man of Law's Prologue and Tale: Constance Adrift
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Man of Law's Prologue and Tale: Constance Adrift

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Manciple silences the drunk, swaying Cook with a trick gourd of wine, then tells the classical fable of Phoebus's speaking white crow, whose truthful report of the god's wife's infidelity gets it blackened and struck dumb — a story the Manciple turns into a long proverbial sermon on the danger of any speech, true or false.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Manciple's Prologue and Tale: The Cook's Gourd, Phoebus's Crow, and the Peril of Speech
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Manciple's Prologue and Tale: The Cook's Gourd, Phoebus's Crow, and the Peril of Speech

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In this fabliau, a cynical Merchant tells of old January, who marries young May, imprisons her behind a walled garden he alone can unlock, goes blind from jealousy's own working, and is out-argued by his wife (with Proserpina's coaching) when a counterfeited key lets Damian cuckold him in a pear tree in plain sight.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Merchant's Tale: The Walled Garden and the Counterfeited Key
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Merchant's Tale: The Walled Garden and the Counterfeited Key

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A drunken miller shoulders his way ahead of the tale-telling order to tell a bawdy Oxford fabliau in which a clerk-lodger's astrology becomes the instrument of a doomsday hoax that gets a jealous carpenter out of the way, only for the seduction to end in a rival suitor's misdirected kiss and a red-hot coulter's revenge.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Miller's Tale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Miller's Tale

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: This closing unit of the volume gathers Chaucer's short, miscellaneous poems—the Marian acrostic prayer known as the A.B.C., courtly ballades to an unnamed lady, the moral complaint 'Lak of Stedfastnesse' addressed to Richard II, comic verse-letters to Bukton and to his own empty purse, the philosophical retreat-poem 'Truth,' and a scatter of proverbs, envoys, and an apocalyptic prophecy—several of which the edition's own notes flag as probably not Chaucer's at all.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Chaucer's Shorter Poems: A.B.C., Ballades, Envoys, and the Complaint to His Purse
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Chaucer's Shorter Poems: A.B.C., Ballades, Envoys, and the Complaint to His Purse

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Monk, prodded by the Host's bawdy jab at clerical celibacy, delivers his catalogue of "tragedies" — a de casibus series running from Lucifer and Adam through Sampson, Hercules, Nebuchadnezzar, Zenobia, Nero, Holofernes, Antiochus, Alexander, Julius Caesar, Croesus, and on into near-contemporary falls (Pedro of Castile, Petro of Cyprus, Bernabò Visconti, Ugolino of Pisa) — each figure raised to greatness only to be broken by Fortune's wheel.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Monk's Tale: The Catalogue of Fortune's Falls
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Monk's Tale: The Catalogue of Fortune's Falls

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A dreaming rooster's fear of a fox becomes the occasion for a mock-heroic beast fable that mounts a full scholastic debate on dream-prophecy and free will only to let vanity and flattery, not philosophy, decide the plot.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Chanticleer and the Fox: The Nun's Priest's Tale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Chanticleer and the Fox: The Nun's Priest's Tale

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Host's shaken reaction to the previous tale gives way to the drunken Pardoner's boastful confession of how he fleeces congregations with fake relics and a stock avarice sermon, followed by his "moral tale" of three Flemish revelers whose quest to kill Death ends in their killing each other over a hoard of gold, after which the frame resumes with the Pardoner trying to sell his relics to the pilgrims and provoking the Host's obscene rebuff.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Pardoner's Prologue and Tale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Pardoner's Prologue and Tale

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Parson refuses to tell a "fable" and instead delivers (in this Purves edition, heavily abridged) a prose penitential treatise on Contrition, Confession, and Satisfaction — complete with a vision of hell's torments, a survey of the Seven Deadly Sins anchored by a furious attack on fashionable dress as the outward sign of Pride — after which Chaucer appends his own closing prayer retracting his secular works and ending the whole Canterbury Tales.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Parson's Tale: Penitence Replaces the "Tale," and Chaucer Retracts
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Parson's Tale: Penitence Replaces the "Tale," and Chaucer Retracts

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Chaucer's Prioress narrates a Marian miracle legend in which a devout seven-year-old "litel clergeon" is murdered by Jews in a walled Jewery for singing a hymn to the Virgin in their midst, and continues to sing miraculously after his throat is cut until an abbot removes a grain the Virgin placed on his tongue, the tale closing with an invocation of the historical child-martyr Hugh of Lincoln.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Prioress's Tale: The Boy-Martyr of the Jewery
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Prioress's Tale: The Boy-Martyr of the Jewery

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Stung by the Miller's tale of a cuckolded carpenter, the aging Reeve Oswald delivers a bitter prologue on desire outliving the body, then tells a fabliau in which two Cambridge clerks avenge a thieving miller's grain-fraud by sleeping with his wife and daughter in one chaotic, dark-room night, leaving him beaten, cuckolded, and still out his stolen meal.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Reeve's Prologue and Tale: Age, Grudge, and the Miller Beguiled
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Reeve's Prologue and Tale: Age, Grudge, and the Miller Beguiled

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Chaucer's Second Nun translates the Legenda Aurea life of Saint Cecilia, who converts her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburce through visions of an angel, then out-argues and outlasts the Roman prefect Almachius before dying a slow three-day martyrdom in her own bath-turned-execution-chamber.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Second Nun's Tale: The Legend of Saint Cecilia
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Second Nun's Tale: The Legend of Saint Cecilia

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: A Saint-Denis merchant's wife, short a hundred francs for her finery, secretly borrows the sum from a visiting monk who poses as the merchant's "cousin," repays him with a night in bed, and when the merchant later asks the monk for his own loan back, the monk claims he already repaid it to the wife in cash — leaving her to settle the debt with her husband the same way she settled it with the monk.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Shipman's Prologue and Tale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Shipman's Prologue and Tale

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Host teases the pilgrim Chaucer for his aloof, portly, 'elvish' bearing and demands a tale, and Chaucer answers with a deliberately terrible tail-rhyme romance about the diminutive knight Sir Thopas, piling up threadbare chivalric clichés and small category-errors of convention until the story breaks off mid-clause partway through its Second Fit.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Prologue and Tale of Sir Thopas (First and Second Fits)
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Prologue and Tale of Sir Thopas (First and Second Fits)

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In revenge for the Friar's tale, the Sompnour tells a fabliau of a hypocritical mendicant friar who fleeces a bedridden parishioner while preaching against wrath, is repaid with a monstrous fart, and is then mocked further when a lord's squire "proves," in a parody of scholastic demonstration, how the fart's sound and stink can be divided equally among the friar's whole convent.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Sompnour's Tale: A Friar's Comeuppance
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Sompnour's Tale: A Friar's Comeuppance

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Chaucer's unfinished romance opens at Cambuscan's Tartar court with a mysterious knight's gift of four marvels — a brass horse, a truth-revealing mirror, a language-granting ring, and a wounding-and-healing sword — then pivots to Canace's rescue of a peregrine falcon whose confession exposes a courtly lover's practiced hypocrisy.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Squire's Tale: Marvels of Sarra and the Falcon's Lament
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Squire's Tale: Marvels of Sarra and the Falcon's Lament

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In the abridged Tale of Melibee, a wronged man's wife Prudence out-argues his impulse toward vengeance for the assault on their household, walking him step by step from rage through a review of good and bad counsel to a negotiated peace and formal act of mercy toward his attackers.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Tale of Melibee: Prudence Talks Her Husband Out of War
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Tale of Melibee: Prudence Talks Her Husband Out of War

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: An editorial headnote frames Chaucer's Troilus and Cressida as his most finished and morally elevated poem before Book One itself begins, narrating how Troilus, having scorned Love's servants, is struck by love at first sight of the widowed Cressida in the temple of Pallas and, after much secret suffering, confesses his passion to her uncle Pandarus, who resolves to help him win her.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Troilus and Cressida: Editor's Preface and the First Book
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Troilus and Cressida: Editor's Preface and the First Book

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Pandarus visits his niece Cressida, argues and maneuvers her from resistance to receptive interest in Troilus, and by the book's end has engineered — through a dream, a letter campaign, and a staged dinner at Deiphobus's house — the private meeting at which Troilus must finally speak his love.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Troilus and Criseyde, Book II: Pandarus's Persuasion
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Troilus and Criseyde, Book II: Pandarus's Persuasion

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: Pandarus's carefully engineered plot succeeds: Troilus and Criseyde are brought together, first at Deiphebus's house where Troilus haltingly declares himself, then at Pandarus's rain-swept house where the lovers are secretly united in body, an episode framed by a cosmic hymn to Venus, an aubade cursing the coming day, and Troilus's Boethian song praising Love as the force that binds the universe.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Troilus and Criseyde, Book III: Pandarus's Engineered Union
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Troilus and Criseyde, Book III: Pandarus's Engineered Union

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Trojan parliament votes to trade Cressida for the captured Antenor over Hector's objection, driving Troilus to near-suicidal grief, prompting Pandarus's cynical counsel to simply love another and a long Boethian excursus on predestination versus free will, before the lovers meet by night, exchange desperate vows, and Cressida overrules Troilus's plan to flee together, promising instead to return within ten nights.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Troilus and Criseyde, Book IV: The Exchange of Cressida and the Lovers' Parting
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Troilus and Criseyde, Book IV: The Exchange of Cressida and the Lovers' Parting

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: In the final book of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde, Criseyde is exchanged to the Greek camp and gradually succumbs to Diomede's courtship, abandoning Troilus, who—devastated by proof of her infidelity—dies in battle and ascends to the eighth sphere to look down in contempt on the vanity of earthly love, as the poet closes by renouncing pagan love for Christian devotion.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: Troilus and Criseyde, Book Five: The Exchange, the Betrayal, and the Death of Troilus
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: Troilus and Criseyde, Book Five: The Exchange, the Betrayal, and the Death of Troilus

commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.summary: The Wife of Bath defends her five marriages and her mastery over each husband in a long autobiographical prologue, then tells an Arthurian tale in which a knight who has raped a maiden is spared only if he can answer what women most desire, and the answer — sovereignty — is what redeems him.
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.term: The Wife of Bath's Prologue and Tale
commons/reading/chaucer-canterbury-tales.title: The Wife of Bath's Prologue and Tale

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Roger Crowley traces Venice's ascent from a marginal, self-governing lagoon settlement into the acknowledged master of the Adriatic, anchored by Doge Pietro Orseolo II's year-1000 campaign against Narentine pirates and by Venice's slow climb within the Byzantine trading system from subject to indispensable-but-resented monopolist, sealed by the Golden Bull of 1082.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Lords of Dalmatia
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Lords of Dalmatia

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In 1201 Venice negotiates and quietly weaponizes the Treaty of Venice — a fully monetized, quantified transport contract for the Fourth Crusade brokered by the elderly, blind Doge Enrico Dandolo — turning a papal call to holy war into a commercial gamble with a concealed target: Egypt, not Jerusalem.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Blind Doge and the Treaty of Venice
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Blind Doge and the Treaty of Venice

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Venice mobilizes its entire economy under contract to build, crew, and provision a fleet for the Fourth Crusade, but when only a third of the promised crusaders arrive and cannot pay the agreed price, the blind ninety-year-old Doge Enrico Dandolo saves the deal — and Venice's solvency — by deferring the debt in exchange for the crusade's first strike falling not on the Holy Land but on the rebel Christian city of Zara, then personally taking the cross to bind the fractured alliance together.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Broken Contract of 1202: Venice, the Fourth Crusade, and the Road to Zara
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Broken Contract of 1202: Venice, the Fourth Crusade, and the Road to Zara

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Venice's Doge Enrico Dandolo leverages the Fourth Crusade's crushing debt to the Republic to redirect the expedition first into sacking the Christian city of Zara and then, via a cynical bargain with the pretender Alexius Angelus, toward Constantinople, all while Pope Innocent III's repeated excommunications are suppressed, ignored, or evaded by the crusade's leadership.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: 'A Dog Returning to its Vomit'
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: 'A Dog Returning to its Vomit'

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In June–August 1203 the Venetian-led Fourth Crusade fleet arrives before Constantinople, forces the Golden Horn by amphibious and naval assault after Doge Enrico Dandolo personally leads the beach landing, burns a swath of the city, and topples the complacent Emperor Alexius III, restoring the blinded Isaac II and crowning his son Alexius IV as a financially indebted puppet.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Fourth Crusade at the Walls of Constantinople
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Fourth Crusade at the Walls of Constantinople

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Constantinople is devastated by a catastrophic fire set by Venetian, Pisan, and crusader looters, and in the ensuing five months Byzantine authority disintegrates through failed payments, mob violence, and a palace coup, leaving four rival emperors in the city before the crusaders manufacture a theological pretext to storm it outright.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Four Emperors: Fire, Betrayal, and the Collapse of Byzantine Legitimacy
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Four Emperors: Fire, Betrayal, and the Collapse of Byzantine Legitimacy

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In April 1204 a second Venetian-Frankish assault finally breaches the sea walls of Constantinople, collapsing Byzantine resistance within hours and unleashing a three-day sack of unprecedented savagery, after which Venice — having prearranged the terms of conquest and outlasted every rival claimant — emerges with an empire it never set out to win.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Sack of Constantinople, 1204
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Sack of Constantinople, 1204

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: After the Fourth Crusade's 1204 partition of Byzantium, Venice converts its share — a merchant's precise "Quarter and Half a Quarter" of the empire — into the Stato da Mar, a lean network of ports, chokepoints, and semi-privatized colonies rather than a territorial state, while draping the new power in captured Byzantine ceremony.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Quarter and Half a Quarter: Venice Builds an Empire of the Sea
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Quarter and Half a Quarter: Venice Builds an Empire of the Sea

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Traces the escalating Venice–Genoa commercial rivalry from the 1256–1258 War of Saint Sabas at Acre through the Genoese-brokered Byzantine recapture of Constantinople in 1261 and the thirteenth-century boom in grain and spice, to the Mamluk destruction of Acre in 1291, which ended the crusader footholds and redirected the two republics' contest toward the Bosphorus and Black Sea.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Genoese Wars and the Economics of Empire, 1250–1291
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Genoese Wars and the Economics of Empire, 1250–1291

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Between the fall of Acre (1291) and the Black Death's eruption in Venice (1348), Venetian and Genoese rivalry for the Black Sea's Mongol-opened trade routes escalates through open war and precarious diplomacy at outposts like Tana and Caffa, until the 1345-46 Mongol siege of Caffa seeds the plague that annihilates roughly two-thirds of Venice's population and permanently darkens its mercantile culture.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Black Sea Emporium: Venice, Genoa, and the Road to the Black Death
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Black Sea Emporium: Venice, Genoa, and the Road to the Black Death

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Between 1348 and 1368 Venice fights a third inconclusive naval war with Genoa over the Black Sea trade while its Ottoman rivals quietly gain a permanent foothold in Europe, and then nearly loses its most vital colony when Crete's own Venetian-born landowning class rises against the mother city in the four-year Revolt of St Titus.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Flag of St Titus
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Flag of St Titus

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: A dispute over precedence at a Cypriot coronation escalates through contests over Black Sea access and the island of Tenedos into the War of Chioggia, in which Venice's fleet is nearly destroyed at Pola, Genoese and allied land forces seize Chioggia at the edge of the lagoon, and the city survives only through total civilian mobilization and a popular revolt that frees the disgraced admiral Vettor Pisani from prison to lead its last-ditch defense.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Bridling St Mark
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Bridling St Mark

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Besieged and starving in the winter of 1379–80, Venice reverses the War of Chioggia by sealing the Genoese fleet inside the lagoon town it had captured, and after ten months of amphibious siege-warfare, near-mutiny, and Carlo Zeno's near-fatal wound, starves Chioggia into unconditional surrender, a victory the author attributes to institutional durability rather than martial superiority.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Siege of Chioggia: Fight to the Finish
