commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Siege of Chioggia: Fight to the Finish

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In the half-century after the Chioggia war (1381), Venice rebuilt and vastly expanded its maritime empire, the Stato da Mar, through a pragmatic mix of purchase, diplomacy, and force, then ran it as a minutely documented, ruthlessly audited extractive system that replicated Venetian institutions across the eastern Mediterranean.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Stato da Mar: Venice's Second Wave of Maritime Empire, 1381–1425
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Stato da Mar: Venice's Second Wave of Maritime Empire, 1381–1425

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Between 1425 and 1500 Venice perfected a tightly regulated, state-run system of galley convoys (the muda), fondaco compounds, and patient diplomacy that let it out-compete Genoa and dominate the Levant spice trade, turning the Rialto into the transaction point of a world market stretching from China to the North Sea.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Like Water in a Fountain: Venice's Levant Trade System, 1425–1500
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Like Water in a Fountain: Venice's Levant Trade System, 1425–1500

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In 1500, at the moment Jacopo de' Barbari's triumphant bird's-eye map proclaims Venice's mastery of the sea, the reality behind the image is anatomized: a proto-industrial state arsenal, a dense body of maritime law, and eyewitness pilgrim accounts of galley life and storms reveal both the machine's disciplined power and its human cost, even as the chapter's close reveals the Stato da Mar was already in hidden decline beneath its most confident self-portrait.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: City of Neptune
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: City of Neptune

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Venice manages the slow, terrifying rise of Ottoman power between the 1416 Battle of Gallipoli and the 1453 fall of Constantinople through a mixture of ruthless naval violence, obsessive intelligence-gathering, and a diplomacy so delicate contemporaries compared it to juggling a glass ball, only to pivot instantly to renewed trade with the victorious Sultan Mehmet II once Byzantium is gone.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Glass Ball: Venice and the Ottoman Ascent, 1400–1453
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Glass Ball: Venice and the Ottoman Ascent, 1400–1453

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In the decade after the fall of Constantinople, Venice becomes the front-line state facing Sultan Mehmet II's relentless expansion, waging a shadow war of espionage and assassination plots even as it fails to rally a fractured, cynical Italy and a moribund papacy into a real crusade.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Shield of Christendom
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Shield of Christendom

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Venice's sixteen-year war with Mehmet II (1463–1479) climaxes in the catastrophic loss of Negroponte through a lawyer-admiral's fatal hesitation, ends in a humiliating peace and the Otranto raid, and closes with Portuguese spies quietly mapping the sea route to India that will render the whole Venetian-Mamluk spice monopoly obsolete.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Long War and the Fall of Negroponte
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Long War and the Fall of Negroponte

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Venetian espionage tracks a two-year Ottoman naval buildup that culminates in the 1499 Battle of Zonchio (Sapienza), where a hesitant, faction-riven Venetian fleet fails to stop the Ottoman armada, the fireball destruction of the corsair Burak Reis's giant carrack becomes the war's signature horror, and the port of Lepanto falls soon after.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Pyramid of Fire: Zonchio and the Fall of Lepanto, 1498–1499
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Pyramid of Fire: Zonchio and the Fall of Lepanto, 1498–1499

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Between 1500 and 1503 Venice absorbs a double blow — catastrophic Ottoman conquests of Modon and Coron following the Lepanto debacle, and the far more durable shock of Vasco da Gama's Cape route to India, which together force the Republic into a peace of vassalage in the east and a pivot from sea to Terra Firma.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: The Double Shock: Ottoman Conquest and the Portuguese Sea Route (1500–1503)
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: The Double Shock: Ottoman Conquest and the Portuguese Sea Route (1500–1503)

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: In the short epilogue to City of Fortune, Crowley closes the book at the 1669 fall of Venetian Crete and traces the two-century unraveling of the Stato da Mar, then pivots from imperial ruin to the intimate motif of "return" — the pull Venice exerted on the merchants, sailors, and officials who scattered across its sea empire and came home.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Return: The Fall of Venetian Crete and the Idea of Homecoming
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Return: The Fall of Venetian Crete and the Idea of Homecoming

commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.summary: Petrarch's 1363 eyewitness account of a merchant galley departing Venice opens Roger Crowley's prologue, which frames Venice as a landless, resourceless "virtual economy" whose entire civic and psychological life was organized around the sea and trade, and which then pivots from that departure to the 1201 arrival of crusading knights that launched the five-century rise of the Stato da Mar.
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.term: Departure: Petrarch's Vision of the Venetian Fleet
commons/reading/crowley-city-of-fortune/.title: Departure: Petrarch's Vision of the Venetian Fleet

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante, lost in a dark wood and blocked by three beasts, is rescued by the shade of Virgil (sent at the intercession of Beatrice, Lucia, and Rachel) and led through the inscribed gate of Hell, past the neutral souls and Charon's crossing, into Limbo among the virtuous pagans, and finally into the second circle, where the whirlwind of the lustful carries Francesca da Rimini, whose account of the love that damned her and Paolo overwhelms him.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Inferno, Cantos I–V: From the Dark Wood to the Circle of Lust
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Inferno, Cantos I–V: From the Dark Wood to the Circle of Lust

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante and Virgil pass through the circles of gluttony, avarice-and-prodigality, and wrath, are refused entry at the walled city of Dis until a heavenly messenger forces the gate, meet the arch-heretics Farinata degli Uberti and Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti among the burning tombs, and finally receive Virgil's systematic taxonomy of all the sins punished in the circles still to come.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Through Gluttony, Avarice, and Wrath to the Gates of Dis
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Through Gluttony, Avarice, and Wrath to the Gates of Dis

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: In Cary's translation, Dante and Virgil cross the three rings of Hell's circle of violence — the river of boiling blood guarded by centaurs, the trackless wood of suicides devoured by Harpies, and the burning sand of blasphemers, sodomites, and usurers (with the Old Man of Crete's allegory and Dante's reunion with Brunetto Latini along the way) — before summoning the fraud-monster Geryon to carry them down toward the eighth circle.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Hell, Cantos XII–XVII: Violence Against Neighbor, Self, and God, and the Descent to Fraud
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Hell, Cantos XII–XVII: Violence Against Neighbor, Self, and God, and the Descent to Fraud

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante and Virgil cross the fraud-pits of Malebolge from the panderers and flatterers through the simoniac popes, the backward-twisted diviners, the pitch-boiled barrators harried by a slapstick company of devils, and into the leaden-gilded hypocrites, where Caiaphas lies crucified underfoot.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Malebolge: From Panderers to Hypocrites (Inferno XVIII–XXIII)
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Malebolge: From Panderers to Hypocrites (Inferno XVIII–XXIII)

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante and Virgil climb into the seventh and eighth chasms of Malebolge, watching serpent-tormented thieves melt and swap bodies before hearing the flame-wrapped Ulysses recount his final forbidden voyage and Guido da Montefeltro recount how a pope's advance absolution damned him for fraudulent counsel.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Thieves, Serpents, and Fraudulent Counselors
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Thieves, Serpents, and Fraudulent Counselors

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante and Virgil cross the eighth and ninth chasms of Malebolge, where sowers of discord (Mohammed, Bertrand de Born) are eternally hacked apart and falsifiers of metal, person, coin, and word (Griffolino, Capocchio, Gianni Schicchi, Myrrha, Master Adam, Sinon) rot with disease, before descending past the giants Nimrod, Ephialtes, and Antaeus into the pit of treachery.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Sowers of Discord and Falsifiers: Malebolge's Ninth Chasm to the Giants' Well (Inf. XXVIII–XXXI)
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Sowers of Discord and Falsifiers: Malebolge's Ninth Chasm to the Giants' Well (Inf. XXVIII–XXXI)

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante and Virgil cross the frozen lake of Cocytus, where traitors to kindred, country, guests, and benefactors lie sealed in ice by degrees of guilt, hearing Count Ugolino's account of starving with his sons in the Tower of Hunger before the poem descends to the three-faced Lucifer chewing Judas, Brutus, and Cassius at the dead center of the universe.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: The Ninth Circle: Traitors in the Ice and the Sight of Lucifer
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: The Ninth Circle: Traitors in the Ice and the Sight of Lucifer

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Guided by Beatrice, Dante ascends past the sphere of fire into the heaven of the Moon, where natural philosophy explains the moon's dark spots and the soul's power to rise, the shade of Piccarda Donati (and the empress Constance) illustrates that perfect blessedness lies in willing what God wills, and Beatrice's long discourse on vows, free will, and violence resolves Dante's doubts before the pair are swept upward into the second heaven, Mercury.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Paradiso I–V: Invocation, the Sphere of the Moon, and the Ascent to Mercury
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Paradiso I–V: Invocation, the Sphere of the Moon, and the Ascent to Mercury

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: In the close of Canto VI and the whole of Cantos VII through X, Justinian narrates the Roman eagle-standard's history and damns both Guelphs and Ghibellines for misusing it, Beatrice resolves the paradox of a just act justly avenged by explaining why God redeemed humanity through the Incarnation and Crucifixion, Charles Martel argues in the sphere of Venus that nature requires a diversity of human vocations that institutions perversely override, Cunizza and Folco speak before Folco denounces Rome's money-corrupted papacy, and Dante ascends into the Sun where Thomas Aquinas introduces the garland of twelve theologian-philosophers.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: The Eagle, the Cross, and the Sun: Paradiso VI (cont.)–X
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: The Eagle, the Cross, and the Sun: Paradiso VI (cont.)–X

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: In the Heaven of the Sun, Thomas Aquinas eulogizes St. Francis while lamenting the Dominican order's decay, Bonaventura mirrors him with a eulogy of St. Dominic and a lament for the Franciscans' decline, Aquinas then explains Solomon's kingly wisdom and warns against rash judgment, and after Beatrice questions the souls about resurrected bodies, Dante ascends to Mars where warrior-souls form a luminous cross around the gleaming figure of Christ.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Paradise, Cantos XI–XIV: Francis, Dominic, and the Ascent to Mars
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Paradise, Cantos XI–XIV: Francis, Dominic, and the Ascent to Mars

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: In the sphere of Mars, Dante's crusader ancestor Cacciaguida praises the austere, close-knit Florence of his own boyhood against the corrupt, swollen city of Dante's day, then delivers a precise prophecy of Dante's coming exile and the Comedy's eventual vindication, before Dante ascends to Jupiter and watches the just souls spell out a call for justice in letters of fire, ending in an eagle's head, while decrying a papacy that wages war with excommunications for gold.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Paradiso XV–XVIII: Cacciaguida's Florence, the Prophecy of Exile, and the Eagle of Justice
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Paradiso XV–XVIII: Cacciaguida's Florence, the Prophecy of Exile, and the Eagle of Justice

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: In the eagle of just rulers formed from the spirits of Jupiter and the golden ladder of contemplatives in Saturn, Dante confronts the limits of human justice, learns that a pagan Trojan (Ripheus) and a pagan Roman emperor (Trajan) sit among the saved, and hears Peter Damian and St. Benedict denounce the corruption of the Church's prelates and monastic orders before he looks back down to see the whole earth reduced to a "petty area."
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: The Eagle of Jupiter and the Ladder of Saturn: Justice, Pagan Salvation, and Institutional Decay
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: The Eagle of Jupiter and the Ladder of Saturn: Justice, Pagan Salvation, and Institutional Decay

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante is examined in turn by Saints Peter, James, and John on the theological virtues of Faith, Hope, and Charity in the Heaven of the Fixed Stars, meets Adam who corrects the legend of the Fall and describes humanity's first vanished language, hears Peter turn red with fury and denounce the corrupted papacy before the pilgrim ascends into the Primum Mobile, and there sees, reflected in Beatrice's eyes, the Point of divine light encircled by nine concentric rings of angels whose order inverts the physical cosmos.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Paradiso XXIII–XXVIII: The Catechism, Peter's Wrath, and the Point of Light
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Paradiso XXIII–XXVIII: The Catechism, Peter's Wrath, and the Point of Light

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Beatrice finishes her discourse on the angels' creation and fall and denounces preachers who trade the Gospel for fables and jests, after which Dante rises into the Empyrean's river of light, beholds the blessed as a vast celestial rose, is handed off from Beatrice to St. Bernard, and through Bernard's prayer to the Virgin Mary receives the poem's closing beatific vision of the triune God.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: The Celestial Rose and the Final Vision: Paradiso XXIX–XXXIII
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: The Celestial Rose and the Final Vision: Paradiso XXIX–XXXIII

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Newly escaped from Hell, Dante and Virgil are received on the shore of Mount Purgatory by its guardian Cato, watch an angel ferry a boatload of souls (including Dante's musician friend Casella) across the sea, and among the late-repentant excommunicate — the slain King Manfred of Sicily and the indolent Belacqua — learn that Purgatory runs on an economy of contrition, intercessory prayer, and patient waiting rather than Hell's fixed decree.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Purgatory, Cantos I–IV: Cato, Casella, and the Late-Repentant on the Mountain's Shore
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Purgatory, Cantos I–IV: Cato, Casella, and the Late-Repentant on the Mountain's Shore

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante and Virgil pass through the crowd of the violently-slain-but-late-repentant (Jacopo del Cassero, Buonconte da Montefeltro, La Pia), are joined by the proud shade Sordello whose greeting of a fellow Mantuan triggers Dante's furious apostrophe against a lawless, emperor-less Italy, then move on to the flower-carpeted Valley of the Princes at dusk, and finally, after a dream of a golden eagle that is really the saint Lucia bearing him in her arms, arrive at the three-stepped Gate of Purgatory where an angel inscribes seven P's on Dante's brow and admits him with two keys under the warning that none who look back after entering may return.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: The Late-Repentant, Sordello's Lament, and the Gate of Purgatory
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: The Late-Repentant, Sordello's Lament, and the Gate of Purgatory

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: On the first terrace of Purgatory the pilgrim views marble carvings of humility and studies the Proud bent double under stones, converses with Omberto Aldobrandeschi and the illuminator Oderisi on the transience of earthly fame, watches Virgil's guiding angel erase a letter P from his brow, then climbs to the second terrace where the Envious sit with eyelids sewn shut by wire while voices proclaim examples of love and Guido del Duca laments the vanished noble houses of the Arno valley and Romagna.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Purgatorio X–XIV: The Terraces of Pride and Envy
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Purgatorio X–XIV: The Terraces of Pride and Envy

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: On the terrace of wrath Dante and Virgil hear Marco Lombardo's discourse on free will and the corrupt fusion of Church and Empire, then pass through the terrace of sloth where Virgil expounds love as the root of every virtue and vice, before a dream-vision of a Siren gives way to the terrace of avarice and Pope Adrian V's confession.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Wrath's Smoke, Sloth's Haste, and the Root of All Sin: Purgatorio XV–XIX
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Wrath's Smoke, Sloth's Haste, and the Root of All Sin: Purgatorio XV–XIX

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: On the fifth terrace Dante hears Hugh Capet curse the avarice of the French royal line he founded, feels the mountain shake and hears the Gloria as a purified soul (revealed to be Statius) rises free, and then climbs with Statius — who recounts how Virgil's Fourth Eclogue secretly converted him to Christianity — onto the terrace of gluttony, where he meets the emaciated Forese Donati, hears Bonagiunta of Lucca name the dolce stil novo, and is finally blessed by the angel of temperance.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Purgatory, Cantos XX–XXIV: Hugh Capet's Curse, Statius's Conversion, and the Terrace of Gluttony
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Purgatory, Cantos XX–XXIV: Hugh Capet's Curse, Statius's Conversion, and the Terrace of Gluttony

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: Dante ascends the seventh terrace of Purgatory, where Statius expounds a scholastic account of embryonic ensoulment and the formation of aerial shadow-bodies, the penitent lustful purge themselves in fire while crying out counter-exemplars of chastity and excess (and Dante converses with poets Guido Guinizelli and Arnaut Daniel), then passes through the flame himself, sleeps on the stairway to a dream of Leah and Rachel, and is crowned by Virgil "sovereign o'er thyself" before entering the Earthly Paradise, where he meets the flower-gathering lady Matelda across the stream of Lethe.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: Purgatory, Cantos XXV–XXVIII: Statius on the Soul, the Fire of Lust, and the Threshold of the Earthly Paradise
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: Purgatory, Cantos XXV–XXVIII: Statius on the Soul, the Fire of Lust, and the Threshold of the Earthly Paradise

commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.summary: In the Earthly Paradise, Dante witnesses an elaborate allegorical pageant of the Church, loses Virgil and is reproved by the newly arrived Beatrice for his infidelity to her memory, confesses and is plunged into Lethe, then beholds the pageant's chariot corrupted by an eagle, fox, dragon, and finally a harlot and giant, before Beatrice charges him to record it all and he is purified in Eunoe, made fit to rise to the stars.
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.term: The Earthly Paradise: Beatrice's Reproof and the Pageant of the Church
commons/reading/dante-divine-comedy/dant.title: The Earthly Paradise: Beatrice's Reproof and the Pageant of the Church

commons/reading/decameron/dec-conclusion.summary: Boccaccio's closing self-defence refutes anticipated charges of licentiousness, partiality toward women, uneven quality, excessive length, and satirising friars, grounding each rebuttal in the reader's own disposition as the decisive variable.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-conclusion.title: DEC 12 — Conclusion of the Author

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-01.md.summary: The famous plague prologue establishes Florence 1348 as a world unmade, from which seven ladies and three men flee to form the brigata—a curated, governed retreat whose first day of free-topic storytelling sets up the Decameron's core arguments about wit, faith, sacred fraud, noble speech, and the persistence of value under moral collapse. Its marquee novellas are Ser Ciappelletto's false deathbed confession, which mints the wickedest of men into a venerated saint, and Abraham the Jew's conversion after witnessing Rome's clerical corruption—faith surviving its ministers.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-01.md.title: DEC 02 — Day the First

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-02.md.summary: Day the Second puts fortune's wheel at full throttle — ten stories of travellers robbed, noblewomen shipwrecked, exiles disgraced, and a princess passed through nine men's hands, all of whom arrive at unexpected restoration through a mixture of wit, luck, and resilient self-possession.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-02.md.title: DEC 03 — Day the Second

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-03.md.summary: Day the Third stages ten tales of successful ingenuity under Neifile's governance: characters across every social station — mute gardeners, horsekeeper impostors, scheming abbots, pilgrim lovers, and a girl in the Theban desert — all deploy wit, disguise, and deliberate deception to obtain desire or recover what was lost, while Boccaccio mounts a sustained satirical assault on clerical hypocrisy throughout.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-03.md.title: DEC 04 — Day the Third

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-04.md.summary: Day the Fourth, governed by the melancholy Filostrato, collects ten novels of tragic love alongside Boccaccio's spirited author's defence — the 'green geese' half-tale — and spans the full range of love's ruin: jealous fathers, murderous brothers, deception, sudden death, and the eaten heart.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-04.md.title: DEC 05 — Day the Fourth

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-05.md.summary: Day Five, governed by Fiammetta, assembles ten stories of love vindicated by persistence, cunning, or fortune after extreme adversity — sea-raids, imprisonment, near-burning, and near-hanging — establishing a structural argument that desire, if noble in origin, is ultimately ratified by Providence or social order.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-05.md.title: DEC 06 — Day the Fifth

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-06.md.summary: Day Six stages wit as a survival technology: ten stories in which the well-timed word — retort, riddle, pun, or improvised sermon — deflects insult, escapes punishment, or exposes the pretensions of rank, all framed by the servants' bawdy quarrel that gives Dioneo the theme for Day Seven.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-06.md.title: DEC 07 — Day the Sixth

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-07.md.summary: Day the Seventh turns the Decameron's comic engine fully toward sexual politics: under Dioneo's anarchic governance ten stories catalogue how wives outwit jealous or credulous husbands — through phantom-conjurations, improvised fictions, disguise, and a surreal enchanted pear-tree — making female wit the unchallenged sovereign of the household.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-07.md.title: DEC 08 — Day the Seventh

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-08.md.summary: Day the Eighth is Boccaccio's most sustained anatomy of trickery as a social art: across ten stories under Lauretta's reign, wit is deployed as currency, disguise, and weapon, culminating in the scholar Rinieri's methodical near-lethal revenge on a widow who mocked him in the snow — a story that refuses comfortable laughter and tests the very limits of justified cruelty.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-08.md.title: DEC 09 — Day the Eighth

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-09.md.summary: Day Nine's free-topic miscellany — presided over by Emilia with no set theme — cycles through female wit outfoxing male desire, institutional hypocrisy laid bare, two more Calandrino hoaxes, and closes on morally uncomfortable Solomon-tale and bawdy conjuration, collectively dramatising the contest between knavery, credulity, and pragmatic intelligence.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-09.md.title: DEC 10 — Day the Ninth

commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-10.md.summary: Day the Tenth, Boccaccio's culminating Day under Pamfilo's governance, presents a sustained philosophical argument that true magnificence — in gifts, friendship, erotic renunciation, and patient suffering — is the highest human virtue, building through ten stories to the ambiguous, disturbing test of Griselda, whose patience Dioneo calls a 'monstrous folly' even as the Day crowns her as its final exemplar.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-day-10.md.title: DEC 11 — Day the Tenth

commons/reading/decameron/dec-proem.md.summary: Boccaccio frames the *Decameron* as an act of gratitude-repayment, dedicating his hundred tales to lovesick ladies as the class least able to seek external relief, while justifying storytelling itself as therapeutic consolation.
commons/reading/decameron/dec-proem.md.title: DEC 01 — Proem & Author's Introduction

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett opens Darwin's Dangerous Idea by arguing that natural selection replaces the ancient premise that Mind must precede and explain all design — surveyed through Locke's deductive proof and Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion — with a mindless, algorithmic process that is scientifically secure yet philosophically dangerous to inherited notions of meaning and purpose.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Tell Me Why
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Tell Me Why

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Darwin's demonstration that species evolved by natural selection dismantles the Platonic-Aristotelian doctrine of fixed essences and reframes natural selection itself as a substrate-neutral, mindless, yet guaranteed algorithmic process capable of producing design without a designer.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: An Idea Is Born
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: An Idea Is Born

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Darwin's idea of natural selection is a 'universal acid' that inverts the pre-Darwinian Cosmic Pyramid — showing how Design accumulates from mere Order via a mindless algorithmic process — and the chapter defends that inversion against two centuries of resistance using the skyhook-versus-crane distinction and a contrast between good and greedy reductionism.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Universal Acid
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Universal Acid

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett formalizes the Tree of Life as a graph of every organism's birth-to-offspring time lines to argue that its two biggest forks (the eukaryotic and multicellular revolutions), the boundary of a species, and the moment of speciation itself all resist essentialist or real-time definition and can only be read off the whole pattern, retrospectively, at the right level of oversimplification.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Tree of Life
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Tree of Life

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett builds a naturalized theory of biological possibility by nesting four grades of possibility (logical, physical, biological, historical) and replacing the vague, all-or-nothing question of what is biologically possible with a measurable notion of accessibility inside an imagined "Library of Mendel" — a Borges-style combinatorial space of every conceivable genome — arguing that many apparent laws of biology are really just contingent, historically locked-in restrictions on what that search process can reach.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Possible and the Actual
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Possible and the Actual

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett distinguishes neutral genetic drift from selection-driven 'lifting' in Design Space, sorts biological and cultural design features into forced moves versus historically contingent 'virtual necessities,' and mounts the chapter's Central Salvo that biological and human-made design occupy a single unified Design Space, evidenced by the same logic of homology and imperfection that textual critics use to trace manuscript descent.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Threads of Actuality in Design Space
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Threads of Actuality in Design Space

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett opens Chapter 7 by arguing that crane-style Darwinian explanation must be pushed back past the origin of life itself, then surveys molecular-evolution research (Eigen, Cairns-Smith, Maynard Smith) showing how meaningless, self-replicating "macros" could bootstrap into the genetic code without a skyhook.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Cranes All the Way Down: Priming Darwin's Pump
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Cranes All the Way Down: Priming Darwin's Pump

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett uses Conway's Game of Life to show how the Anthropic Principle and cosmic fine-tuning collapse the line between Order and Design, turning God the Artificer into God the Lawfinder, then turns to Nietzsche's eternal recurrence to ask whether life can hold meaning once science has removed its metaphysical foundations.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Laws of the Game of Life and Eternal Recurrence
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Laws of the Game of Life and Eternal Recurrence

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett argues that engineering is not a demeaning metaphor but the literal, obligatory organizing principle of Darwinian biology, tracing how mindless molecular mechanisms — from Eigen's quasi-species dynamics to Monod's code-plus-environment solution to protein folding — give rise, by gradual and non-teleological steps, to function, error, and finally meaning itself.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Biology Is Engineering: Function, Fitness, and the Origins of Meaning
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Biology Is Engineering: Function, Fitness, and the Origins of Meaning

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Reverse-engineering organisms as artifacts exposes two disanalogies between evolution and human design (bait-and-switch discard-only redesign, and blindness to side effects that both wrecks and occasionally blesses complex systems), and Stuart Kauffman's self-organization research is reframed not as a rival to Darwinism but as a deepening of it into a general science of 'meta-engineering,' the constraints that govern any design process at all.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Reverse Engineering, Bait-and-Switch, and Stuart Kauffman's Meta-Engineering
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Reverse Engineering, Bait-and-Switch, and Stuart Kauffman's Meta-Engineering

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett grounds adaptationist reasoning in the intentional stance's reverse-engineering method, then defends it against Gould and Lewontin's Panglossian caricature by proposing the fairer label 'the Leibnizian Paradigm.'
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Power of Adaptationist Thinking: From the Intentional Stance to the Leibnizian Paradigm
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Power of Adaptationist Thinking: From the Intentional Stance to the Leibnizian Paradigm

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett defends game-theoretic adaptationism — the Prisoner's Dilemma, evolutionarily stable strategies, and the resulting rarity of cooperation in nature — and then answers Gould and Lewontin's charge that adaptationism ignores "hidden constraints" by showing, via a chess analogy, how such constraints can be empirically discovered rather than merely asserted against the adaptationist program.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Playing with Constraints: Game Theory, Cooperation, and Hidden Constraints in Adaptationism
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Playing with Constraints: Game Theory, Cooperation, and Hidden Constraints in Adaptationism

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett argues that both of Stephen Jay Gould's self-styled revolutions against orthodox neo-Darwinism — punctuated equilibrium and the Burgess Shale's 'radical contingency' — collapse back into the modern synthesis once their rhetoric is stripped away, revealing Gould as a covert hunter for skyhooks rather than a discoverer of new cranes.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Gould's Two Revolutions That Weren't: Punctuated Equilibrium and Radical Contingency
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Gould's Two Revolutions That Weren't: Punctuated Equilibrium and Radical Contingency

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett argues that Stephen Jay Gould's decades of announced revolutions against neo-Darwinism, culminating in the Gould-Lewontin 'Spandrels of San Marco' paper, are a myth that dissolves on close reading, and traces the pattern to Gould's underlying discomfort with Darwin's algorithmic, no-skyhooks idea.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Crying Wolf: The Myth of Gould's Revolutions and the Spandrels of San Marco
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Crying Wolf: The Myth of Gould's Revolutions and the Spandrels of San Marco

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett triages every controversy raised against Darwinism into three bins — harmless heresies that wouldn't touch the theory even if confirmed (panspermia, intergalactic gene-splicing, multiple origins of life), fatal-if-true heresies that are ruled out on logical or empirical grounds (Teilhard's Omega-point, Lamarckism, directed mutation), and one genuine but low-stakes controversy, the units-of-selection/gene's-eye-view debate, that carries none of the anxiety people project onto it.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Controversies Contained: Heresies, Losers, and the Gene's-Eye View
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Controversies Contained: Heresies, Losers, and the Gene's-Eye View

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett traces a century of resistance to human Darwinism before formally introducing Dawkins' meme as a second replicator, modeled on the eukaryotic-endosymbiosis story, that runs its own selection process through minds, vehicles, and filters in what he calls the infosphere.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Memes as a Second Replicator: From Ape-Ancestry Anxiety to the Infosphere
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Memes as a Second Replicator: From Ape-Ancestry Anxiety to the Infosphere

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett argues that a rigorous science of memetics is unlikely, because cultural information has no uniform syntactic medium the way genes have DNA, but that the meme's-eye view remains philosophically indispensable for explaining how minds, selves, and autonomy are themselves products of meme colonization rather than its sovereign judges.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Meme's-Eye View: A Doubtful Science, an Essential Philosophy
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Meme's-Eye View: A Doubtful Science, an Essential Philosophy

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett builds a four-tier Tower of Generate-and-Test (Darwinian, Skinnerian, Popperian, Gregorian creatures) culminating in language-equipped human minds, then shows how Chomsky, Gould, and Searle each block a Darwinian, engineering-style account of language and mind, casting all three as reluctant champions of skyhooks.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Losing Our Minds to Darwin
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Losing Our Minds to Darwin

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett argues, via the two-bitser vending machine, a frog's-eye fly-detector re-selected for food pellets, Putnam's Twin Earth, and his own "two black boxes" and cryogenic-robot fables, that all meaning is conferred by selective and functional history rather than being intrinsic or original, so that the philosophical wall between an artifact's "derived" intentionality and a human's "real" intentionality cannot hold.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Evolution of Meanings
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Evolution of Meanings

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett refutes Roger Penrose's Godel-based argument that human minds cannot be algorithmic, tracing Penrose's mistake to a confusion between what a class of algorithms can be proven to do and what a particular, evolved algorithm might in fact accomplish, and diagnosing Penrose's proposed quantum-gravity escape hatch as an as-yet-unfound skyhook.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Emperor's New Mind, and Other Fables
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Emperor's New Mind, and Other Fables

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett recasts the naturalistic fallacy as "greedy ethical reductionism" — the real error shared by Skinner's behaviorism, E. O. Wilson's sociobiology, the Hutterites' communalism, and biblical literalism alike — then sketches how genuine morality could still evolve gradually, through parental investment, kin selection, reciprocal altruism, and iterated Prisoner's Dilemma tournaments, without any single architect or skyhook.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Some Varieties of Greedy Ethical Reductionism
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Some Varieties of Greedy Ethical Reductionism

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett reads Hobbes's social-contract account and Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals as rival Darwinian "Just So Stories" of how an amoral state of nature gave way to morality, using the genes-eye puzzle of multicellular cooperation — solved by Brian Skyrms's "Darwinian Veil of Ignorance" — to explain why a body's own cells do not rebel, and credits Nietzsche with an early, independent statement of the origin/function distinction Dennett calls exaptation, against the Social Darwinists' genetic fallacy.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Two Just So Stories of Morality: Hobbes's Social Contract and Nietzsche's Genealogy
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Two Just So Stories of Morality: Hobbes's Social Contract and Nietzsche's Genealogy

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett tries to separate sociobiology's two faces — careful science of nonhuman social behavior versus reckless megaphone claims about human nature — by insisting that in humans, unlike other species, adaptive plausibility never by itself licenses an inference to a genetic cause, since culture is always available as an alternative explanation.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Sociobiology: Good and Bad, Good and Evil
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Sociobiology: Good and Bad, Good and Evil

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett argues that no ethical theory, utilitarian or Kantian, has ever produced a computable decision procedure, and that real moral reasoning is instead Herbert Simon's "satisficing" all the way down, so a workable ethics must be redesigned as situational, a-rational "conversation-stoppers" rather than a completed algorithm.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Redesigning Morality
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Redesigning Morality

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Closing Darwin's Dangerous Idea, Dennett extends Design Space thinking to value itself, arguing that biodiversity, cultural artifacts, and even religious traditions are precious in proportion to the design work embedded in them, that faiths must be selectively tolerated, caged, or left to go extinct like species, and that Darwinism remains a universal acid whose corrosive power, handled with care, leaves stronger versions of our most cherished ideas intact.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: The Future of an Idea
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: The Future of an Idea

commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.summary: Dennett explains why so many thinkers resist Darwin's idea and defends his choice to persuade through storytelling rather than formal philosophical argument, before thanking colleagues, students, and correspondents who shaped the book.
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.term: Preface: Why Dennett Tells a Story Instead of Making an Argument
commons/reading/dennett-darwins-dangerou.title: Preface: Why Dennett Tells a Story Instead of Making an Argument

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: Walter Wriston's crusade to free global finance from state control instead built the dollar-clearing system, SWIFT, the Internet's physical backbone, and the semiconductor supply chain into concentrated chokepoints that gave the United States more leverage over the world, not less.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.term: Walter Wriston's World: How Escaping the State Built New Chokepoints
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: Walter Wriston's World: How Escaping the State Built New Chokepoints

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: The STORMBREW leak reveals how the U.S. turned literal maps of internet cable choke points and SWIFT's financial-messaging network into instruments of empire, using NSA telecom surveillance and Treasury/OFAC dollar-clearing power to police, coerce, and cut adversaries like North Korea and Iran out of the global system.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: The STORMBREW Map

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: The Huawei-Meng Wanzhou saga shows how the United States turned its financial and technological chokepoints—dollar clearing through HSBC and control over semiconductor intellectual property—into weapons to cripple China's most important technology champion, prompting China to pursue its own, far weaker, countermeasures.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.term: War Without Gunsmoke: The Weaponization of Huawei
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: War Without Gunsmoke: The Weaponization of Huawei

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: Trump's sanctions war over the Iran deal and Nord Stream 2, followed by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, shocks the European Union out of its founding faith that trade guarantees peace and pushes it, haltingly and still dependent on American financial infrastructure, toward building the instruments of a geopolitical power.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: Europe's Awakening into Winter

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: Through the coerced tanker captain, Microsoft's decades of diplomatic improvisation, TSMC's fraying neutrality, and crypto's failed attempts to build money beyond state reach, the chapter shows businesses trapped between rival powers that have weaponized the same global networks companies once treated as neutral infrastructure.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.term: Hook's Captain: Corporations Trapped Between Empires
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: Hook's Captain: Corporations Trapped Between Empires

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: America's underground empire of weaponized financial and technological interdependence emerged not from grand design but from ad hoc improvisation, and now, as it grows more visible and China responds in kind, it risks spiraling toward the same kind of catastrophic feedback loop that once nearly produced nuclear war and once helped precipitate World War II -- so Farrell and Newman close by arguing for Schelling-style strategic frameworks, new institutions, and a possible turn toward using the empire's coercive machinery for climate and anti-corruption goals instead of unbounded rivalry.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.term: The Empire of Wind and Light
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: The Empire of Wind and Light

commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.summary: Farrell and Newman introduce the "underground empire" thesis: the fiber-optic cables, SWIFT messaging, dollar clearing, and semiconductor supply chains that make up the global economy's infrastructure were built for private profit but, centered on the United States by Cold War-era path dependence, became instruments of American surveillance and financial coercion after 9/11, an unplanned drift toward empire now becoming visible and provoking resistance from China, Europe, and the businesses caught between them.
commons/reading/farrell-underground-empi.title: All Roads Lead to Rome

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Wisdom is an attentional, anticipatory orientation to a necessarily uncertain, possibility-open world, while knowledge is intentional and predictive and mistakes not-knowing for mere ignorance.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: Abstract: Attention, Not-Knowing, and the Wisdom of a Possible World
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Abstract: Attention, Not-Knowing, and the Wisdom of a Possible World

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: The back matter reveals that the essay began as a 2020 University College Cork keynote and was assembled from fragments of three earlier Ingold books, and lists a reference lineage running from phenomenology and process philosophy through the anthropology of skill and perception to new-materialist theory.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: Back Matter: Acknowledgements, Notes, and References
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Back Matter: Acknowledgements, Notes, and References

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Ingold distinguishes correspondence — a longitudinal, middle-voiced joining-with things that unfolds without predetermined ends — from interaction's transverse exchange of interests, then argues that living correspondence well means choosing undercommoning's shared uncertainty over the false security of settled understanding, sustaining the same prolonged, uncategorizing astonishment that Erin Manning locates in autistic attention and in artists.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: Correspondence versus Interaction, Understanding versus Undercommoning
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Correspondence versus Interaction, Understanding versus Undercommoning

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: A childhood memory of finding a stranger watching the moon through a telescope becomes Ingold's occasion for distinguishing knowledge from wisdom and the self from the soul, arguing that knowledge encloses the world within explanatory categories while wisdom exposes us, undefended, to its living presence.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: The Man in the Moon: Knowledge, Wisdom, Self and Soul
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: The Man in the Moon: Knowledge, Wisdom, Self and Soul

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Ingold replaces the image of generations as discrete stacked layers with an intergenerational braid of overlapping lives, then distinguishes the perpetual astonishment of open, attentive engagement with the world from the surprise that punctuates failed scientific prediction, arguing that not-knowing is not ignorance.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: Generations as a Braid, and Astonishment Without Surprise
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Generations as a Braid, and Astonishment Without Surprise

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Ingold contrasts the Western idea of ‘fulfilling one’s potential’ — a progressive narrowing from many possibilities to one fixed destination — with the Pintupi sense of life as a ‘one-possibility thing’ that is continually replenished rather than spent, then applies the same distinction to Dewey’s doing and undergoing, arguing that undergoing overflows every discrete act so that a life is a longitudinal becoming rather than a sequence of targeted, self-contained deeds.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: Replenishing Potential, Not Fulfilling It: Doing and Undergoing
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Replenishing Potential, Not Fulfilling It: Doing and Undergoing

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Ingold closes the essay by distinguishing fake freedom, which smuggles in a predetermined objective the way a jigsaw puzzle smuggles in its solution, from real freedom as the attentive, singular correspondence of the path — then indicts education, science, and the state as machines that manufacture the ignorance they claim to cure, proposing not-knowing as wisdom instead.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Real Problems; Real Freedom

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Wisdom lies beyond what facts and data-extraction can capture, Ingold argues, and the uncertainty we mourn as a knowledge deficit is really — following Bergson — the very excess that makes genuine possibility, rather than mere probability, real.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: Turning Toward the World: Wisdom, Post-Truth, and Uncertainty as Possibility
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: Turning Toward the World: Wisdom, Post-Truth, and Uncertainty as Possibility

commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.summary: Attention has two sides — exposure (submission to a restless, unfinished world) and attunement (a perceiver's honed responsiveness to a settled one) — which alternate in one fixed direction, illustrated by the bodily jeopardy of walking and used to distinguish open-ended anticipation from closed prediction.
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.term: The Two Sides of Attention: From Exposure to Falling Forwards
commons/reading/ingold-2023-possible-wor.title: The Two Sides of Attention: From Exposure to Falling Forwards

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes's two prefaces frame Revolution in Time as a triptych — cultural, technical, and socio-economic history of timekeeping — born of a collector's accident in 1972 Paris; the 1999 second-edition preface updates the story with atomic clocks, the Swiss-luxury/East-Asian-digital bifurcation, and the observation that ubiquitous cheap precision has made knowledge of time far outrun the timeliness of action.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 01 — Prefaces & front matter
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 01 — Prefaces & front matter

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes frames the medieval European mechanical clock (c. 1300) as a movable-type-class invention whose oscillating-digital principle underlies all subsequent timekeeping and whose portability converted external time obedience into internalized time discipline.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 02 — Introduction — why the clock matters
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 02 — Introduction — why the clock matters

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes reconstructs Su Sung's 1086–94 astronomical water-wheel clock to argue Chinese horology was a magnificent dead end: technically superb but demand-starved and politically monopolized, it could not and did not seed the oscillating-escapement revolution that Europe's mechanical clock began.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 03 — A Magnificent Dead End (Ch. 1)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 03 — A Magnificent Dead End (Ch. 1)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: China got a second chance at the horological revolution when Ricci's 'self-ringing bells' reached the Ming court (1580s–1601), but with no social demand for precision time the clock was metabolized as a toy — a rejection Landes traces through K'ang-hsi's palace workshop, the 1782 dismissal of Western machines as 'intricate oddities,' Ch'ien-lung's 1793 edict, and the Opium War.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 04 — Why Are the Memorials Late? (Ch. 2) — China's second chance refused
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 04 — Why Are the Memorials Late? (Ch. 2) — China's second chance refused

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes locates the demand that produced the mechanical clock in Western monasticism's uniquely point-based, collective prayer discipline — refuting Price's 'fallen angel' thesis that timekeeping was a by-product of astronomical automation.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 05 — Are You Sleeping, Brother John? (ch. 3)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 05 — Are You Sleeping, Brother John? (ch. 3)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes traces how the mechanical clock emerged from monastic bell-discipline into the medieval city, where work bells, labor conflict, and the shift to equal hours made standardized public time the infrastructure of a new commercial order — a discipline workers contested and then claimed for themselves.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 06 — "The Greatest Necessity for Every Rank of Men" (Ch. 4)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 06 — "The Greatest Necessity for Every Rank of Men" (Ch. 4)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes argues that miniaturization (mainspring + fusee, c. 1430) turned the clock into a personal possession, and that this privatization of time — driven by plague-era anxiety, salvation-accounting, and Protestant time-thrift — bred the punctual, self-monitoring individual of Western modernity, with armies and transport networks adopting synchronized time only slowly and through private watch ownership.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 07 — My Time Is My Time (Ch. 5)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 07 — My Time Is My Time (Ch. 5)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes maps the fork in Renaissance horology — German complexity-toys and French ornament-jewels versus the Anglo-Dutch precision instrument — and shows how Puritan demand, astronomy, and the longitude problem pulled the trade onto the precision main line.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 08 — Of Toys and Ornaments and Serious Things (ch. 6)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 08 — Of Toys and Ornaments and Serious Things (ch. 6)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes narrates the seventeenth-century precision revolution — Huygens's pendulum (1656) and balance spring (1675) — that cut variance from quarter-hours to seconds, made clocks agree with each other, dethroned the sun in favour of mean time, and laid the material basis for punctuality.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 09 — My Time Is Your Time (ch. 7)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 09 — My Time Is Your Time (ch. 7)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes shows precision horology entering its asymptotic phase — the last, hardest gains against temperature and friction won through compensation devices, jewelled bearings, machine tools, and four escapements that defined two centuries of timekeeping.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 10 — Approaching the Asymptote (ch. 8)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 10 — Approaching the Asymptote (ch. 8)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes retells the Harrison–longitude story against the David-and-Goliath myth: the Board's insistence on a reproducible, accessible method was partly wise, Maskelyne's lunars were conviction not conspiracy, and Harrison's legacy was proof of feasibility — his ingenious devices left almost no descendants.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 11 — The Man Who Stayed to Dinner (ch. 9)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 11 — The Man Who Stayed to Dinner (ch. 9)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes argues that Harrison's proof bore fruit mainly in France, where Pierre Le Roy invented the conceptual prototype of every later chronometer (detached escapement, inertia-based compensation, isochronized spring) and grasped that reproducibility, not a single masterpiece, solved longitude — yet French chronometry ran through his rival Berthoud, whose state-purveyor monopoly left French chronometers rare and unconscionably expensive.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 12 — The French Connection (Ch. 10)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 12 — The French Connection (Ch. 10)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes turns the chronometer's endgame into a study of credit versus merit — the Arnold–Earnshaw spring-detent priority war, fought through patents, patronage (Banks), and pamphlets, while the market quietly industrialized Earnshaw's design and precision ran on past nature itself.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 13 — Fame Is the Spur (ch. 11)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 13 — Fame Is the Spur (ch. 11)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes reconstructs the early turret-clock trade from account books and contracts — Perpignan 1356 (a nine-month, million-dollar royal build), the Nieppe contract of 1379, and the Cambrai cathedral accounts — to show that clockmaking was from the start a collaborative, division-of-labour craft whose products were hostages to fortune, demanding as much expenditure on maintenance and repair as on original construction.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 14 — Clocks in the Belfry (Ch. 12)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 14 — Clocks in the Belfry (Ch. 12)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes demolishes both nostalgia for the integral pre-industrial craftsman and the revisionist claim that division of labour was a capitalist imposition: specialization at all three levels (among crafts, within crafts, in the shop) predates the factory and even the guild, while guild monopolies — restrictive, rent-extracting, anti-commercial — leaked everywhere sovereignty ran out, from Friedberg and Fürth to the guild-free Jura and free-trading London.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 15 — The Good Old Days That Never Were (Ch. 13)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 15 — The Good Old Days That Never Were (Ch. 13)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes explains Britain's century of horological supremacy (c. 1675–1775) as talent plus structure — five great London makers atop a high-wage, urbanized, time-conscious market served by deep division of labour — while France kept the genius (Le Roy, Breguet) but lost the industry to Geneva's cheaper imitation of 'the French style of watch,' the whole trade riding on forgery, outside work, smuggling, and failing protectionism.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 16 — The Ups and Downs of International Competition (Ch. 14)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 16 — The Ups and Downs of International Competition (Ch. 14)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes on how tiny Calvinist Geneva — refugee skill, the établissage putting-out system, merchant credit, and ruthless commercial opportunism — became the world's second watch industry, then was undercut by the very logic of cheap-labor devolution it pioneered when the Jura out-Geneva'd Geneva.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 17 — Multum in Parvo (Ch. 15)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 17 — Multum in Parvo (Ch. 15)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes explains the improbable rise of Jura watchmaking — a barren, snowbound highland whose winter-bred jack-of-all-trades peasants, organized by établissage and supercharged by Japy's mass-produced standard ébauches (100,000/yr at 2.5 francs by ~1805), built a cheap, thin, going-barrel 'watch for everyman' and a congeries of specialized sub-branches that pleased every market the British disdained.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 18 — Notwithstanding the Barrenness of the Soil (Ch. 16)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 18 — Notwithstanding the Barrenness of the Soil (Ch. 16)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes traces the British watch trade's self-inflicted collapse (1797–1870s) — Pitt's tax, a quality-destroying race to the bottom, complacent rejection of Ingold's machine manufacture — just as railway time, the telegraph, and Greenwich standardization democratized the watch and handed the booming market to the Swiss.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 19 — "Nor Could He Compete with Us" (ch. 17, pp. 293–309)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 19 — "Nor Could He Compete with Us" (ch. 17, pp. 293–309)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes explains the nineteenth-century reversal of horological fortunes — Swiss observatory trials, swarm-like emulation, and Protestant literacy versus British craft conservatism and merchant complacency — and rejects the New Economic History claim that British decline was foreordained.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 20 — "Ah, But He Could!" (ch. 18)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 20 — "Ah, But He Could!" (ch. 18)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes shows how the American system of manufacture — interchangeable parts cut by single-purpose machines, universal micrometer gauging, and statistical sorting in place of craft fitting — took watchmaking through its third tenfold scale jump in a century (Terry's clocks, Jerome's brass-clock invasion of England, Waltham/Elgin's duopoly), until Favre-Perret's 1876 Philadelphia report forced the Swiss to concede that a randomly drawn machine-made Waltham beat 'one in fifty thousand' of their own.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 21 — Not One in Fifty Thousand (Ch. 19)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 21 — Not One in Fifty Thousand (Ch. 19)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes answers the title's nursery-rhyme question — who killed the American watch industry? — with a double autopsy: the Swiss survived the American challenge through selective mechanization, dispersed multiplicity, and product variety, while the American pioneers killed themselves via financial extraction (Dumaine's Waltham), marketing-over-technique, and an interchangeability ideal that was 'puff and bluff' until the 1930s.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 22 — "Who Killed Cock Robin?" (ch. 20, pp. 347–364)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 22 — "Who Killed Cock Robin?" (ch. 20, pp. 347–364)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes narrates the double assault on Swiss horology — Timex perfecting the old mass-production logic (8 million disposable pin-levers by 1960, 45% of the US market by 1973), then quartz abolishing the mechanical paradigm itself — and locates the Swiss failure not in science (CEH, Battelle, FASELEC had it all) but in entrepreneurship killed by monopoly rents, symbolized by the 26 April 1968 suspension of the chronometry competitions when quartz scores humiliated the regleurs.
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 23 — The Quartz Revolution, Part I (Ch. 21)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 23 — The Quartz Revolution, Part I (Ch. 21)

commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.summary: Landes closes the book with the quartz revolution's aftermath — Swiss collapse and Jura deindustrialization, leadership churning from Japan to Hong Kong, the Swatch's engineered renaissance, the luxury-mechanical retreat into meaning — and a final meditation: craftsmen no longer give us time, physicists do, but 'the timekeeper remains.'
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.term: RIT 24 — The Quartz Revolution, II (ch. 21, second half + conclusion)
commons/reading/landes-revolution-in-tim.title: RIT 24 — The Quartz Revolution, II (ch. 21, second half + conclusion)

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel traces the Saint-Simonian church of 1828-1832 as it turns Enfantin's doctrine of rehabilitated flesh and free love into a full theology of history, diagnosing the age's crisis as an atrophy of love, redefining man as tripartite (reason, action, feeling), and recasting Kantian antagonism as the engine of humanity's arithmetic progress toward universal association.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Children of Saint-Simon: The Triumph of Love
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Children of Saint-Simon: The Triumph of Love

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel traces the mature Saint-Simonian doctrine of hierarchical meritocracy ("each according to his capacity, each capacity according to its works") and its centralized-bank utopia of finance capital, then follows the movement's turn toward an "education for love" meant to complete humanity's moral development, culminating in the 1832 obscenity/subversion trial where Enfantin staged his defense of the "rehabilitation of the flesh," and finally the sect's dissolution into respectable Second Empire technocrats (Chevalier, the Pereires) even as Enfantin himself lived out thirty more years as a mystic of universal love.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: The Saint-Simonian Religion: Hierarchy, Love, Trial, and Aftermath
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: The Saint-Simonian Religion: Hierarchy, Love, Trial, and Aftermath

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel narrates Auguste Comte's stormy break with his mentor Saint-Simon, his catastrophic marriage and mental breakdowns, his transfiguring love for the dying Clothilde de Vaux, and the split between his rationalist "Cours de philosophie positive" and the mystical Religion of Humanity he built afterward as self-proclaimed "Grand Prêtre de l'Humanité."
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Auguste Comte: Embodiment in the Great Being
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Auguste Comte: Embodiment in the Great Being

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel dissects Auguste Comte's systematization of the philosophy of history into the law of the three states, the encyclopedic hierarchy of sciences, and a psychology of historical regression, then traces how Comte's late religion of Humanity subordinates the individual, capitalists, women, and eventually labor and science itself to a mystical cult of altruistic love centered on the Great Being.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Order and Progress, Moral Love and Gay Science
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Order and Progress, Moral Love and Gay Science

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel portrays Condorcet as an emotionally tormented 'snow-capped volcano' whose secular Esquisse turned Turgot's providential history of progress into a self-contained statistical science of prediction — an attempt literally to 'tame the future' — and pushed that science toward the democratization of genius and the equalization of nations, ending in an unexamined Eurocentric universalism.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Condorcet: Taming the Future

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel reconstructs Condorcet's late, fragmentary blueprint (from his commentary on Bacon's New Atlantis and the Esquisse) for a self-organizing, quantifying world republic of science, and traces how his doctrine of infinite, moral-absolute progress culminates in a technocratic vision of a state run by "social mathematics" and a quasi-religious cult of futurity.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Condorcet's Republic of Science and the Cult of Progress
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Condorcet's Republic of Science and the Cult of Progress

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel closes his study of Turgot, Condorcet, Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Comte with a comparative epilogue that weighs what united and divided the five prophets of philosophical history — their attitudes toward system-building, action versus contemplation, revolution, love and the family, religion, property and labor — and argues that their common blind spot was a refusal to confront the tragic, meaningless destructiveness of fate.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Epilogue: Comparing the Prophets of Paris
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Epilogue: Comparing the Prophets of Paris

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel profiles Charles Fourier as an obsessive, autodidact traveling salesman who built the doctrine of passionate attraction and the phalanstery entirely from introspection and marketplace observation, then argues that Fourier's method of ecart absolu required a total rejection of philosophy, morality, and "civilization" itself rather than their reform.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Fourier: Life of a Salesman, Death to Philosophy
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Fourier: Life of a Salesman, Death to Philosophy

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Fourier catalogues twelve innate human passions—organized like a tree into a luxurious, a group (affective), and a serial (distributive) branch under the trunk of 'unityism'—and argues that civilization's repression of these passions perverts them into malignant 'counterpassions' and manias, while a rightly engineered phalanstery could channel even sadistic and destructive drives into harmless or productive expression without sublimation.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Fourier's Twelve Passions: Taxonomy, Repression, and the Theodicy of Desire
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Fourier's Twelve Passions: Taxonomy, Repression, and the Theodicy of Desire

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel lays out Fourier's phalanstery program of uncoerced child-rearing, passional free love, abundance-neutralized inequality, and cosmic "harmonious armies," then turns to psychobiography, arguing that Fourier's self-described "mask of Harlequin" concealment strategy and his megalomaniacal fantasies of vengeance against France and Paris betray a sadistic, possibly masochistic substrate beneath his utopia of love.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Fourier's Phalanstery: The Economy of Passion and the Mask of Harlequin
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Fourier's Phalanstery: The Economy of Passion and the Mask of Harlequin

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: In the preface and prolegomenon to The Prophets of Paris, Frank Manuel defends his portraiture-driven method and then defines a distinct nineteenth-century French type — the secular prophet — arguing that Turgot, Condorcet, Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Comte, despite founding rival and mutually hostile systems, share a common psychology of crisis-consciousness, future-intoxication, contempt for the state, and millennial optimism.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Preface and Prolegomenon: The Prophets of Paris
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Preface and Prolegomenon: The Prophets of Paris

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel narrates Saint-Simon's picaresque life of speculation, imprisonment, and self-reinvention, then traces his shifting theory of the scientist's social role from Newtonian high priest to subordinated commodity, and his late turn from Enlightenment egalitarianism to a physiology-based organicism of three unequal, functionally specialized human types.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Saint-Simon: From Sans-Culotte Speculator to the Prophet of Organicism
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Saint-Simon: From Sans-Culotte Speculator to the Prophet of Organicism

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel analyzes Saint-Simon's late doctrine that the industrial-scientific order will dissolve the power drive by redirecting human aggression from man onto nature and will reduce government to pure administration, then traces how this technocratic vision culminated in the *Nouveau Christianisme*, Saint-Simon's deathbed reformulation of Christianity around a single commandment—labor for the poorest and most numerous class—meant to fill the spiritual void left by the collapsing Catholic order.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Saint-Simon: The Twilight of Power and the New Christianity
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Saint-Simon: The Twilight of Power and the New Christianity

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel traces Turgot's 1750 Sorbonne discourses and scattered fragments to show him inventing the modern secular idea of progress — grounded in sensationalist epistemology, driven by an innate human urge to innovate against institutional routine, channeled through genius and language, and confirmed by the stadial record of ethnology and four unevenly-developing 'progressions' (technology, fine arts, morals, science).
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Turgot: The Architect of the Idea of Progress
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Turgot: The Architect of the Idea of Progress

commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.summary: Manuel reconstructs Turgot's twin arguments for the inevitability of progress — an empirical proof from the past and a demonstration that regression is now structurally impossible — and then shows how this doctrine of progress functioned as a modern theodicy, converting the self-interested passions and crimes of history into unwitting instruments of a providential design.
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.term: Turgot: The Demonstration of Inevitability and Progress as Theodicy
commons/reading/manuel-prophets-of-paris.title: Turgot: The Demonstration of Inevitability and Progress as Theodicy

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Thomas More, in Antwerp on a diplomatic mission for Henry VIII, is introduced by his friend Peter Giles to Raphael Hythloday, a Portuguese philosopher who sailed with three of Amerigo Vespucci's four voyages, traveled from parched equatorial deserts into flourishing, well-governed nations, and is prized above all for describing wisely run commonwealths rather than monsters.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Meeting Raphael Hythloday
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Meeting Raphael Hythloday

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday refuses Peter Giles’ and More’s urging that he enter a king’s service as counsellor, arguing that courts run on flattery and self-regard and shield themselves from better ideas by appeal to ancestral custom, so a wise man’s advice is structurally unwelcome there.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Raphael’s Refusal: Counsel, Flattery, and the Uselessness of Wisdom at Court
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Raphael’s Refusal: Counsel, Flattery, and the Uselessness of Wisdom at Court

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: At Cardinal Morton's dinner table, the narrator rebuts an English lawyer's satisfaction that thieves are hanged "twenty on one gibbet" by arguing that idle noble retainers, France's standing armies, and sheep-pasture enclosures manufacture the very thieves the law then hangs, closing with the charge that lawmakers "first make thieves and then punish them."
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Sheep Devouring Men: Hythloday's Case Against Hanging Thieves
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Sheep Devouring Men: Hythloday's Case Against Hanging Thieves

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday rebuts the Counsellor's defense of hanging thieves by describing the Polylerits, a Persian tributary people whose penal code replaces execution with restitution and unchained public labor secured by visible marks rather than walls, and the scene closes on the same proposal being scorned when Raphael offers it but applauded when the Cardinal repeats a hedged version of it.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Restitution, Not the Gallows: The Polylerits and Whose Ideas Get Heard
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Restitution, Not the Gallows: The Polylerits and Whose Ideas Get Heard

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: A comic set-piece in which Cardinal Morton's jester goads a Friar into a scripture-quoting rage over care for the poor gives way to Raphael Hythloday's argument that courtiers only ever echo power, capped by the Achorians' cautionary tale of a kingdom ruined by holding a conquest it should never have taken.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Cardinal's Fool and the Achorians: Court Flattery and the Case Against Conquest
