commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Cardinal's Fool and the Achorians: Court Flattery and the Case Against Conquest

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday anatomizes five stratagems corrupt counsellors use to swell a prince's treasury — currency manipulation, feigned wars, revived defunct laws, sold dispensations, and a captured judiciary — then answers them by arguing a king's safety lies in his people's wealth rather than his own, capped by the Macarian law binding kings by oath never to hoard more than a thousand pounds of gold.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Corrupt Counsel, Captured Courts, and the Macarian Vow Against Treasure
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Corrupt Counsel, Captured Courts, and the Macarian Vow Against Treasure

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: The persona More argues, through the analogy of an actor who must not interrupt a comedy with a tragic speech, that a philosopher should adopt a pliable 'civil philosophy' that plays its part inside a corrupt court to make outcomes only as little bad as possible, while Raphael Hythloday rejects this as complicity — his honesty forecloses the compromise, court participation launders others' guilt onto him regardless, and Plato's simile of a man sheltering from unstoppable rain shows that self-preserving withdrawal is the only integrity left available.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Play in Progress: Civil Philosophy versus Principled Withdrawal
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Play in Progress: Civil Philosophy versus Principled Withdrawal

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday argues that as long as private property and money exist no nation can be governed justly or happily, is challenged by Peter Giles on grounds of incentive and civil order, answers by invoking his five years living among the Utopians, and — after a digression on Utopia's antiquity and a shipwreck through which the Utopians absorbed Roman and Egyptian learning — agrees to describe the island in full, setting up Book 2.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Against Private Property, For a Community of Goods
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Against Private Property, For a Community of Goods

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: More's Utopia opens Book Two with the island's crescent geography and its single hidden channel, the founding conquest by Utopus who severed it from the continent by forced (and self-shared) labor, and the resulting order of fifty-four identical cities and rotating farm labor that together secure Utopia against both foreign attack and domestic scarcity.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Shape of Utopia: Utopus's Island and Its Ordered Countryside
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Shape of Utopia: Utopus's Island and Its Ordered Countryside

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: More's Utopia describes Amaurot, the exemplary town of Utopia and seat of its supreme council, as a uniformly planned settlement where all fifty-four towns share one template, houses are owned by no one and redistributed by lot every ten years, and a founder's original design was deliberately left for later generations to complete.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Amaurot: The Legible Anatomy of a Utopian Town
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Amaurot: The Legible Anatomy of a Utopian Town

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: More's Utopia describes a tiered elective magistracy — Syphogrants, Tranibors, and a lifelong Prince chosen by secret ballot — engineered with procedural chokepoints (mandatory multi-stage consultation, a one-day cooling-off rule before any debate, and a capital ban on off-channel political meetings) specifically to prevent the Prince and Tranibors from conspiring to seize and enslave the state.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Of Their Magistrates
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Of Their Magistrates

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: In Utopia every citizen is trained in agriculture plus one craft, dresses identically in undyed durable cloth, and works a magistrate-audited six-hour day, because abolishing idle classes and money-driven luxury trades leaves labor abundant enough to redirect the surplus toward public lectures, reading, and the stated purpose of the whole design: the improvement of the mind.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Of Their Trades, and Manner of Life
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Of Their Trades, and Manner of Life

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday details the administrative machinery beneath Utopian 'traffic' — patriarchal households capped and rebalanced by demographic quota, colonization justified by a natural-law claim on uncultivated land, and a moneyless economy of common storehouses, communal dining halls, and public hospitals engineered to eliminate want and the pride it breeds.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Of Their Traffic
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Of Their Traffic

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: In Utopia, travel between towns is licensed and tracked by passport, daily life is organized to prevent idleness and factionalism through constant visibility, provisions are pooled and redistributed among towns as if the island were one family, and gold and silver are deliberately degraded — used for chamber pots and slaves' chains — so that wealth cannot buy social esteem, a policy dramatized when boastfully gold-clad Anemolian ambassadors are mistaken for slaves.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Travel, Legibility, and the Utopian Contempt for Gold
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Travel, Legibility, and the Utopian Contempt for Gold

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: More's Utopians ground happiness in a religiously-warranted hedonism, defining virtue as the rational pursuit of pleasure that binds self-love to duty toward others, all resting on empirical natural philosophy rather than scholastic abstraction or astrology.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Utopian Ethics of Reasoned Pleasure
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Utopian Ethics of Reasoned Pleasure

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday explains how the Utopians build their ethics on a rational calculus of pleasure, dismissing status display, hoarded wealth, and hunting as false pleasures while ranking bodily health and the mind's contemplation of virtue and truth as the only genuine ones.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: True and False Pleasures: The Utopians' Rational Calculus of Delight
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: True and False Pleasures: The Utopians' Rational Calculus of Delight

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Utopians pair bodily vigor and relentless land-improvement with an explosive, self-motivated mastery of Greek learning, then — after being shown only a crude account of Aldine printing — independently reinvent papermaking and the press well enough to multiply their small library into thousands of copies, while insisting on managing their own foreign trade to preserve navigational skill.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Utopian Vigor, Greek Learning, and the Reinvention of Printing
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Utopian Vigor, Greek Learning, and the Reinvention of Printing

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Utopia regulates slavery by calibrated crime rather than conquest, sanctions priest-approved euthanasia for the incurably ill, subjects marriage to age limits, premarital chastity law, and a mutual nude inspection, replaces lawyers with plainly-worded laws pled in person, lends its own incorruptible magistrates to neighboring nations, and refuses all treaties with foreign powers, contrasting its plain-law ethos with European princes’ deliberately ambiguous treaty language.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Slaves, Marriages, Voluntary Death, and the Rule of Plain Law in Utopia
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Slaves, Marriages, Voluntary Death, and the Rule of Plain Law in Utopia

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: The Utopians treat war as a brutal last resort permitted only for narrow just causes, then wage it through priced assassination bounties, expendable hired mercenaries, and calculated tribute extraction rather than glory-seeking battle.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Calculated Restraint of Utopian War
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Calculated Restraint of Utopian War

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Utopia's many local cults converge toward a shared natural theology of one Supreme Being called Mithras, and founder Utopus's law of toleration protects freedom of conscience through persuasion alone, punishing only sedition while civically excluding — but never punishing — those who deny an afterlife and providence.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Religions of Utopia: Natural Theology, Christian Reception, and the Law of Toleration
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Religions of Utopia: Natural Theology, Christian Reception, and the Law of Toleration

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Utopia's ascetic religious order, the Brutheskas, and its small elected priesthood, which shapes children's moral formation, holds full civil immunity, and accompanies armies to broker mercy, derive all their authority from voluntary reverence rather than coercive force.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: The Brutheskas and the Priesthood of Utopia
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: The Brutheskas and the Priesthood of Utopia

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Thomas More's Utopians worship one imageless Divine Essence they call Mithras in deliberately dim temples whose unified public liturgy — confession, household seating, incense, and passion-tuned music instead of blood sacrifice — absorbs a plurality of private sects without contradicting any of them.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Temples of a Single Divine Essence: The Utopians' Architecture of Worship
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Temples of a Single Divine Essence: The Utopians' Architecture of Worship

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Raphael Hythloday closes his defense of Utopia by declaring common ownership the only true foundation of a just commonwealth, indicts money-based governments as "a conspiracy of the rich," and the narrator then withholds full assent even while wishing such laws could be followed at home.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Utopia's Peroration: The Conspiracy of the Rich and the Case Against Private Property
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Utopia's Peroration: The Conspiracy of the Rich and the Case Against Private Property

commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.summary: Henry Morley's editorial introduction traces Thomas More's life — from Cardinal Morton's household and Oxford's Greek studies through his legal and parliamentary career and the 1515 Flanders embassy — to the composition, Continental publication, and translation history of *Utopia*, arguing that beneath its 'veil of a playful fiction' lies 'a noble English argument' against the political and social evils of More's own England.
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.term: Thomas More's Life and the Making of *Utopia*
commons/reading/more-utopia/more-utopia-.title: Thomas More's Life and the Making of *Utopia*

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: The appendix reprints, verbatim and without commentary, David Hume's autobiographical essay "My Own Life" and Adam Smith's letter to William Strahan describing Hume's cheerful, unreligious death, the two primary documents that first made Hume's serene skeptical death a public controversy.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Hume's My Own Life and Smith's Letter to Strahan
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Hume's My Own Life and Smith's Letter to Strahan

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Traces David Hume's life from his 1711 birth at Ninewells through 1749, covering his early education, the failed reception of A Treatise of Human Nature, his turn to essay-writing, his rejection from the Edinburgh chair over charges of heterodoxy, his secretarial-military service abroad, and the composition of the Philosophical Essays (First Enquiry), including the famous arguments against miracles and design, on the eve of his friendship with Adam Smith.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Young Hume: Life, the Treatise, and the Making of a Skeptic (1711–1749)
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Young Hume: Life, the Treatise, and the Making of a Skeptic (1711–1749)

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Adam Smith's biography from his 1723 birth in Kirkcaldy through Glasgow, a disillusioning stint at Oxford, the composition of his early manuscript on the history of astronomy, and his probable first meeting with Hume in autumn 1749 traces the formation of a mind already quietly Humean before the two men ever spoke.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Smith's Early Life and First Meeting with Hume
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Smith's Early Life and First Meeting with Hume

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Adam Smith settles into the Chair of Moral Philosophy at Glasgow while David Hume, twice passed over for a university post, becomes Keeper of the Advocates' Library in Edinburgh, and between 1751 and 1754 the two men's intellectual partnership deepens through Hume's Second Enquiry and Political Discourses (which Smith visibly absorbs into his own lectures), the opening of their surviving correspondence, and the founding of Edinburgh's Select Society.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Separate Chairs, Converging Minds: Smith at Glasgow, Hume in Edinburgh (1751-1754)
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Separate Chairs, Converging Minds: Smith at Glasgow, Hume in Edinburgh (1751-1754)

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Hume's monumental History of England becomes his greatest popular and financial triumph even as the Kirk's Popular Party mounts a failed campaign to excommunicate him and his Natural History of Religion deepens the scandal, all while his correspondence with Adam Smith tracks the widening but affectionate distance between Edinburgh's leading skeptic and its pious establishment.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Hume's History of England and the Kirk's Attempt to Excommunicate Him
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Hume's History of England and the Kirk's Attempt to Excommunicate Him

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: In 1759 Adam Smith publishes The Theory of Moral Sentiments as a sustained but unnamed dialogue with Hume's moral philosophy, diverging on sympathy, utility, justice, and religion even as he builds squarely on Hume's foundations, and Hume responds with a teasing letter, a laudatory anonymous review, and further private correspondence that together display the depth of their friendship.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: The Theory of Moral Sentiments and Hume's Delighted Response (1759)
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments and Hume's Delighted Response (1759)

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Between 1759 and 1766 Adam Smith leaves his Glasgow professorship to tutor the Duke of Buccleuch across the Continent while David Hume, serving as secretary to Britain's ambassador, becomes the improbable idol of Parisian high society, and their letters chart a running, never-resolved negotiation over where the two friends should finally settle together.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Fêted in France: Hume's Paris Apotheosis and Smith's Grand Tour (1759–1766)
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Fêted in France: Hume's Paris Apotheosis and Smith's Grand Tour (1759–1766)

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Rasmussen narrates the collapse of David Hume's friendship with Jean-Jacques Rousseau in 1766-67, showing how Rousseau's persecution-fueled paranoia turned Hume's rescue of him into an imagined conspiracy, and how Adam Smith's counsel that Hume stay silent went unheeded when Hume published their correspondence anyway.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: The Quarrel with the Wild Philosopher: Hume, Rousseau, and the Limits of Friendship
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: The Quarrel with the Wild Philosopher: Hume, Rousseau, and the Limits of Friendship

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Between 1766 and early 1776 Hume and Smith live largely apart—Hume settling into contented Edinburgh domesticity and a brief stint as Under-Secretary of State while Smith retreats to Kirkcaldy in near-total seclusion to write The Wealth of Nations—so that their friendship is sustained mainly through affectionate, needling letters, culminating in Hume's declining health and his anxious pleas for Smith to finish the book and finally come home.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Mortally Sick at Sea: The Long-Distance Friendship, 1766–1776
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Mortally Sick at Sea: The Long-Distance Friendship, 1766–1776

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Comparing The Wealth of Nations (1776) against Hume's earlier writings, Rasmussen argues that Smith's central claims about commerce's promotion of liberty, its refutation of mercantilism, and its case for free trade were substantially anticipated by Hume, even as Smith broke from Hume in dwelling on commercial society's costs and in favoring church disestablishment.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: The Wealth of Nations and the Debts Smith Owed Hume
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: The Wealth of Nations and the Debts Smith Owed Hume

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Rasmussen reconstructs the dispute over Hume's request that Smith publish his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, arguing that the episode was far less acrimonious than commonly claimed and that Smith's refusal reflected ordinary caution about public controversy rather than cowardice or philosophical discomfort with Hume's skepticism.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Hume's Dialogues and the Dispute Over Posthumous Publication
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Hume's Dialogues and the Dispute Over Posthumous Publication

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: In the months before his death on 25 August 1776, David Hume deliberately staged a composed, cheerful, irreligious end—writing the terse autobiography My Own Life, parrying Boswell's and Strahan's probes about the afterlife, and joking with Adam Smith about his lack of an excuse to give Charon—while Smith prepared to complete the record with a public letter that would prove a skeptic could die well.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: The Death of David Hume: Dying as a Philosopher Should
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: The Death of David Hume: Dying as a Philosopher Should

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: After Hume's funeral, Adam Smith composes the Letter to Strahan eulogizing Hume as a model of wise and virtuous living and dying without religion, and the resulting public backlash from Horne, Johnson, Boswell, Wesley, and others brings Smith, by his own account, ten times more abuse than The Wealth of Nations had.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: The Letter to Strahan and the Backlash Against Smith
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: The Letter to Strahan and the Backlash Against Smith

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: In the epilogue, Adam Smith spends his last dozen years in Edinburgh as a customs officer and literary lion, and the extensive revisions he makes to the sixth edition of The Theory of Moral Sentiments just before his 1790 death are read as a covert, sustained tribute to David Hume.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Epilogue: Adam Smith's Last Years and His Tribute to Hume
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Epilogue: Adam Smith's Last Years and His Tribute to Hume

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: The book's introduction argues that David Hume and Adam Smith's decades-long friendship is the greatest philosophical friendship in the Western tradition, sets out the sources (fifty-six surviving letters, contemporaries' memoirs) that make it recoverable despite both men's aversion to publicity, situates the friendship within the sudden efflorescence of the Scottish Enlightenment, and dismantles three common caricatures that would otherwise divide the pair (abstract philosopher vs. practical economist, Tory vs. Whig, atheist vs. believer).
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Hume and Smith: A Case Study in Philosophical Friendship
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Hume and Smith: A Case Study in Philosophical Friendship

commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.summary: Rasmussen's preface frames his dual biography of David Hume and Adam Smith around the arc of their personal friendship from 1749 to Hume's death, flagging the book's central puzzle: the two thinkers held broadly similar private views on religion but adopted starkly different public postures toward it.
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.term: Preface: The Friendship That Shaped Modern Thought
commons/reading/rasmussen-infidel-and-pr.title: Preface: The Friendship That Shaped Modern Thought

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Matthew Stewart frames the secret 1676 meeting between Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and Baruch Spinoza in The Hague as the hidden pivot of modern philosophy, with Spinoza embodying an affirming response to modernity and Leibniz a reactive one.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: The Hague, November 1676

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Chapter 2 traces Baruch "Bento" Spinoza's life from his Sephardic family's flight from Iberian persecution to tolerant Amsterdam through his rabbinical education, his radicalization under Frans van den Enden and Descartes, and his harsh 1656 excommunication, arguing that his lifelong status as a double exile forged both his personality and his philosophy of freedom.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Bento

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Leibniz's childhood, education, and rapid rise as a courtier-diplomat unfold against the ruin of the Thirty Years War, revealing a psychology of restless ambition and insatiable need for approval that will define his philosophy and his eventual encounter with Spinoza.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.term: Gottfried: The Making of a Courtier-Philosopher
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Gottfried: The Making of a Courtier-Philosopher

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Stewart reconstructs Spinoza's Rijnsburg-to-The-Hague years as the deliberate enactment of a philosophy born from a personal crisis of vanitas, arguing that his ascetic, materialist, and paradoxically sociable way of living was itself the argument for his system, and sets up his November 1676 encounter with Leibniz.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: A Life of the Mind

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Chapter 5 lays out the young Leibniz's instrumental, other-directed "philosophy of philosophy" — a legalistic, conciliatory, reason-grounded theocratic project defined by its opposition to modern philosophy, in sharp contrast to Spinoza's solitary, truth-seeking monomania.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: God's Attorney

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Spinoza's secret self-portrait as the martyred Neapolitan rebel Masaniello opens Stewart's account of how the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus turned the reclusive philosopher into a secular political revolutionary whose self-interest-based theory of the state provoked Europe-wide condemnation and left unresolved the paradox of whether a liberal can be a hero.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: The Hero of the People

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Leibniz's covert 1671-72 courtship of Spinoza, conducted in parallel with public denunciations of the Tractatus, reveals a philosopher of ineradicable “multiplicity” whose demand that everything have a sufficient reason quietly converges with the necessitarian God he was publicly attacking.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: The Many Faces of Leibniz

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Chapter 8 follows Spinoza through his perilous final years in The Hague, where mob violence, the execution of his old mentor Frans van den Enden, and a cast of unreliable new acquaintances set the stage for the chain of introductions—through Georg Hermann Schuller and Walther von Tschirnhaus—that finally carries Spinoza's secret manuscripts into Leibniz's hands in Paris.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.term: The Hague Years: Mob Violence, Betrayal, and the Road to Leibniz's Letter
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: The Hague Years: Mob Violence, Betrayal, and the Road to Leibniz's Letter

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Leibniz's four glamour-hungry years in Paris (1672–1676) — chasing status, patronage, and a diplomatic mission, while independently discovering calculus and making his first, rebuffed overtures toward Spinoza through Tschirnhaus.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.term: Leibniz in Love: The Paris Years (1672–1676)
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Leibniz in Love: The Paris Years (1672–1676)

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Stewart reconstructs Spinoza's Ethics from the inside as one system in which God is Nature, man is no "kingdom within a kingdom" but a part of Nature bound by its laws, mind and body are one thing seen under two attributes, and salvation is an intellectual love of a God that cannot love back, and he reads the whole as the first active embrace of modernity.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.term: God, or Nature: Spinoza's Secret Philosophy of the Whole of Things
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: God, or Nature: Spinoza's Secret Philosophy of the Whole of Things

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Leibniz's private Paris notebooks and his 1676 sea-and-canal journey toward The Hague show him drafting, in Spinoza's own logical form, the very substance-monism he simultaneously denounces and censors in himself.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Approaching Spinoza

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Stewart reconstructs the November 1676 meeting itself, staging the personal and philosophical collision between Leibniz's needy vanity and Spinoza's self-sufficient indifference around a single surviving document: Leibniz's ontological proof and his claim that Spinoza pronounced it "sound."
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Point of Contact

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: In his first years in Hanover, Leibniz chases salary, title and a silver-mine fortune while turning against Spinoza's philosophy almost as soon as the 1676 meeting ends; after Spinoza's death he tries to buy the Ethics manuscript, dreads the publication of his own letters, privately confesses and repudiates a near-fall into necessitarianism, names Spinoza the source of atheism, and then spends decades shrinking the record of their contact.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Surviving Spinoza

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Leibniz's mature metaphysics of 1676-1686 — the Discourse on Metaphysics and the monadology that grew from it, including the pre-established harmony — was constructed point-by-point as a systematic rebuttal to Spinoza's God, mind, and vision of salvation.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.term: Building the Antidote: Leibniz's Monadology Against Spinoza's God
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Building the Antidote: Leibniz's Monadology Against Spinoza's God

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Across four decades after The Hague, Leibniz's political maneuvering, church-reunion diplomacy, feuds with Locke and Newton, admiration for Chinese philosophy, and eventual defense against charges of Spinozism all reveal the same underlying anxiety: an obsessive, lifelong struggle against the ghost of Spinoza.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: The Haunting

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Stewart argues that when Leibniz's transcendent God, individualist monadology, and ethics of self-realization are followed to their logical ends, each collapses into a system observationally indistinguishable from the one Spinoza had already built and openly embraced.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: The Return of the Repressed

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Stewart narrates Leibniz's humiliating final decade of political house arrest, unpaid salaries, and diplomatic exile alongside his sunset metaphysical writings, arguing that the monadological optimism was an elegiac fiction masking a life that, contrary to Leibniz's own philosophy, was actually lived on Spinozist premises of self-interest, deception, and ontological insecurity.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Leibniz's End

commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.summary: Stewart's closing chapter tracks how posthumous reception distorted Leibniz and Spinoza into misleading caricatures before arguing that they represent modernity's two enduring responses—active affirmation versus reactive longing—which still structure philosophy today.
commons/reading/stewart-courtier-and-her.title: Aftermath

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Following the poet-official Prapanca on a 1359 CE royal progress through eastern Java, this chapter uses his court gossip, travel notes, and a monastery-hosted recitation of dynastic legend to reconstruct daily life, social hierarchy, and the two centuries of religious and political history that produced the Majapahit empire.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Prapanca's Royal Progress and the Chronicle of Kings
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Prapanca's Royal Progress and the Chronicle of Kings

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: In 1359 the court poet Prapanca hears a Buddhist abbot read the secret legend of Ken Arok — a divinely-fathered robber, rapist, and murderer who seized Ken Dedes, commissioned a cursed magical keris, assassinated the ruler of Singasari, and crowned himself King Rajasa — only for the same cursed blade to claim his own life and drive his queen to ritual self-immolation, a hidden origin story that clashes with the sanitized official genealogy of the Rajasa dynasty Prapanca had always been taught.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: From Robber to Royal: The Legend of Ken Arok
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: From Robber to Royal: The Legend of Ken Arok

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: A Chinese harbormaster's 1225 ethnography of cosmopolitan Singasari frames a chronicle of how Ken Arok's royal line devoured itself in a fratricidal succession war (1220-1250), while a 1359 frame narrative shows that same bloody dynasty being retroactively remade into a myth of divine kingship.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Game of Thrones, Java Style: Ken Arok's Dynasty Devours Itself (1220-1250)
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Game of Thrones, Java Style: Ken Arok's Dynasty Devours Itself (1220-1250)

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: After two decades of royal assassinations in Singasari, court elders engineer a compromise succession—installing the illegitimate Wisnuwardhana as king (later co-ruling with Narasingamurti and crowning his own son Kertanegara as boy-king) to fuse Ken Arok's bloodline back together, even as Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty conquers mainland Southeast Asia and priestly omens begin to frame the coming Mongol threat as a cosmic and magical crisis rather than merely a political one.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Three Kings: Wisnuwardhana's Fix and the Mongol Shadow over Kertanegara's Java
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Three Kings: Wisnuwardhana's Fix and the Mongol Shadow over Kertanegara's Java

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: King Kertanegara of Singasari fuses tantric Shaivist-Buddhist ritual with statecraft to purge his father's old guard, launch the Pamalayu naval expedition and conquer Bali and southern Sumatra, then provokes Kublai Khan into war by mutilating his envoy.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Kertanegara: Tantric Kingship, the Pamalayu Expedition, and the Road to War with Kublai Khan
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Kertanegara: Tantric Kingship, the Pamalayu Expedition, and the Road to War with Kublai Khan

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: In 1292 the resentful governor of Kediri, egged on by a spurned rival governor's cryptic tip-off, sacks Singasari and kills King Kertanegara, sending the heir Prince Widjaya through a year of flight, feigned surrender, and covert alliance-building that ends with the founding of the village of Majapahit.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: The Fall of Singasari and the Founding of Majapahit
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: The Fall of Singasari and the Founding of Majapahit

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Kublai Khan's 1293 punitive naval expedition against Java is hijacked by Prince Widjaya, who uses the Mongol army to crush his rival Jayakatwang at Kediri, then massacres the drunken Chinese garrison and is crowned king of the newly founded Majapahit.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: The Mongol Invasion of Java and the Founding of Majapahit (1293)
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: The Mongol Invasion of Java and the Founding of Majapahit (1293)

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Between Widjaya's coronation and Jayanegara's murder, Majapahit's founding circle of loyalists devours itself in a cascading sequence of patronage slights, revolts, and court intrigue, out of which the low-born guard commander Gajah Mada emerges as the indispensable strongman allied with the dowager queen Gayatri.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Friends Turn Foes: The Rise of Gajah Mada (1294–1328 CE)
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Friends Turn Foes: The Rise of Gajah Mada (1294–1328 CE)

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Between 1331 and 1355, the commoner-born Gajah Mada claws his way to the position of patih of Majapahit, swears the Palapa Oath to unite the archipelago as Nusantara, and prosecutes conquests of Sumatra and Bali under the patronage of the dowager queen Gayatri, while young prince Hayam Wuruk grows up amid courtly ritual and is crowned king, the chapter closing with a month-long Caitra festival of spectacle and administration that pointedly foreshadows the massacre to come at his wedding.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: The Golden Age of Majapahit

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Gajah Mada's scheme to marry King Hayam Wuruk to the Sundanese princess Citra Rashmi as a covert annexation collapses into a diplomatic insult-exchange and the Battle of Bubat, wiping out the Sundanese royal party and briefly toppling Gajah Mada before the Majapahit court discovers it cannot govern without him.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Wedding Disaster: The Battle of Bubat, 1357
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Wedding Disaster: The Battle of Bubat, 1357

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: King Hayam Wuruk's ceremonial 1359 progress through eastern Java showcases Majapahit's tribute economy and ritual statecraft at its height, while the chapter then fast-forwards through Queen Gayatri's 1362 death rites, Gajah Mada's 1364 death and the succession crisis it triggers, and a 1370s-80s diplomatic rupture with Sumatra that ends with the rise of Islamic Malacca on Majapahit's doorstep.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: The Royal Progress and the Seeds of Decay
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: The Royal Progress and the Seeds of Decay

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: The death of King Hayam Wuruk in 1389 leaves Majapahit's throne split between his daughter's line and his popular illegitimate son Wirabumi, and that unresolved fracture curdles over four decades into the Paregreg civil war, a disastrous massacre of Chinese envoys, cascading vassal defections, and finally earthquakes, river-silting, and famine that bracket King Wikramawardhana's own death in 1429.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: The Death of Hayam Wuruk and the Paregreg Civil War
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: The Death of Hayam Wuruk and the Paregreg Civil War

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Drawing on the Ming translator-official Ma Huan's eyewitness notes from Zheng He's fourth treasure-fleet voyage, the chapter reconstructs a walking tour of 1413–15 Majapahit — its markets, keris-craft, unwalled cityscape, hydraulic royal temple, religious pluralism, and a witnessed sati — as the only foreign first-person account of the empire at its height.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: A Stroll Around Town (1415 CE)

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Queen Suhita rules Majapahit from 1429 to 1446, using pragmatic statecraft — famine relief through irrigation works, accommodation of Muslim and Chinese merchant interests, and deliberately transgressive new temples — to hold together an empire that the chapter explicitly frames as entering its terminal decline.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Suhita: Pragmatism at the Twilight of Majapahit
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Suhita: Pragmatism at the Twilight of Majapahit

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: Between 1450 and 1527, Majapahit's Hindu-Buddhist kingdom hollows into ceremonial and economic irrelevance as a wandering Sundanese prince records its last interior view, Portuguese traders arrive at Malacca and marvel at Javanese seacraft and cartography, and the rising Muslim sultanate of Demak finally storms and burns the capital, ending the empire and seeding the coastal outpost that becomes Jakarta.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: The Final Blow: The Fall of Majapahit, 1450–1527
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: The Final Blow: The Fall of Majapahit, 1450–1527

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: After Majapahit's 1527 collapse, the empire survived not as ruins but as a migrating tradition — reborn in Bali, nearly lost and rescued in manuscript form, and repurposed by twentieth-century Indonesia as the founding myth of its national identity.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Majapahit's Afterlife: Ruins, Legends, and the Making of Indonesia
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Majapahit's Afterlife: Ruins, Legends, and the Making of Indonesia

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: The introduction narrates the piecemeal rediscovery of the vanished Majapahit empire in Java — from Raffles's 1815 expedition to Singasari and the Wardenaar survey, through Engelhard's earlier looting, to Brandes's rescue of the Nagarakertagama manuscript amid the 1894 Lombok massacre, and Stutterheim's suppressed 1941 reconstruction of the palace — showing how a great Hindu-Buddhist civilization was reduced to overgrown brick and folk memory before being reassembled, and repurposed, centuries later.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.term: Raffles, Ruins, and the Rediscovery of Majapahit
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Raffles, Ruins, and the Rediscovery of Majapahit

commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.summary: The preface to Herald van der Linde's Majapahit opens with the 1290 Singasari–Mongol diplomatic clash that led to Kublai Khan's failed invasion of Java, then frames the book's aim: to introduce English-speaking readers to Majapahit, a powerful, religiously plural, and now largely forgotten Southeast Asian empire whose rise, fall, and jungle-swallowed ruins the author connects to modern Indonesia's resurgence.
commons/reading/vanderlinde-majapahit/va.title: Preface: An Empire Asia Forgot

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Sun Wukong spends decades secretly training under the Patriarch Subodhi, rejecting every conventional path to enlightenment until he masters the seventy-two transformations and the cloud-somersault, is banished for showing off his powers, and returns to Flower-Fruit Mountain to annihilate the Monstrous King of Chaos and free his kidnapped monkey subjects.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Monkey's Secret Teachings and the Defeat of the Monstrous King of Chaos
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Monkey's Secret Teachings and the Defeat of the Monstrous King of Chaos

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Sun Wukong drills his monkey subjects into an army, uses sorcery and nuisance to extort a shape-shifting iron staff and a suit of armor from the Dragon King of the Eastern Ocean, strikes his own name from the Underworld's register of death, and provokes Heaven's court into offering him a government post rather than risking a war it fears it cannot win.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Monkey Arms His Kingdom and Defies Death
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Monkey Arms His Kingdom and Defies Death

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey King rebels against the lowly rank Heaven assigns him, wages a brief war against the Jade Emperor's forces, and is pacified only when Heaven grants him the empty, dutyless title of Great Sage Equal to Heaven.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Monkey King Becomes the Great Sage Equal to Heaven
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Monkey King Becomes the Great Sage Equal to Heaven

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Made caretaker of the Peach Orchard to keep him harmlessly occupied, Monkey secretly devours the immortal peaches, impersonates a guest to crash the Queen Mother's Peach Festival and drink Laozi's elixir, then flees to boast of it at Flower-Fruit Mountain as the Jade Emperor musters a heavenly army to punish him.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Great Sage Steals the Peaches, the Wine, and the Elixir of Immortality
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Great Sage Steals the Peaches, the Wine, and the Elixir of Immortality

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Guanyin briefs the Jade Emperor on Sun Wukong's rampage through Heaven, then the demigod Erlang Shen out-transforms and out-fights the Great Sage in an escalating shapeshifting duel before Laozi's magic diamond circlet brings him down for binding and a sentence of execution.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Capture of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Capture of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Unable to kill Monkey through blades, fire, thunderbolts, or Laozi's forty-nine-day alchemical brazier, Heaven turns to the Buddha, who out-wagers him with a cosmic sleight of hand and seals him beneath Five-Phases Mountain, alive but immobilized, pending an unspecified future release by a Tang pilgrim.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Buddha's Wager and Monkey's Imprisonment Under Five-Phases Mountain
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Buddha's Wager and Monkey's Imprisonment Under Five-Phases Mountain

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: The Buddha commissions Guanyin to find a scripture pilgrim in the east, and on her journey she converts three banished, monstrous exiles — the future Sandy and Pigsy, and a condemned dragon prince — into disciples-in-waiting, then visits Sun Wukong, still imprisoned beneath Five-Phases Mountain, and extracts his promise to join the pilgrimage.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Guanyin Assembles the Pilgrimage
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Guanyin Assembles the Pilgrimage

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Chen Guangrui wins the examination top prize and marries Yin Wenjiao, only to be murdered by a boatman who steals his post and his wife, setting in motion the karmic rescue, hidden birth, and eventual vindication of their son, the monk who will become Xuanzang.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The River Hong Murder and the Birth of Xuanzang
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The River Hong Murder and the Birth of Xuanzang

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: A local dragon king cheats on a Heaven-decreed rainfall forecast to spite a Chang'an fortune-teller, and his subsequent execution under Heavenly law—botched by the sleeping prime minister Wei Zheng after the Tang emperor Taizong fails to save him—leaves Taizong guilt-haunted, mortally ill, and about to journey into the underworld.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Dragon King's Wager and the Death of Emperor Taizong
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Dragon King's Wager and the Death of Emperor Taizong

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Emperor Taizong's soul is dragged into the Chinese underworld to answer a wronged dragon's lawsuit, has his death sentence overturned through a judge's personal favor and a corrected ledger entry, is marched past the tortures, bridges, and hungry ghosts of Hell, and returns to life to repay his debts and reform his rule.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Taizong's Journey Through Hell
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Taizong's Journey Through Hell

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Liu Quan and his wife Cuilian are revived through a bureaucratic soul-swap into Princess Yuying's body, after which Emperor Taizong stages a grand Buddhist mass at which Guanyin unveils herself, exposes the presiding monk's ignorance of the Mahayana, and recruits him—now renamed Tripitaka—to journey to India for the scriptures that will save the empire's ghosts.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Grand Mass and the Calling of Tripitaka
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Grand Mass and the Calling of Tripitaka

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Newly departed from the Tang empire, the monk Tripitaka loses both attendants to a den of cannibalistic demons, is saved first by the divine Planet Venus and then by the hunter Liu Boqin, and is left alone at the Mountain of Two Frontiers just as an unknown voice cries out from within it.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: First Perils on the Road West: Demons, Providence, and the Hunter Liu Boqin
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: First Perils on the Road West: Demons, Providence, and the Hunter Liu Boqin

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Tripitaka frees Sun Wukong — the “Great Sage Equal to Heaven,” trapped for five centuries beneath the Mountain of Two Frontiers — who joins him as disciple and bodyguard, but Monkey's casual slaughter of a tiger and then six robbers provokes the pilgrimage's first moral rupture, after which Guanyin (disguised as an old woman) equips Tripitaka with a golden fillet and binding spell that gives him permanent, pain-based control over his volatile disciple.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Freeing of Monkey and the Golden Fillet
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Freeing of Monkey and the Golden Fillet

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey battles the horse-eating dragon of the Brook of Eagle's Sorrow, only to discover Guanyin had already destined the dragon to become Tripitaka's mount, and after confronting her over the coercive golden hoop, Monkey accepts the transformed dragon-horse and receives three life-saving hairs.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Jade Dragon Becomes the White Horse
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Jade Dragon Becomes the White Horse

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Tripitaka and Monkey arrive at Gao Village, where Monkey bullies information out of a reluctant local, poses as an exorcist, disguises himself as the imprisoned bride to trap her monstrous husband, and exposes the demon (soon to be Zhu Bajie) by needling him into confessing his own backstory before the mere mention of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven sends him fleeing.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Monkey Unmasks the Pig Demon of Gao Village
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Monkey Unmasks the Pig Demon of Gao Village

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey subdues the shape-shifting pig-demon terrorizing the Gao household and discovers he is Zhu Bajie (Pigsy), a banished Heavenly marshal already recruited by Guanyin to join Tripitaka's scripture pilgrimage.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Pigsy Joins the Pilgrimage
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Pigsy Joins the Pilgrimage

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Pigsy repeatedly battles the monstrous guardian of the River of Flowing Sand to a stalemate, until Guanyin reveals the fiend to be Sandy, a banished immortal already assigned to the pilgrimage, and arranges his submission and a magic boat that carries Tripitaka safely across.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Crossing the River of Flowing Sand: The Recruitment of Sandy
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Crossing the River of Flowing Sand: The Recruitment of Sandy

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Sun Wukong (Monkey) kills the shapeshifting White-Bone Demon in three successive disguises to protect Tripitaka, but Pigsy's jealous slander convinces their master that each killing is murder, and after the third reveals her true skeletal form Tripitaka banishes Monkey from the pilgrimage anyway.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Chapter Nineteen: Three Strikes Against the White-Bone Demon
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Chapter Nineteen: Three Strikes Against the White-Bone Demon

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Left without Sun Wukong, Tripitaka wanders off after Pigsy's hunger-nap and is captured by the indigo-faced Yellow-Robe demon at the Cave of the Tidal Moon, escaping only because the demon's long-captive wife, Princess Baihuaxiu of Precious Image, tricks her husband into releasing him so she can smuggle a rescue letter to her parents — after which Pigsy's boastfulness and cowardice let the same demon capture Sandy.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Chapter Twenty: The Yellow-Robe Demon of Casserole Mountain
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Chapter Twenty: The Yellow-Robe Demon of Casserole Mountain

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Sandy shields the princess from Yellow-Robe's wrath and the demon infiltrates Precious Image's court in disguise to frame Tripitaka as a man-eating tiger, and after the dragon-horse's solo rescue attempt fails, Pigsy fetches Monkey, who tricks and defeats Yellow-Robe—revealed as the truant Wood-Wolf Star—restoring Tripitaka and the princess and reuniting the pilgrim band.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Wood-Wolf Star's Masquerade and Downfall
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Wood-Wolf Star's Masquerade and Downfall

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: On a demon-haunted mountain, the shapeshifting Silver Horn captures Pigsy, Sandy, and Tripitaka for the man-eating Golden Horn and Silver Horn of the Lotus-Flower Cave, while Monkey—pinned beneath three sacred mountains by stolen magic—breaks free, dupes the demons' goblin messengers with a fake treasure gourd, and enlists the Jade Emperor and Nezha in a staged eclipse to steal back the real capturing vessels.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Golden Horn and Silver Horn: The Lotus-Flower Cave
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Golden Horn and Silver Horn: The Lotus-Flower Cave

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey King brings down the demon brothers Golden Horn and Silver Horn by stealing and weaponizing their five heavenly treasures, only for Laozi to reveal at the end that the "demons" are his own runaway attendants and the entire ordeal was adversity engineered by Guanyin to test the pilgrims.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Monkey Defeats Golden Horn and Silver Horn with Their Own Treasures
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Monkey Defeats Golden Horn and Silver Horn with Their Own Treasures

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Tripitaka is kidnapped by Red Boy, the fire-breathing demon son of Monkey's sworn brother Bull Demon King, and after a cascade of failed mutual impersonations between Monkey and the boy, Guanyin herself subdues Red Boy with an ocean of magic water, a concealed sword-throne, and five golden hoops, taking him into her service as a disciplined attendant.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Red Boy and the Taming of a Demon Son
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Red Boy and the Taming of a Demon Son

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey infiltrates Cart-Slow Kingdom, discovers that three Taoist "immortals" who ended a twenty-year drought have enslaved and are killing the local Buddhist monks, kills two of the sect's young enforcers after they refuse to free the slaves, and that night leads Pigsy and Sandy in a raid on the Taoists' temple, impersonating the Three Pure Ones and dumping their statues in a latrine before the trio is nearly caught.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Cart-Slow Kingdom: The Slaves of the Three Pure Ones
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Cart-Slow Kingdom: The Slaves of the Three Pure Ones

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey and his fellow pilgrims humiliate Cart-Slow Kingdom's three Taoist state preceptors by disguising urine as holy water, then Monkey talks his way out of a murder charge and wins a life-or-death rain-making contest by personally commandeering the wind, cloud, thunder, lightning, and dragon-king deities.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Rain-Making Contest at Cart-Slow
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Rain-Making Contest at Cart-Slow

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: In the kingdom of Cart-Slow, Monkey King defeats three Taoist state-immortals through a rigged meditation contest, a box-guessing game, and a triple execution ordeal, exposing them as a tiger, a deer, and an antelope spirit and freeing the persecuted Buddhist monks.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Three Immortals Unmasked at Cart-Slow
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Three Immortals Unmasked at Cart-Slow

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: The pilgrims cross the River to Heaven on the back of a self-taught, centuries-old turtle who begs Tripitaka to ask the Buddha how he might finally acquire a human body, then travel on into the all-female kingdom of Western Liang, where Tripitaka and Pigsy accidentally fall pregnant by drinking from the Mother-and-Child River and Monkey must trick a vengeful immortal out of Abortion Spring water to cure them.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The River Turtle and the Land of Women
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The River Turtle and the Land of Women

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: In the Land of Women, the queen tries to marry Tripitaka to secure an heir, so Monkey engineers a sham wedding to get their travel papers stamped and escape, only for a mysterious woman to abduct Tripitaka in a whirlwind at the very moment the plan succeeds.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Land of Women: A Sham Marriage
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Land of Women: A Sham Marriage

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: The pilgrims track a cyclone to the Cave of the Lute, where a scorpion-spirit holding Tripitaka captive as an unwilling bridegroom stings both Monkey and Pigsy in successive fights before Guanyin redirects them to the Star Lord Orionis, whose true rooster form kills the demon and frees Tripitaka.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Scorpion-Spirit of the Cave of the Lute
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Scorpion-Spirit of the Cave of the Lute

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Monkey wages a two-round war of impersonation and shapeshifting against Princess Iron-Fan and her estranged husband King Bull Demon to win the real Palm-Leaf Fan and finally extinguish Flame Mountain, letting the pilgrims pass west.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Flame Mountain and the Palm-Leaf Fan
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Flame Mountain and the Palm-Leaf Fan

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: In the City of Young Sons (formerly the Kingdom of Bhikku), Monkey Xingzhe uncovers that the ailing king's chief advisor, the self-styled Royal Father-in-Law, is a fugitive demon-deer plotting to cure the king with soup made first from 1,111 little boys' hearts and then from Tripitaka's own, and after spiriting the children to safety and swapping faces with Tripitaka, Monkey exposes the demon and its fox-spirit consort and restores the kingdom to health.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The City of Young Sons
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The City of Young Sons

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: A three-year drought in the Indian prefecture of Phoenix-Immortal turns out to be deliberate Heavenly punishment for a prefect's petty impiety, and Monkey can only end it by working Heaven's own administrative channels and staging a citywide display of piety rather than by force.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Monkey Petitions Heaven for Rain in Phoenix-Immortal
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Monkey Petitions Heaven for Rain in Phoenix-Immortal

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Tripitaka and his three disciples cross a river of transcendence to reach the Buddha at Thunderclap Monastery, where they are first fobbed off with blank scrolls for lack of a bribe and only receive the written scriptures after surrendering a golden alms bowl, closing a pilgrimage that Guanyin tallies to a preordained number of days.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: The Pilgrims Reach the Buddha and Are Charged for the Scriptures
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: The Pilgrims Reach the Buddha and Are Charged for the Scriptures

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Guanyin's audit reveals Tripitaka is one ordeal short of the required eighty-one, so the Buddha's attendants engineer a final mishap before the pilgrims complete their return to Chang'an, deliver the scriptures, and are recalled to Thunderclap for apotheosis, ending the novel with promotions to Buddhahood, an origin story for a torn sutra, and the vanishing of Monkey's control-hoop.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Journey's End: The Pilgrims' Return and Apotheosis
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Journey's End: The Pilgrims' Return and Apotheosis

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Gene Luen Yang's personal foreword on inheriting the Monkey King from his immigrant mother and Julia Lovell's scholarly introduction on the novel's contested authorship, Ming-dynasty context, comic/allegorical duality, and five centuries of political reinvention together frame this translation of Journey to the West.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: Framing the Monkey King: Yang's Foreword and Lovell's Introduction
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: Framing the Monkey King: Yang's Foreword and Lovell's Introduction

commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.summary: Julia Lovell explains the principles behind her abridged translation of Journey to the West before the novel proper opens with the stone monkey's birth from an egg on Flower-Fruit Mountain, his winning of kingship by daring the waterfall, and his ten-year voyage to the Patriarch Subodhi, who names him Sun Wukong after mortality-fear drives him from his four-hundred-year paradise.
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.term: A Note on the Translation, and the Birth of Monkey
commons/reading/wu-monkey-king/wu-monkey.title: A Note on the Translation, and the Birth of Monkey

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Andrea Wulf traces Alexander von Humboldt's childhood in a cold, controlling aristocratic Prussian household, his restless wanderlust and string of career compromises (Frankfurt, Göttingen, Hamburg finance, the Freiberg mining academy), and his self-experiments in animal electricity, showing how personal loneliness, Enlightenment mechanistic science, and an emerging vitalist counter-current all converged to shape the naturalist who would later travel to the Americas.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Young Humboldt: Restlessness, Mechanism, and the Making of a Naturalist
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Young Humboldt: Restlessness, Mechanism, and the Making of a Naturalist

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Between 1794 and 1797 in Jena and Weimar, Alexander von Humboldt's friendship with Goethe fuses Humboldt's empirical rigor with Goethe's organicist, imaginative approach to nature, and this synthesis—forged through shared dissection, electrical experiments, and immersion in Kantian philosophy—reshapes Humboldt's science into the holistic, feeling-infused method he will carry to South America.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: The Jena Circle: Humboldt, Goethe, and the Fusion of Science and Imagination
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: The Jena Circle: Humboldt, Goethe, and the Fusion of Science and Imagination

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Freed by his mother's death and a large inheritance, Alexander von Humboldt spends two years assembling instruments and knowledge for an expedition with no fixed destination, watches one route after another close due to the French Revolutionary Wars, finally secures an unprecedented Spanish passport to the Americas, and arrives with Aimé Bonpland at Cumaná, Venezuela, in July 1799 to begin the journey that will remake him as a scientist.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Free at Last: Humboldt's Search for a Ship to the New World
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Free at Last: Humboldt's Search for a Ship to the New World

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: In Cumaná, Caracas, and the Aragua Valley, Humboldt catalogues nature obsessively, survives an earthquake that shatters his faith in the earth's stability, and at Lake Valencia becomes the first scientist to identify human-caused deforestation as a driver of climate change.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Cumaná, Caracas, and the Discovery of Deforestation at Lake Valencia
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Cumaná, Caracas, and the Discovery of Deforestation at Lake Valencia

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Humboldt crosses the scorching Llanos, experiments on electric eels at Calabozo, and paddles the Rio Apure, Orinoco, and Casiquiare into deep rainforest, where mapping the Amazon-Orinoco waterway and watching predator and prey collide reshapes his view of nature from a harmonious divine machine into a single, conflict-driven web of life, crystallized in his discovery of the Mauritia palm as a keystone species.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: The Llanos and the Orinoco: Humboldt's Web of Life
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: The Llanos and the Orinoco: Humboldt's Web of Life

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: After abandoning a bid to rendezvous with Captain Baudin's circumnavigation, Humboldt and Bonpland cross the Andes overland from Cartagena to Quito, visiting the botanist Mutis in Bogotá, nearly losing their instruments and collections on the murderous Quindío Pass, and then spending months systematically climbing every reachable volcano around Quito (Pichincha, Cotopaxi, Antisana) to test whether volcanoes are locally isolated or subterraneously connected, all while Wulf lays out the emotionally intense, likely homoerotic friendships (culminating in Carlos Montúfar) that structured Humboldt's private life.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Across the Andes: Chasing Baudin, Climbing Volcanoes
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Across the Andes: Chasing Baudin, Climbing Volcanoes

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Humboldt's failed but record-setting 1802 ascent of Chimborazo becomes the moment he synthesizes years of scattered observations into a single vision of nature as an interconnected web, which he renders as the Naturgemälde before crossing the Andes once more and sailing north out of South America for the last time.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Chimborazo and the Naturgemälde
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Chimborazo and the Naturgemälde

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: In June 1804, fresh off a near-fatal hurricane crossing from Cuba, Humboldt spends a week in Washington with Thomas Jefferson trading scientific data for political intelligence, discovering deep agreement on agrarian republicanism and a sharp, unresolved rift over slavery and racial equality.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Humboldt and Jefferson: Politics and Nature in Washington, 1804
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Humboldt and Jefferson: Politics and Nature in Washington, 1804

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: After five years in the Americas, Humboldt returns to a Paris transformed by Napoleon's rise, becomes the toast of European science, forges a formative friendship with the young Simón Bolívar, and travels on to Rome and Naples (witnessing a Vesuvius eruption) as Europe tips into war and Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz ends the Holy Roman Empire.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Return to a Changed Paris: Humboldt, Bolívar, and the Eve of Austerlitz
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Return to a Changed Paris: Humboldt, Bolívar, and the Eve of Austerlitz

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Returning from South America to a provincial, war-battered Berlin, Humboldt chafes under royal patronage and watches Prussia collapse to Napoleon while completing the Essay on the Geography of Plants and Views of Nature, works in which he recasts nature as an interconnected living organism rather than a mechanistic taxonomy, before decamping permanently to Paris in 1807.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Berlin, the Naturgemälde, and Views of Nature
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Berlin, the Naturgemälde, and Views of Nature

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Between his return from South America and Napoleon's fall, Humboldt builds a frenetic Paris life of publication and correspondence, forges his closest friendship with Arago while alienating his patriotic brother Wilhelm, endures Napoleon's jealous suspicion of his rival scientific empire, and finally watches the occupying Allied armies fill the city he calls his second fatherland.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Humboldt's Paris Years: Fame, Rivalry, and the Fall of Napoleon
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Humboldt's Paris Years: Fame, Rivalry, and the Fall of Napoleon

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Simón Bolívar's decade-plus campaign to liberate Spanish South America is narrated as inseparable from Alexander von Humboldt's influence — his statistics-laden critique of colonialism supplying revolutionary ammunition, his descriptions of Andean landscapes supplying Bolívar's rhetorical language, and his rebuttal of Buffon's degeneracy thesis supplying the continent a claim to natural and civilizational parity with Europe.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Bolívar's Revolution, Written in Humboldt's Language
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Bolívar's Revolution, Written in Humboldt's Language

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: In London in 1817, Humboldt is refused a travel permit to the Himalaya by the East India Company even as his books on Spanish America ignite the British Romantics—Coleridge, Wordsworth, Byron, and Mary Shelley—who embrace his vision of nature as one living, interconnected organism against the era's mechanistic, classifying science.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Refused by Empire, Embraced by the Poets: Humboldt in London, 1817
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Refused by Empire, Embraced by the Poets: Humboldt in London, 1817

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Blocked for a decade from mounting a new expedition to India by the East India Company, the fifty-something Humboldt cycles restlessly between scientific patronage, financial ruin, and Restoration-era Paris politics until his own king finally orders him back to Berlin in 1827.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Going in Circles: Humboldt Stalled Between Paris and Berlin
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Going in Circles: Humboldt Stalled Between Paris and Berlin

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Returning to Berlin in 1827, Humboldt submits to a gilded captivity at Friedrich Wilhelm III's reactionary court while using his royal access to fund science, withdraws from a politics he finds disillusioning across Prussia, Britain, the German Confederation, Bolívar's crumbling South America, and slaveholding America, and instead throws himself into democratizing knowledge through wildly popular public lectures, a new kind of interdisciplinary scientific congress, a renewed intellectual partnership with Goethe and his brother Wilhelm, and finally the diplomatic opening — via a query about Russian platinum currency — that will let him complete his global Naturgemälde with an expedition into the Russian Empire.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Return to Berlin: Court Captivity and the Democratization of Science
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Return to Berlin: Court Captivity and the Democratization of Science

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: At fifty-nine, Humboldt undertakes his last great expedition—a tsar-funded, mining-focused journey across Russia to the Urals, Siberia, the Altai Mountains, and the Caspian Sea—where he predicts diamonds by comparative geology, chafes under police-state surveillance and a gag order on political commentary, escapes his official itinerary to reach the wild frontier he craves, and returns to launch a worldwide network of geomagnetic observation stations while articulating one of the first scientific accounts of human-caused climate change.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Humboldt's Russian Expedition: Diamonds, Surveillance, and the Magnetic Crusade
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Humboldt's Russian Expedition: Diamonds, Surveillance, and the Magnetic Crusade

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Charles Darwin's five-year Beagle voyage (1831-1836) is recounted as a sustained act of reading Humboldt's Personal Narrative against the world, with Humboldt's observations on species distribution, ecological interdependence, and population pressure among the raw materials Darwin later fused with Malthus into the theory of natural selection culminating in the Origin of Species' entangled-bank metaphor.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Darwin's Humboldtian Voyage: The Beagle, Natural Selection, and the Entangled Bank
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Darwin's Humboldtian Voyage: The Beagle, Natural Selection, and the Entangled Bank

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: At sixty-five, Humboldt begins Cosmos, a decade-long attempt to synthesize the entire physical universe into one book just as science is fracturing into specialized disciplines, and the book becomes an international bestseller that shapes Darwin, Emerson, Poe, and Whitman even as its author grows old, grieves his brother's death, and chafes under a Prussian king's court duties.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: The Making and Reception of Cosmos
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: The Making and Reception of Cosmos

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Between 1849 and 1854, Henry David Thoreau's immersion in Alexander von Humboldt's Cosmos, Personal Narrative, and Views of Nature transforms his Walden Pond journals from scattered Transcendentalist fragments into disciplined scientific field notes, fusing poetry and empirical observation into the book that became Walden.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Thoreau, Humboldt, and the Making of Walden
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Thoreau, Humboldt, and the Making of Walden

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Alexander von Humboldt spends his final decade caught between the Prussian court and the 1848 revolutions, races to finish the last volumes of Cosmos amid a global flood of fame and correspondence, and dies in May 1859 to a worldwide outpouring of grief that cements his afterlife in Darwin's work, Frederic Church's painting The Heart of the Andes, and a century of borrowed influence.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Revolution, Twilight Labor, and Death: Humboldt's Final Years
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Revolution, Twilight Labor, and Death: Humboldt's Final Years

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: George Perkins Marsh, a polyglot Vermont autodidact and lifelong admirer of Humboldt, converts firsthand observation of deforested, exhausted landscapes in Egypt, the Levant, and Italy into Man and Nature (1864), the book that first argued at global scale that humankind was destroying the earth and that founded the American conservation movement.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: George Perkins Marsh and the Making of Man and Nature
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: George Perkins Marsh and the Making of Man and Nature

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Ernst Haeckel channels the grief and identity crisis triggered by Humboldt's death into a scientific-artistic career that coins the word "ecology," builds a monist religion of nature's unity, and supplies the visual vocabulary for Art Nouveau.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Ernst Haeckel: Grief, Ecology, and the Art Forms of Nature
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Ernst Haeckel: Grief, Ecology, and the Art Forms of Nature

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: John Muir builds his entire life's trajectory as a re-enactment of Humboldt's, walking from Indianapolis to Florida to the Sierra Nevada, discovering Yosemite's glacial origins and a mystical vision of ecological unity, and ultimately converting Humboldt's holistic science into the American preservationist movement (Yosemite National Park, the Sierra Club, and the losing fight to save Hetch Hetchy) before finally reaching South America at age seventy-three.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: John Muir: Walking Into Humboldt's Cosmos
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: John Muir: Walking Into Humboldt's Cosmos

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: The epilogue reflects on why Humboldt was forgotten in the Anglophone world—the fracturing of science into narrow disciplines and anti-German sentiment after the World Wars—and argues for reclaiming him as the founding father of ecological, interconnected thinking now urgently needed to confront climate change.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Epilogue: Reclaiming Humboldt
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Epilogue: Reclaiming Humboldt

commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.summary: Wulf's prologue frames Alexander von Humboldt's harrowing 1802 ascent of Chimborazo as the crucible moment when he conceived of nature as one interconnected living web, then traces how thoroughly that idea (and Humboldt's own fame) has been absorbed into modern thought while his name has faded from popular memory.
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.term: Prologue: The Man Who Invented Nature
commons/reading/wulf-invention-of-nature.title: Prologue: The Man Who Invented Nature

commons/summaries/a-good-dictionary.md.summary: A practical and philosophical case for richer dictionaries, tracing from Zinsser through McPhee to the superiority of the 1913 Webster's over modern abridged editions.
commons/summaries/a-good-dictionary.md.title: A Good Dictionary

commons/summaries/adams-education.md.summary: Henry Adams's third-person account of his own miseducation (1918 Massachusetts Historical Society edition, ed. Henry Cabot Lodge), built as the twentieth-century-multiplicity counterweight to Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres and ending in an explicit mechanics of history — a law of acceleration measured in coal.
commons/summaries/adams-education.md.title: The Education of Henry Adams

commons/summaries/ai-explainable-enough..summary: Aneesh Sathe argues from product experience that AI must be 'explainable enough' — calibrated to the cognitive level of the domain expert user — rather than fully transparent or fully opaque, yielding an AI-human causal prediction machine.
commons/summaries/ai-explainable-enough..title: AI: Explainable Enough

commons/summaries/baumol-cost-disease-to.summary: Alex Mayyasi argues that Baumol's cost disease is the underappreciated structural cause of America's rising social isolation — making communal, labor-intensive experiences increasingly expensive while scalable, solitude-inducing products get cheaper.
